- Numeric or verbal scale at rest and on movement.
- Record with sedation score, respiratory rate and side effects.
- Use observational tools in dementia or ventilated patients.
- Investigate unexpected severe pain for a complication.

> **Closing point:** Assess pain, sedation and function together.

Past exam: 2024.1 Q1

items.title: What must be excluded in a patient with severe, unexpected postoperative pain?
items.q: What must be excluded in a patient with severe, unexpected postoperative pain?
items.a:
- Surgical causes: bleeding, compartment syndrome, tight dressing or cast, ischaemia.
- Anaesthetic causes: block failure, nerve injury.
- Other: myocardial ischaemia, pneumothorax, retention, malignant hyperthermia.
- Check drugs already given.

> **Closing point:** Treat as a possible emergency.

Past exam: 2024.1 Q1

items.title: What is the role of the acute pain service?
items.q: What is the role of the acute pain service?
items.a:
- A multidisciplinary service supporting complex pain, PCA, neuraxial/regional catheters and high-risk infusions.
- Provides protocols, staff education, daily review, 24-hour escalation arrangements and incident audit.
- Reviews function, adverse effects, opioid stewardship and discharge transitions.
- Identifies persistent-pain risk and arranges follow-up; it cannot guarantee chronic-pain prevention.

> **Closing point:** Safe delivery and transition matter as much as prescribing.

items.title: What are the limitations of pain scales?
items.q: What are the limitations of pain scales?
items.a:
- Need cognition and communication.
- Measure intensity only.
- Influenced by culture, mood and stoicism.
- Single scores miss function and goals.

> **Closing point:** Combine with function and observation.

items.title: How is pain assessed in a patient with dementia?
items.q: How is pain assessed in a patient with dementia?
items.a:
- Use an observational tool (Abbey, PAINAD).
- Seek carers’ views on usual behaviour.
- Look for delirium and reversible causes.
- Assess at rest and on movement.

> **Closing point:** Behaviour is the language of pain.

Past exam: 2012.2 Q1

items.title: What are the principles of opioid stewardship?
items.q: What are the principles of opioid stewardship?
items.a:
- Maximise useful analgesia while limiting harm to patients, families and the community.
- Safe storage, labelling, controlled-drug documentation, witnessed wastage and appropriate disposal.
- Individualised perioperative prescribing, function-based review and avoidance of routine new modified-release opioids.
- Discharge only what is needed, with a stop/taper plan, safe-use education, follow-up and naloxone for appropriate risk.

> **Closing point:** Stewardship spans handling, prescribing, discharge and community harm.

Past exam: 2024.2 Q14

items.title: What should an opioid discharge prescription include?
items.q: What should an opioid discharge prescription include?
items.a:
- A limited supply of immediate-release opioid.
- A tapering plan and a review date.
- Advice on safe use, storage and disposal.
- Consider naloxone in high-risk patients.

> **Closing point:** Small supply, clear plan.

Past exam: 2024.2 Q14

items.title: What are the analgesic options after open colorectal surgery?
items.q: What are the analgesic options after open colorectal surgery?
items.a:
- **Preop:** discuss thoracic epidural versus catheter/block alternatives for incision, comorbidity, antithrombotics and preference.
- **Intraop:** TEA is a strong open-surgery option; rectus-sheath/wound or fascial techniques need additional visceral analgesia.
- **Postop:** regular appropriate non-opioids, monitored rescue opioid and daily functional/side-effect review.
- Do not combine active regional LA with IV lignocaine; ERAS does not automatically mean omitting TEA in open surgery.

> **Closing point:** Match the plan to open surgery and the available service.

items.title: What are the benefits and risks of thoracic epidural analgesia?
items.q: What are the benefits and risks of thoracic epidural analgesia?
items.a:
- TEA can provide strong dynamic/visceral analgesia and reduce systemic opioid use; pulmonary/bowel benefits depend on context.
- Hypotension, urinary retention, motor block, pruritus, failure and catheter problems may hinder recovery.
- Rare haematoma/abscess can cause catastrophic neurological injury; insertion/removal require antithrombotic planning.
- Requires trained review, rescue analgesia and urgent escalation for new back pain/weakness.

> **Closing point:** Its benefit depends on both patient selection and delivery quality.

items.title: Why are long-acting opioids avoided in acute pain?
items.q: Why are long-acting opioids avoided in acute pain?
items.a:
- Acute pain changes rapidly; prolonged onset/offset makes some long-acting formulations hard to adjust.
- Accumulation and ventilatory impairment can persist as surgical pain falls.
- ANZCA advises **avoiding routine modified-release prescription** unless need, close monitoring and a cessation plan are established.
- This does not mean every long-acting molecule or established maintenance regimen must be stopped.

> **Closing point:** Distinguish formulation, indication and monitoring.

Past exam: 2023.2 Q1

items.title: When is a long-acting opioid appropriate?
items.q: When is a long-acting opioid appropriate?
items.a:
- Established chronic/cancer therapy may need continuation or safe replacement to avoid withdrawal, with review for toxicity and route changes.
- Selected **single-dose intraoperative methadone** protocols have a role with expertise and prolonged monitoring.
- Maintenance buprenorphine for opioid use disorder should **not routinely be stopped**.
- These roles do not justify routine new fentanyl patches or modified-release oxycodone for acute postoperative pain.

> **Closing point:** A legitimate selected role is different from routine discharge prescribing.

Past exam: 2023.2 Q1

items.title: Why are fentanyl patches unsuitable for post-discharge pain after hip replacement?
items.q: Why are fentanyl patches unsuitable for post-discharge pain after hip replacement?
items.a:
- Transdermal fentanyl has delayed onset and prolonged, variable offset from a skin depot after removal.
- It is poorly matched to falling acute pain and is unsafe for opioid-naive postoperative patients.
- Heat/fever can increase uptake; respiratory depression, accidental exposure and diversion remain concerns.
- Use appropriate non-opioids and a limited immediate-release rescue prescription with review. Existing patch users need an individual baseline-opioid plan.

> **Closing point:** A patch is not a safe convenience prescription for new acute pain.

Past exam: 2018.2 Q3

items.title: What is the role of tramadol?
items.q: What is the role of tramadol?
items.a:
- Tramadol combines μ-opioid activity (especially its CYP2D6-generated M1 metabolite) with serotonin/noradrenaline reuptake inhibition.
- It can treat selected moderate acute pain but has variable efficacy and opioid-class harm.
- Consider renal dosing, nausea, seizures, serotonergic interactions and poor/ultra-rapid metabolism.
- Chronic neuropathic benefit is limited and does not justify routine long-term use; it is not a risk-free opioid substitute.

> **Closing point:** Dual mechanism brings additional variability and interactions.

Past exam: 2013.2 Q11

items.title: How does codeine produce its effect and why is it unreliable?
items.q: How does codeine produce its effect and why is it unreliable?
items.a:
- Much of codeine's opioid analgesia depends on CYP2D6 conversion to morphine.
- Poor metabolisers may get little benefit; ultra-rapid metabolisers can develop toxicity at usual doses.
- CYP2D6 inhibitors can cause reduced activation; CYP2D6 is not clinically inducible like CYP3A4.
- Renal dysfunction increases metabolite toxicity. Avoid restricted paediatric/breastfeeding use; choose a more reliable alternative when needed.

> **Closing point:** “Weak opioid” does not mean predictable or harmless.

Past exam: 2011.1 Q11

items.title: Which opioids are preferred in renal impairment?
items.q: Which opioids are preferred in renal impairment?
items.a:
- **Fentanyl** often suits monitored parenteral acute analgesia because it lacks active renally cleared metabolites.
- Morphine, codeine and pethidine are problematic because metabolites accumulate.
- Hydromorphone and oxycodone can be used cautiously with reduced doses/longer intervals: **H3G can accumulate and cause neuroexcitation**.
- Review pain, sedation, ventilation and renal trajectory; methadone/buprenorphine need an appropriate specialist plan.

> **Closing point:** Renal suitability is relative, not permission for standard unmonitored dosing.

items.title: How do you distinguish tolerance from opioid-induced hyperalgesia?
items.q: How do you distinguish tolerance from opioid-induced hyperalgesia?
items.a:
- **Tolerance:** reduced response to a given opioid dose. **OIH:** opioid-associated increased pain sensitivity, sometimes diffuse/allodynic.
- Worsening despite escalation raises concern, but response to an extra dose is **not a validated diagnostic test**.
- Exclude surgical pathology, withdrawal and inadequate delivery; mechanisms may coexist.
- Use specialist-guided multimodal treatment and cautious dose adjustment/rotation rather than reflex escalation or abrupt withdrawal.

> **Closing point:** Reassess the cause before changing the dose.

items.title: How do you manage an opioid-tolerant patient having surgery?
items.q: How do you manage an opioid-tolerant patient having surgery?
items.a:
- **Preop:** establish baseline regimen, indication, organ function, tolerance and withdrawal/relapse risk; agree a pain-service plan.
- **Intraop:** usually continue/safely replace baseline therapy, use appropriate regional/non-opioid analgesia and titrated rescue opioid.
- **Postop:** monitor pain/function and ventilation, adjust for toxicity, taper the added acute component and hand back to the prescriber.
- Do not automatically stop maintenance buprenorphine or stack sedating adjuncts.

> **Closing point:** Prevent withdrawal while treating the new surgical pain safely.

items.title: What changes when a surgical patient takes naltrexone?
items.q: What changes when a surgical patient takes naltrexone?
items.a:
- **Preop:** identify indication/formulation and involve the prescriber; elective opioid-requiring surgery commonly needs oral cessation 72 h beforehand or ≥25 days after a depot injection.
- **Intraop:** emergency blockade may require expert high-dose opioid titration plus regional/non-opioid care and ventilatory capability.
- **Postop:** as blockade wanes, opioid sensitivity/toxicity can increase; monitor and coordinate opioid-free restart with the prescriber.
- Interruption also needs relapse/overdose support.

> **Closing point:** Antagonism now can become respiratory risk later.

items.title: Should maintenance buprenorphine be stopped for surgery?
items.q: Should maintenance buprenorphine be stopped for surgery?
items.a:
- **Preop:** confirm indication/dose and agree a plan with the patient, usual prescriber and acute pain/addiction teams.
- **Do not routinely stop or taper** buprenorphine for opioid use disorder; interruption risks recurrence/overdose.
- **Intraop:** regional/non-opioid analgesia and monitored full-agonist rescue can still work; high affinity does not make analgesia impossible.
- **Postop:** specialist divided dosing may help; taper extra acute opioids and ensure maintenance supply/handover.

> **Closing point:** Continue treatment continuity while planning additional analgesia.

items.title: What are the advantages of opioid-free anaesthesia in bariatric surgery?
items.q: What are the advantages of opioid-free anaesthesia in bariatric surgery?
items.a:
- Reducing unnecessary opioids is attractive in obesity/OSA because of respiratory and PONV risk.
- OFA may reduce opioid use/PONV in selected regimens, but an opioid-free label does not prove better respiratory or long-term outcomes.
- Non-opioid drugs have their own haemodynamic, sedating and toxicity effects.
- Prefer a justified multimodal plan with monitored rescue opioid available.

> **Closing point:** Judge recovery and harm, not the opioid total alone.

Past exam: 2019.2 Q12

items.title: What are the drawbacks of opioid-free techniques?
items.q: What are the drawbacks of opioid-free techniques?
items.a:
- Complex regimens can substitute bradycardia/hypotension, sedation or LA toxicity for opioid harm.
- **POFA** was stopped after five severe bradycardia events; its adverse-event composite was worse with dexmedetomidine-based OFA.
- TAP/infiltration does not cover every visceral pain mechanism.
- Do not overlap active regional/infiltrated LA with an IV lignocaine analgesic infusion; provide rescue analgesia.

> **Closing point:** Opioid-free is not automatically safer.

Past exam: 2019.2 Q12

items.title: When does paracetamol dosing need to be modified?
items.q: When does paracetamol dosing need to be modified?
items.a:
- Neonates/children need age-, weight- and route-specific dosing; do not extrapolate an adult schedule.
- Low weight, frailty, malnutrition, liver disease, prolonged poor intake and severe renal dysfunction require review of dose/interval.
- Count all oral, IV and combination-product doses together.
- A healthy >50-kg adult commonly has a 4-g/day short-term maximum; lower limits often apply. IV ≤50-kg dosing commonly caps at 60 mg/kg/day and 3 g/day, product-specific.

> **Closing point:** Weight, route and total daily exposure matter.

Past exam: 2023.1 Q12

items.title: How is paracetamol toxicity managed?
items.q: How is paracetamol toxicity managed?
items.a:
- Establish amount, time, formulation and single versus repeated exposure; contact toxicology/poisons services.
- A ≥4-hour level and nomogram apply to an appropriate known-time acute ingestion—not unknown-time or repeated supratherapeutic exposure.
- Start **NAC promptly** when indicated; avoid delaying beyond 8 hours while awaiting assessment.
- Standard Australasian IV treatment is **200 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h**; massive/complex poisoning needs a separate pathway and protocol stopping tests.

> **Closing point:** Correct pathway, early NAC and laboratory-guided continuation.

Past exam: 2023.1 Q12

items.title: What are the mechanisms and risks of NSAIDs?
items.q: What are the mechanisms and risks of NSAIDs?
items.a:
- COX inhibition reduces prostaglandin-mediated sensitisation and can provide useful opioid-sparing analgesia.
- Assess hypovolaemia/AKI/CKD, GI bleeding, cardiovascular disease, antithrombotics and NSAID hypersensitivity.
- COX-2 selectivity largely spares platelets and reduces **but does not eliminate** GI risk; renal/CV risk remains.
- Use the lowest effective dose for a defined short period. Pregnancy risks are gestation-dependent; avoid routine use and recognise fetal renal risk from about 20 weeks.

> **Closing point:** Screen the patient and operation rather than applying blanket reassurance or avoidance.

items.title: What is the evidence for IV lignocaine infusions?
items.q: What is the evidence for IV lignocaine infusions?
items.a:
- Older small abdominal trials suggested early analgesic/opioid and bowel-recovery benefits.
- **ALLEGRO** found no improvement in 72-hour GI recovery after minimally invasive colon surgery: **57.3% vs 59.0%**, adjusted RR 0.97 (95% CI 0.88–1.07).
- That result does not answer every operation, but routine bowel-recovery claims are outdated.
- Selected use requires a procedure-specific rationale and a high-risk medicine protocol.

> **Closing point:** Historical promise is not current proof of routine benefit.

Past exam: 2018.1 Q15

items.title: What is the toxic risk of combining lignocaine infusion with regional blocks?
items.q: What is the toxic risk of combining lignocaine infusion with regional blocks?
items.a:
- IV lignocaine and regional/infiltrated LA can produce additive systemic toxicity; merely adding the doses is insufficient.
- **Do not overlap** an analgesic IV infusion with an active LA block/catheter/wound infusion.
- The consensus specifies at least **4 h after a nerve block before IV infusion**, and **4 h after stopping IV infusion before a block**; respect longer LA action/local policy too.
- Small-dose single-shot spinal LA is a consensus exception; catheter transitions have specific rules. Recognise LAST and use the rescue algorithm.

> **Closing point:** Choose and time the LA strategy deliberately.

Past exam: 2018.1 Q15

items.title: What is the role of gabapentin in postoperative pain?
items.q: What is the role of gabapentin in postoperative pain?
items.a:
- Modern evidence does **not** support routine perioperative initiation: small opioid reductions have not produced clinically meaningful pain/recovery benefit.
- Verret 2020 and **GAP 2025** temper older favourable teaching.
- Sedation, dizziness, falls and respiratory interaction with opioids are important, especially with frailty/renal dysfunction.
- Continue established treatment appropriately or consider a goal-based trial for neuropathic features; it does not reliably prevent CPSP/phantom pain.

> **Closing point:** A selective neuropathic role is not routine postoperative prophylaxis.

Past exam: 2008.1 Q13

items.title: What are the practical features of gabapentin pharmacology?
items.q: What are the practical features of gabapentin pharmacology?
items.a:
- Oral **α2δ calcium-channel ligand**, not a GABA-receptor agonist; an analgesic for selected neuropathic conditions.
- Saturable absorption means bioavailability falls as dose rises.
- Excreted unchanged by the kidneys: adjust dose/interval to renal function.
- Few CYP interactions, but important additive opioid/sedative respiratory effects. Titrate slowly; avoid abrupt cessation of established long-term treatment.

> **Closing point:** Renal clearance and pharmacodynamic interactions drive safety.

Past exam: 2008.1 Q13

items.title: What guidelines are needed for ward ketamine infusions?
items.q: What guidelines are needed for ward ketamine infusions?
items.a:
- Define indications, selection, approved route/concentration/pump, dose limits and authorised bolus staff/location.
- Specify a **named sedation scale**, ventilation, oxygenation, BP/HR, pain and psychotomimetic observations with escalation rules.
- Include stop criteria, emergency response, daily review and a short stop/review date.
- Active psychosis or uncontrolled cardiovascular disease needs caution; raised ICP is **not universally an absolute contraindication**.

> **Closing point:** A ward protocol must tell staff what to do when harm appears.

Past exam: 2016.2 Q7

items.title: What are the typical doses and uses of sub-anaesthetic ketamine?
items.q: What are the typical doses and uses of sub-anaesthetic ketamine?
items.a:
- Selected use includes severe/opioid-resistant pain, opioid tolerance or hyperalgesia within multimodal care.
- A monitored example is **0.1–0.3 mg/kg slowly IV**, then around **0.1–0.2 mg/kg/h**, according to local protocol and patient factors.
- Ward boluses require authorised staff and monitoring; SC use is service-specific/off-label.
- Watch sedation, dysphoria and haemodynamics. A PCA is not compulsory and a short infusion does not always need tapering.

> **Closing point:** Example doses are not a universal ward prescription.

items.title: What are the roles of dexamethasone and magnesium in analgesia?
items.q: What are the roles of dexamethasone and magnesium in analgesia?
items.a:
- **Dexamethasone** helps prevent PONV and can modestly improve pain/opioid use in selected operations; it is not immediate rescue analgesia.
- Consider transient hyperglycaemia and the patient's infection/diabetes context.
- **Magnesium** has NMDA-related opioid-sparing effects in some studies but is not a mandatory adjunct.
- Magnesium can cause hypotension, accumulate in renal dysfunction and potentiate neuromuscular blockade; use an appropriate monitoring/protocol plan.

> **Closing point:** Add an adjunct for a clinical benefit, not just a mechanism.

items.title: What must you check before stopping an opioid PCA?
items.sub: Recovery, day surgery and oral transition
items.eyebrow: Recovery, day surgery and oral transition
items.q: What must you check before stopping an opioid PCA?
items.a:
Confirm oral intake and absorption, improving pain and function and no surgical deterioration. Review delivered doses and all other opioid exposure, agree a conservative oral plan and time the switch to avoid a gap or stacking. Recheck pain and sedation after the first oral dose.

**Sources:** [Australian Acute Pain Opioid Analgesic Stewardship Clinical Care Standard](https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/clinical-care-standards/opioid-analgesic-stewardship-acute-pain)

items.title: How do you ensure PCA safety?
items.sub: PCA, opioid infusions and ventilatory impairment
items.eyebrow: PCA, opioid infusions and ventilatory impairment
items.q: How do you ensure PCA safety?
items.a:
- Select a patient who can understand/use the handset; **no PCA by proxy**.
- Standard concentration, locked pump, dose/lockout checks, protected line and no routine background infusion in opioid-naive patients.
- Monitor pain/function, consciousness, ventilation and oxygenation; use risk-appropriate continuous monitoring.
- Specify escalation/naloxone orders and require an authorised plan for extra opioids/sedatives; provide 24-hour support.

> **Closing point:** Device safety and observation must work together.

Past exam: 2012.1 Q11

items.title: What should a PCA order form include?
items.sub: PCA, opioid infusions and ventilatory impairment
items.eyebrow: PCA, opioid infusions and ventilatory impairment
items.q: What should a PCA order form include?
items.a:
- Patient details, weight and allergies.
- Drug, concentration, bolus and lockout.
- Background infusion (usually none) and limits.
- Monitoring instructions, signature and review time.

> **Closing point:** Unambiguous orders prevent errors.

Past exam: 2012.1 Q11

items.title: How do you manage a drowsy patient on PCA with a respiratory rate of 6?
items.sub: PCA, opioid infusions and ventilatory impairment
items.eyebrow: PCA, opioid infusions and ventilatory impairment
items.q: How do you manage a drowsy patient on PCA with a respiratory rate of 6?
items.a:
- **Stop PCA and call an emergency response now**; do not flush retained opioid from the line.
- Open the airway, give oxygen and assist ventilation immediately as required.
- Titrate naloxone (e.g. 40–100 micrograms IV increments in a breathing patient); profound depression/apnoea may need larger rescue doses without delay.
- Repeat/infuse if renarcotisation occurs; investigate pump/drug errors and other causes, monitor at higher acuity and revise analgesia.

> **Closing point:** Ventilate first; a rate of six with drowsiness is already an emergency.

items.title: What factors influence the spread of intrathecal local anaesthetic?
items.q: What factors influence the spread of intrathecal local anaesthetic?
items.a:
- Core controllable factors: **injection level, baricity, dose and position** during/after injection.
- Lumbosacral CSF volume, pregnancy, age and spinal anatomy contribute to variability.
- Dose matters, but does not universally dominate baricity/position; height and BMI are weak standalone predictors in ordinary adult ranges.
- Needle direction/injection speed effects are less reliable. Always test the achieved block.

> **Closing point:** Several interacting factors determine spread.

Past exam: 2018.1 Q11

items.title: How does baricity affect spinal block?
items.q: How does baricity affect spinal block?
items.a:
- Baricity is the **dimensionless density ratio** of solution to CSF at the same temperature (usually 37°C).
- Hyperbaric solutions settle under gravity; hypobaric solutions rise. Position and spinal curves influence distribution.
- “Isobaric” solutions have less gravity-dependent but still variable spread.
- Lateral positioning can favour unilateral block but does not guarantee it; no position ensures a fixed T4 endpoint.

> **Closing point:** Baricity only makes sense in relation to temperature and position.

Past exam: 2018.1 Q11

items.title: What are the advantages and disadvantages of intrathecal morphine?
items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of intrathecal morphine?
items.a:
- A single hydrophilic spinal opioid can provide 12–24-hour analgesia and reduce systemic opioid requirements.
- No catheter/pump; morphine itself produces little motor/sympathetic block.
- Pruritus, PONV, retention and **early/delayed respiratory depression**; the dose cannot be removed or titrated.
- Requires appropriate patient selection and monitoring; no pump does not mean suitable for routine same-day discharge.

> **Closing point:** Prolonged analgesia comes with prolonged surveillance.

Past exam: 2026.1 Q6

items.title: What dose of intrathecal morphine is used?
items.q: What dose of intrathecal morphine is used?
items.a:
- Use **preservative-free morphine**, prescribe in micrograms and double-check preparation.
- Around **50–150 micrograms** is common in obstetric/arthroplasty pathways; selected major surgery uses **100–300 micrograms**.
- Choose the lowest procedure-specific effective dose; do not apply a universal mg/kg rule or efficacy ceiling.
- For TKA, 100 micrograms may be selected, but routine IT opioid is less attractive when ACB plus infiltration works well.

> **Closing point:** Dose and indication are procedure-specific.

Past exam: 2026.1 Q6

items.title: How should patients be monitored after intrathecal morphine?
items.q: How should patients be monitored after intrathecal morphine?
items.a:
- General adult single-shot hydrophilic-opioid guidance: **at least 24 h**, hourly for 12 h then every 2 h for 12 h.
- Assess **ventilation, consciousness and oxygenation**, not respiratory rate alone.
- Increase surveillance for OSA, frailty, additional opioids/sedatives and clinical deterioration; low-dose obstetric pathways may differ.
- Oxygen can mask hypoventilation on SpO2. Have trained rescue staff and naloxone available.

> **Closing point:** An uneventful PACU period does not exclude delayed depression.

Past exam: 2008.1 Q5

items.title: Why is intrathecal morphine riskier in an obese patient?
items.q: Why is intrathecal morphine riskier in an obese patient?
items.a:
- Obesity may coexist with OSA, upper-airway obstruction and reduced respiratory reserve.
- **BMI alone does not diagnose OSA** or automatically prohibit intrathecal morphine.
- Screen for sleep-disordered breathing, sedative exposure and other risk; use low procedure-specific dose or an alternative technique.
- Ensure appropriate postoperative surveillance/CPAP arrangements and avoid unplanned additive depressants.

> **Closing point:** Assess actual respiratory risk rather than assuming it from weight.

Past exam: 2008.1 Q5

items.title: How do you manage an epidural that is not working?
items.q: How do you manage an epidural that is not working?
items.a:
- Assess pain/cause, dermatomal block, motor function, BP, catheter depth/site, connections and pump settings.
- **New weakness, severe back pain, high block or toxicity: stop infusion and escalate; do not bolus.**
- If safe, a trained clinician may use a fractionated protocol bolus, repositioning or limited sterile withdrawal.
- Do not advance exposed catheter; replace only after antithrombotic review or provide an alternative analgesic plan.

> **Closing point:** Exclude complications before troubleshooting coverage.

items.title: What are the signs of epidural haematoma?
items.q: What are the signs of epidural haematoma?
items.a:
- New/progressive back pain, motor weakness, sensory deficit or bladder/bowel dysfunction; severe pain may be absent.
- **Stop infusion, call senior anaesthesia and spinal/neurosurgical teams, and obtain emergency imaging.**
- Review anticoagulants/coagulation, but do not delay imaging while waiting for results or block regression.
- Compression may require urgent decompression; an “8–12-hour window” is not a reason to wait.

> **Closing point:** New neurological deficit is a time-critical emergency.

items.title: What is the timing of neuraxial catheter removal with anticoagulants?
items.q: What is the timing of neuraxial catheter removal with anticoagulants?
items.a:
- Catheter **removal is a neuraxial intervention**, requiring the same attention to drug, dose, timing and renal clearance as insertion.
- Use the current drug-specific ASRA/local table, not one interval for all anticoagulants.
- Low-dose LMWH often requires at least 12 h before removal and ≥4 h afterwards before the next dose; **once- versus twice-daily regimens differ**.
- Therapeutic LMWH/DOACs need longer/different intervals; deep plexus/deep peripheral blocks need neuraxial precautions.

> **Closing point:** Check the exact regimen and renal function before touching the catheter.

items.title: How does a high spinal present and what do you do?
items.q: How does a high spinal present and what do you do?
items.a:
- Arm weakness/tingling, dyspnoea, hypotension/bradycardia progressing to apnoea/unconsciousness suggests high/total spinal; an ordinary T4 caesarean level alone does not.
- Call help, stop dosing, oxygenate/ventilate, intubate if needed and support circulation with uterine displacement and appropriate drugs.
- Arrest: supine CPR/manual displacement and **1 mg adrenaline per adult ALS**, not microgram peri-arrest dosing.
- Prepare resuscitative delivery immediately when indicated; continue sedation after intubation and debrief afterwards.

> **Closing point:** Prioritise oxygenation and maternal resuscitation.

items.title: What should you do if BP falls after an epidural rate increase?
items.q: What should you do if BP falls after an epidural rate increase?
items.a:
Pause or reduce the infusion as appropriate, check block level and perfusion, and consider bleeding, sepsis or cardiac causes. Treat the physiology, recognise high block and review the analgesic plan before restarting.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Blue Book 2017, Deacon and Hartley on thoracic epidural analgesia](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

items.title: What are the risks of continuous peripheral nerve catheters on the ward?
items.q: What are the risks of continuous peripheral nerve catheters on the ward?
items.a:
- Dislodgement/leak/failure, infection, bleeding, nerve injury and **LAST**.
- Motor weakness/falls, pressure/thermal injury to an insensate limb and delayed recognition of compartment syndrome.
- Interscalene catheters can impair diaphragmatic function; assess respiratory reserve.
- Use site-specific monitoring, cumulative LA limits, antithrombotic precautions and a 24-hour rescue plan; suspected compartment syndrome needs immediate orthopaedic assessment.

> **Closing point:** Targeted analgesia still requires a trained ward system.

items.title: What is a typical infusion for a peripheral nerve catheter?
items.q: What is a typical infusion for a peripheral nerve catheter?
items.a:
- Dilute ropivacaine (e.g. 0.2%) is commonly used; rate depends on site, weight, boluses and other LA exposure.
- An example range such as 4–10 mL/h is **not universally safe**; prescribe mg/hour and total limits.
- Do not overlap with IV lignocaine analgesia. Review motor block, pain/function, site and toxicity daily.
- Establish oral analgesia before cessation; a short infusion does not automatically need tapering.

> **Closing point:** Calculate the full LA exposure rather than memorising one rate.

items.title: How do you justify the analgesic strategy for an above-knee amputation?
items.q: How do you justify the analgesic strategy for an above-knee amputation?
items.a:
- **Preop:** treat severe rest pain, assess neuropathic features/current opioids, renal function and antithrombotics; explain phantom/residual pain.
- **Intraop:** suitable neuraxial or regional-plus-GA plan; AKA coverage may need femoral, sciatic, obturator and cutaneous contributions.
- **Postop:** effective catheter/non-opioid baseline, titrated rescue and selective neuropathic treatment; rehabilitation/psychology and early follow-up.
- No single regimen reliably prevents chronic phantom pain.

> **Closing point:** Treat current pain well without promising prevention.

Past exam: 2025.2 Q6

items.title: What can be done before amputation to reduce pain afterwards?
items.q: What can be done before amputation to reduce pain afterwards?
items.a:
- Assess and treat ischaemic/traumatic pain, neuropathic features, distress and existing opioid needs.
- Regional analgesia, suitable non-opioids and titrated opioids improve acute comfort and facilitate care.
- Explain painless phantom sensations versus phantom pain, and prepare rehabilitation/support.
- **Routine pre-emptive gabapentin, tricyclics or a catheter have not reliably prevented chronic PLP**; use each treatment for a justified individual indication.

> **Closing point:** Good acute care matters despite uncertain chronic-pain prevention.

Past exam: 2025.2 Q6

items.title: What is the role of a perineural catheter after below-knee amputation?
items.q: What is the role of a perineural catheter after below-knee amputation?
items.a:
- A sciatic perineural catheter can reduce acute residual-limb pain and systemic opioid requirements.
- Below-knee incisions may also need saphenous/femoral coverage, depending on level/tourniquet.
- Prescribe individualised LA limits and monitor motor function, toxicity, infection and catheter performance.
- Transition to oral analgesia before cessation; do not claim the catheter reliably prevents chronic phantom pain.

> **Closing point:** Acute analgesic efficacy is different from prevention efficacy.

Past exam: 2022.2 Q2

items.title: Which drugs reduce phantom limb pain?
items.q: Which drugs reduce phantom limb pain?
items.a:
- PLP-specific drug evidence is limited; a goal-based trial of a gabapentinoid, tricyclic or another neuropathic agent may be reasonable.
- Adjust for renal function, sedation, falls and anticholinergic/cardiac risk; stop ineffective treatment.
- Selected ketamine/opioid or interventional trials need specialist review; memantine/calcitonin are not established routine second line.
- Combine rehabilitation, psychological care and selected mirror/imagery approaches with realistic expectations.

> **Closing point:** Avoid presenting a confident drug ladder where evidence is uncertain.

Past exam: 2006.2 Q4

items.title: How do you distinguish phantom limb pain, phantom sensation and stump pain?
items.q: How do you distinguish phantom limb pain, phantom sensation and stump pain?
items.a:
- Phantom sensation: non-painful awareness of the limb.
- Phantom pain: painful sensation in the absent limb.
- Stump pain: pain in the residual limb.
- Causes of stump pain: neuroma, ischaemia, infection, prosthesis.

> **Closing point:** Do not confuse the three.

Past exam: 2006.2 Q4

items.title: What analgesic approach suits a fractured femur in the emergency department?
items.q: What analgesic approach suits a fractured femur in the emergency department?
items.a:
- Assess ABC, blood loss, associated injury and baseline limb neurology while treating pain promptly.
- Splint; use traction only for a suitable fracture without contraindicating associated injury.
- Titrate monitored IV opioid, give appropriate paracetamol and consider selected ketamine.
- Femoral/fascia-iliaca block may help according to fracture level; **PENG is hip-focused, not a universal shaft block**. Calculate LA dose and maintain compartment surveillance.

> **Closing point:** Analgesia and trauma reassessment proceed together.

items.title: What are the early signs of compartment syndrome?
items.q: What are the early signs of compartment syndrome?
items.a:
- Increasing pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and escalating analgesic requirement raise concern.
- Paraesthesia/weakness and tense swelling may occur; **normal pulses do not exclude** compartment syndrome.
- Pain can be absent or obscured by sedation/block, so use serial objective observations and pressure measurement when needed.
- Call orthopaedics urgently; do not wait for a block to wear off before assessment/decompression decisions.

> **Closing point:** Delayed diagnosis threatens the limb.

items.title: What is the functional target when treating rib fracture pain?
items.q: What is the functional target when treating rib fracture pain?
items.a:
Restore an effective cough, deep inspiration and mobilisation while preserving ventilation. Track oxygen requirement, work of breathing and ability to clear secretions. Escalate respiratory support or regional analgesia if function worsens.

**Sources:** [BJA Education Anaesthetic and surgical management of rib fractures](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7807920/)

items.title: What are the features of trigeminal neuralgia?
items.q: What are the features of trigeminal neuralgia?
items.a:
- Brief unilateral electric-shock/lancinating attacks in a trigeminal distribution, commonly V2/V3, triggered by light touch, chewing or talking.
- Attacks usually last seconds to two minutes, with trigger zones/refractory periods; background pain may coexist.
- Sensory loss or bilateral symptoms suggest a secondary cause, but normal examination does not exclude one.
- MRI is recommended for all; classical TN requires compressive morphological nerve change, not incidental vessel contact alone.

> **Closing point:** Diagnose the syndrome and investigate its cause.

Past exam: 2015.2 Q4

items.title: How is trigeminal neuralgia treated?
items.q: How is trigeminal neuralgia treated?
items.a:
- **Carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine** first line; titrate and monitor sodium, rash, interactions and other toxicity.
- Consider ancestry-appropriate HLA testing before carbamazepine; alternatives/add-ons include lamotrigine or baclofen with weaker evidence.
- Microvascular decompression gives durable relief for suitable classical compression; ablative procedures/radiosurgery trade less invasive treatment for recurrence/sensory effects.
- Routine opioids generally do not treat the paroxysms; severe crises may need specialist rescue.

> **Closing point:** Compare efficacy, tolerability and procedural risk.

Past exam: 2015.2 Q4

items.title: How do you treat acute herpes zoster pain?
items.q: How do you treat acute herpes zoster pain?
items.a:
- Start an appropriate renally adjusted antiviral promptly, ideally within 72 h; later treatment may help with ongoing lesions or complicated/immunocompromised cases.
- Treat acute pain with suitable baseline/rescue analgesia and a cautious neuropathic-agent trial if needed.
- Topical lignocaine belongs on **intact skin**, not active vesicles; capsaicin is usually considered after healing.
- Antivirals do not reliably prevent PHN; vaccination prevents future zoster, not this episode's PHN or established pain.

> **Closing point:** Separate acute treatment from future prevention.

items.title: What are the analgesic issues in sickle cell crisis?
items.q: What are the analgesic issues in sickle cell crisis?
items.a:
- Respect the patient-specific plan; offer analgesia **within 30 minutes**, with titrated opioid/PCA and appropriate non-opioids.
- Assess for acute chest syndrome, infection and other causes; avoid pethidine.
- Maintain warmth/euvolemia, avoid fluid overload and give oxygen if hypoxaemic; monitor ventilation/sedation.
- Uncomplicated pain crisis does not require routine exchange transfusion. Perioperative transfusion/Hb/HbS targets are individualised with haematology.

> **Closing point:** Treat pain promptly while detecting complications.

items.title: What turns an acute headache into an urgent diagnostic problem?
items.q: What turns an acute headache into an urgent diagnostic problem?
items.a:
Thunderclap onset, focal neurology, fever, meningism, pregnancy or postpartum hypertension, anticoagulation or a major change in pattern. Treat pain while investigating the suspected secondary cause.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: Which analgesics are acceptable in early pregnancy?
items.q: Which analgesics are acceptable in early pregnancy?
items.a:
- Paracetamol is preferred when needed, within an appropriate daily limit; short-term titrated opioids can treat severe fracture pain.
- Regional LA is reasonable: TGA **lignocaine A, bupivacaine A, ropivacaine B1**; categories are not a simple safety ranking.
- Avoid routine NSAIDs; use only if benefits justify risks, recognising additional fetal renal risk from about 20 weeks and third-trimester contraindication.
- Do not call standard clinical GA a proven human teratogen; maintain maternal physiology and obtain obstetric input.

> **Closing point:** Balance treatment benefit, gestation and maternal safety.

Past exam: 2009.2 Q5

items.title: What are the key points in analgesia for an elderly patient with a hip fracture?
items.q: What are the key points in analgesia for an elderly patient with a hip fracture?
items.a:
- Use simple self-report where possible; dementia may need PAINAD/Abbey-type assessment, carers' input and movement/function observation.
- Appropriate fascia-iliaca/femoral regional analgesia reduces opioid need; do not equate every block or spinal anaesthesia with proven delirium prevention.
- Regular risk-adjusted paracetamol and small titrated rescue opioid; assess renal function, sedation and ventilation.
- Reorient, mobilise and support hearing/vision, sleep, nutrition and bladder/bowel care; avoid undertreatment.

> **Closing point:** Proactively assess pain because the patient may not request treatment.

Past exam: 2012.2 Q1

items.title: How are pain and delirium linked in the elderly?
items.q: How are pain and delirium linked in the elderly?
items.a:
- Both unrelieved pain and excessive sedating medication can contribute to delirium.
- Aim for adequate pain/function with an individualised, least harmful regimen; avoiding every opioid can undertreat pain.
- Use regional analgesia where suitable, appropriate baseline non-opioids and carefully titrated rescue.
- Address infection/hypoxia, hydration, sleep, orientation, sensory aids and mobilisation; spinal versus GA alone does not reliably prevent delirium.

> **Closing point:** Pain treatment and delirium prevention must be balanced.

items.title: Which drugs should be avoided in delirium-prone patients?
items.q: Which drugs should be avoided in delirium-prone patients?
items.a:
- Avoid pethidine and minimise benzodiazepines, anticholinergics and unnecessary sedating polypharmacy.
- Gabapentinoids/tricyclics and opioids require an individual indication and cautious dosing, not automatic substitution.
- Treat causes and use non-drug de-escalation first; antipsychotics are reserved for severe distress/danger, not routine prophylaxis.
- Check QT risk and avoid/seek specialist advice for **Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia** before dopamine-blocking drugs.

> **Closing point:** Choose drugs for benefit while actively checking cognitive and respiratory harm.

items.title: Which psychosocial factors increase postoperative pain?
items.q: Which psychosocial factors increase postoperative pain?
items.a:
- Anxiety, depression, catastrophising, poor sleep, previous pain/trauma, expectations and limited support can affect pain and recovery.
- Culture, language and practical stresses influence communication and access to care.
- Compensation/litigation associations do **not** prove causation or malingering.
- Listen and validate, use interpreters, set realistic goals and offer psychological/multidisciplinary support without dismissing physical causes.

> **Closing point:** Psychosocial assessment should improve care, not stigmatise pain.

items.title: What non-drug measures help acute pain?
items.q: What non-drug measures help acute pain?
items.a:
- Reassurance/education, splinting/positioning, rehabilitation and a supportive environment.
- Selected relaxation, music/distraction, CBT-based approaches or TENS may help; effects vary.
- Protect skin with cold/heat, especially in ischaemia, neuropathy or a blocked limb.
- Breastfeeding/sucrose/skin-to-skin can help brief neonatal procedures but do not replace major-surgery analgesia.

> **Closing point:** Offer appropriate adjuncts without delaying effective analgesia.

items.title: How does the placebo effect influence pain?
items.q: How does the placebo effect influence pain?
items.a:
- Positive expectation reduces pain through endogenous opioids.
- Negative expectation (nocebo) increases it.
- Language and communication matter.
- Placebo is not evidence of "unreal" pain.

> **Closing point:** What you say changes what they feel.

items.title: How do you manage perioperative pain in a cancer patient on opioids?
items.q: How do you manage perioperative pain in a cancer patient on opioids?
items.a:
- **Preop:** establish pain types, goals, baseline opioid/adjuvants, organ function and palliative-care plan.
- **Intraop:** continue/safely replace baseline opioid, use appropriate regional/non-opioid treatment and titrated additional rescue.
- **Postop:** monitor sedation/ventilation, treat breakthrough pain and adverse effects, then taper the acute addition.
- No universal percentage predicts extra opioid need; rotation, especially methadone, needs specialist conversion and clear handover.

> **Closing point:** Preserve baseline comfort while safely treating the new pain.

items.title: How can you tell whether a knee arthroplasty analgesic plan is helping recovery?
items.q: How can you tell whether a knee arthroplasty analgesic plan is helping recovery?
items.a:
Assess movement pain, quadriceps power, safe transfers and physiotherapy alongside adverse effects, opioid use and ventilation. A below-target pain score can coexist with weakness, falls or sedation.

**Sources:** [BJA Education Anaesthesia and analgesia for total knee arthroplasty 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.03.004)

items.title: 1. Pathophysiology of acute pain and how multimodal analgesia targets it
items.q: Describe the pathophysiology of acute postoperative pain and explain how multimodal analgesia targets the different mechanisms.
items.a:
## Pathways

- **Transduction**: tissue injury releases prostaglandins, bradykinin, substance P, ATP, hydrogen ions and cytokines, which sensitise and activate **nociceptors** (Aδ and C fibres): **peripheral sensitisation**.
- **Transmission**: signals pass by Aδ and C fibres via the dorsal root ganglion to the **dorsal horn** (laminae I, II and V), then cross and ascend in the **spinothalamic tract** to thalamus and cortex.
- **Modulation**: at the dorsal horn, excitatory (glutamate via AMPA and **NMDA** receptors, substance P) and inhibitory (GABA, glycine, endogenous opioids, noradrenaline and context/receptor-dependent serotonergic descending effects) inputs balance. Repeated C-fibre input can cause **wind-up**, a short-term frequency-dependent response; **central sensitisation** is a broader increase in central nociceptive responsiveness, contributing to hyperalgesia/allodynia. They are related, not identical.
- **Perception**: cortical, limbic and affective components, modified by anxiety, expectation and context.

## Multimodal analgesia (different sites with additive or synergistic effects)

| Level | Target | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Periphery | Inflammatory mediators | **NSAIDs**, steroids (dexamethasone) |
| Peripheral nerve | Conduction | **Local anaesthetic** (infiltration, blocks, catheters); IV lignocaine has separate systemic effects and is not a peripheral block |
| Dorsal horn | Opioid receptors, NMDA, calcium channels | **Neuraxial block**, intrathecal opioid, **ketamine**, selected neuropathic agents (not routine perioperative gabapentinoids), magnesium in selected protocols |
| Descending modulation and brain | Opioid, alpha-2 and monoamine mechanisms | **Opioids**, **paracetamol**, **clonidine/dexmedetomidine**, tramadol |
| Cognitive | Anxiety, expectation | Education, reassurance, non-drug therapies |

## Principles

- Combine drugs with **different mechanisms** to improve analgesia and function while reducing individual drug exposure. **Opioid sparing does not guarantee less overall harm** if replacement drugs add sedation, haemodynamic effects or toxicity.
- Start an appropriate plan early; pre-incision dosing does not universally prevent persistent pain. Give suitable baseline agents regularly and reserve titrated rescue treatments for need.
- Tailor to the **procedure, patient** (age, renal function, OSA) and **setting** (day surgery versus inpatient).
- Reassess pain and side effects and adjust.

Apply the mechanism to a patient who cannot cough after laparotomy. Treat movement-related somatic pain with an appropriate regional or local option where feasible, supplement inflammatory pain with a suitable NSAID and use titrated rescue opioid if needed. Adjust if a weak patient cannot mobilise or becomes hypoventilated. Reassess pain during movement, sedation and the ability to breathe deeply. Worsening pain also requires an examination for a surgical complication.

**Sources:** Evidence · [ANZCA acute pain evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence); [ANZCA PS41](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/558316c5-ea93-457c-b51f-d57556b0ffa7/PS41-Guideline-on-acute-pain-management).

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes transduction, transmission, modulation and perception
- Explains peripheral and central sensitisation and wind-up
- Identifies neurotransmitters and receptors (NMDA, opioid, GABA)
- Links drugs to sites of action
- States benefits of combining mechanisms (opioid sparing)
- Describes principles: timing, regular dosing and individualisation

[ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence) · [ANZCA acute pain statement PS41](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/558316c5-ea93-457c-b51f-d57556b0ffa7/PS41-Guideline-on-acute-pain-management)

items.title: 2. Methods of assessing acute postoperative pain and their limitations
items.q: Discuss the methods of assessing acute pain in the postoperative period and their limitations.
items.a:
## Why assess?

Pain is subjective, and assessment guides **titration and safety**. Record it with **vital signs** and review after every intervention. It should include **function** (ability to cough, breathe deeply, mobilise), and side effects (sedation, nausea).

## Self-report scales

- **Numeric rating scale** (0 to 10), **verbal rating scale** (none, mild, moderate, severe) and **visual analogue scale**: quick and validated in adults, but need cognition and communication, affected by culture, mood and expectation, and measure only intensity.
- **Faces scales** (Wong-Baker, Faces Pain Scale-Revised) in children and some adults.
- Assess both **rest and movement** (dynamic pain): the pain with cough or movement is more relevant to complications.

## Observational tools (cognitive impairment, sedation, ventilation)

- **Abbey Pain Scale, PAINAD, Doloplus** (dementia); **FLACC, COMFORT, CRIES** (infants and children); **Behavioural Pain Scale and CPOT** (ventilated).
- Use each tool as validated: CPOT/BPS are principally behavioural tools. Vital signs may prompt assessment but **do not alone establish or quantify pain**. Training and serial assessment are needed.

## Multidimensional and functional assessment

- Location, quality (neuropathic features, **DN4**/**LANSS**), timing and radiation, aggravating factors, effect on sleep and function.
- Psychosocial: anxiety, catastrophising, previous pain, coping, expectations.
- Medication history (opioid tolerance, use) and **side effects** (sedation score, respiratory rate).

## Limitations and pitfalls

Single scores do not reflect the patient's goals; some patients under-report (stoicism); delirium, language barrier, sedation and developmental stage limit validity; individual pain experiences and coping differ; and **pain does not always equal harm**. Investigate unexpected severe pain (surgical complication, compartment syndrome).

**Summary:** use a simple validated tool at rest and movement, adapt to the patient, record regularly with sedation, and act on the results.

Compare ratings obtained in the same context, such as at rest and when coughing or sitting up. Ask what is acceptable to the patient and what activity remains limited. Escalating scores may represent a blocked drain, urinary retention or a surgical complication. Note how communication barriers, fear and cognition affect what is observed. Use an interpreter and supported self-report where possible. Record the intervention, expected onset, reassessment time and adverse effects. A low pain score with excessive sedation does not represent safe analgesia.

Use an agreed assessment context such as coughing or transferring, and record how much help the patient needed.

**Sources:** Evidence · [ANZCA PS41](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/558316c5-ea93-457c-b51f-d57556b0ffa7/PS41-Guideline-on-acute-pain-management).

## Self-marking checklist

- Self-report tools: numeric, verbal, visual analogue
- Pain at rest and on movement
- Observational tools for cognitive impairment, children and ventilated patients
- Multidimensional and functional assessment
- Assessment of neuropathic features
- Limitations of scales
- Link to sedation and side effects
- Act on unexpected pain
- Documents a functional goal, a reproducible reassessment and adverse effects

[ANZCA acute pain statement PS41](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/558316c5-ea93-457c-b51f-d57556b0ffa7/PS41-Guideline-on-acute-pain-management) · [ANZCA professional documents including PS45 and PG67](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents)

items.title: 3. Analgesic options for elective open colorectal resection
items.q: Compare the analgesic options for a patient having an elective open colorectal resection, and justify your choice.
items.a:
## Options

| Option | Strengths | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| **Thoracic epidural** (local anaesthetic ± opioid) | Strong option for dynamic and visceral analgesia in open surgery; fewer pulmonary complications and ileus | Hypotension, failure rate, haematoma risk, anticoagulation constraints, motor block, less routine use in laparoscopic surgery; open-surgery ERAS use remains reasonable |
| **Spinal morphine** | Single shot, 12 to 24 hours analgesia | Short, side effects, delayed respiratory depression |
| **Rectus sheath catheters / wound infusion** | Effective somatic analgesia, opioid sparing, bleeding risk depends on site/depth and antithrombotics | No visceral coverage, leak, requires surgeon |
| **TAP, quadratus lumborum, erector spinae blocks** | Alternatives avoiding epidural sympathectomy in selected patients | Variable coverage; deep sites are not automatically safe with anticoagulation; LAST risk |
| **IV lidocaine infusion** | Possible selected adjunct without neuraxial bleeding risk | Benefit uncertain; ALLEGRO negative in minimally invasive colon surgery; **do not overlap with active regional/infiltrated LA** |
| **IV PCA opioid** | Universally available | Sedation, nausea, ileus, respiratory depression |
| **Adjuncts** | Paracetamol, NSAID (if safe), ketamine, dexamethasone, gabapentinoid only for a specific established indication, not routine initiation | Drug-specific risks |

## Preop

For this **open resection**, discuss TEA versus a catheter/block-based alternative, considering incision, cardiopulmonary risk, anticoagulation, patient preference and service capability. TEA is a strong option, not a universal requirement, and ERAS alone is not a reason to omit it.

## Intraop

If suitable, site a thoracic epidural covering the incision, with careful haemodynamic management and a rescue plan. Otherwise choose rectus-sheath/wound catheters or a suitable fascial block **plus systemic analgesia for visceral pain**. Do **not** add IV lignocaine to active regional LA. ALLEGRO does not establish benefit in open surgery and directly argues against promising improved recovery in minimally invasive colon surgery.

## Postop

Use appropriate regular non-opioids, PONV prophylaxis and titrated rescue opioid/PCA. Review pain, function, BP, motor block and complications daily with the pain service. Remove catheters when no longer beneficial, after planning oral transition and **drug-specific anticoagulant timing**, rather than at a mandatory 48–72 hours. Support early mobilisation, feeding and discharge planning.

For open surgery, a thorough discussion also identifies the conditions in which the planned epidural or abdominal wall technique may fail to provide the expected functional benefit. Consent includes the possibility of hypotension, motor block or incomplete visceral coverage. Treat rescue requirements as part of the pathway and track ability to cough and mobilise.

For emergency laparotomy, the 2025 Blue Book emphasises dynamic analgesia and organ reserve. Shock, sepsis, coagulopathy and the risk of sympathectomy can change the preferred technique or monitoring level. Reassess once source control and haemodynamics improve.

**Sources:** Evidence · historical [Blue Book 2017 TEA/lignocaine chapters](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-(the-blue-book)); [ALLEGRO](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2827435?resultClick=1); [lignocaine safety consensus](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.15270).

## Self-marking checklist

- Lists epidural, spinal morphine, wound/rectus sheath, fascial blocks, lidocaine, PCA
- Gives strengths and limitations of each
- Chooses the epidural for open surgery with justification
- Identifies alternative when epidural is contraindicated
- Includes multimodal adjuncts
- Mentions ERAS context
- Follow-up with acute pain service
- Adapts the strategy for shock, sepsis or coagulopathy if surgery is urgent

[ANZCA Blue Book 2025, emergency laparotomy analgesia and non-obstetric surgery in pregnancy](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305) · [ASA perioperative regional analgesia guideline 2026](https://doi.org/10.1097/ALN.0000000000005790)

items.title: 4. Comparing opioids and choosing one in renal impairment
items.q: Compare the opioids commonly used for acute pain after major surgery and justify your choice of opioid for a patient with renal impairment.
items.a:
## Comparison

| Opioid | Features | Cautions |
|---|---|---|
| **Morphine** | Standard; active metabolite **M6G** (analgesic) and M3G | **Accumulation in renal failure** (sedation, respiratory depression), histamine release |
| **Oxycodone** | Good oral bioavailability, predictable; popular for acute pain | Some active metabolites; reduce dose in renal and hepatic failure |
| **Hydromorphone** | Potent; oral and IV conversion ratios differ. **H3G accumulates in renal impairment and can cause neuroexcitation** | Reduce dose/extend interval, monitor for toxicity; high risk of dosing errors when interchanged with morphine |
| **Fentanyl** | Short-acting IV (PCA, titration); no active metabolites | Context-sensitive accumulation, chest wall rigidity; patches inappropriate in acute pain |
| **Alfentanil/remifentanil** | Short-acting, intraoperative | Remifentanil hyperalgesia; needs transition analgesia |
| **Tramadol/tapentadol** | Tramadol: μ plus serotonin/noradrenaline; tapentadol: μ plus mainly noradrenaline reuptake inhibition | Serotonin syndrome (tramadol), seizures; tapentadol less data |
| **Methadone** | Long half-life, NMDA antagonism, no active metabolites | QT, accumulation, specialist use |
| **Pethidine** | Not recommended: **norpethidine** causes seizures; poor analgesic | Avoid, particularly in renal failure |
| **Codeine** | Weak, variable (CYP2D6) | Avoid in renal impairment |

## Choice in renal impairment

- **Fentanyl** is often preferred for monitored parenteral acute analgesia because it lacks active renally cleared metabolites. **Hydromorphone or oxycodone** may be used cautiously with reduced doses/longer intervals; neither is free of renal accumulation/toxicity. **Methadone or buprenorphine** require an appropriate specialist plan and are not simple ward substitutes.
- **Avoid**: morphine (accumulation of M6G/M3G), **codeine**, **pethidine**, and tramadol at high doses.
- **Principles**: start low, titrate to effect, extend dosing intervals, **combine with multimodal and regional analgesia**, monitor sedation and respiratory rate, and review regularly.
- **Adjuncts**: paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs with AKI, hypovolaemia or advanced CKD; assess any short course in milder stable CKD individually; consider regional block.

Distinguish an isolated monitored IV rescue dose from an infusion or a repeated oral course. In advanced kidney disease a carefully titrated IV fentanyl dose can suit a monitored setting, while repeated exposure still requires reassessment and oral discharge planning. Examine renal trend and dialysis timing, other sedatives, prior opioid response and respiratory risk. Watch for neuroexcitation as well as sedation, especially with accumulated metabolites. The choice depends on acuity, route and follow-up. Discuss longer-term options with the acute pain team before prescribing a long-acting formulation or sending the patient home.

**Sources:** Evidence · [ANZCA acute pain evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence). Compare route, duration, active metabolites and monitoring; equianalgesic tables are approximate and not a substitute for titration.

## Self-marking checklist

- Compares opioids with strengths and weaknesses
- Notes the renal accumulation of M6G/M3G
- Chooses fentanyl, hydromorphone or oxycodone with justification
- Avoids morphine, codeine and pethidine
- Dose reduction and extended interval
- Multimodal and regional strategies
- Monitoring and review

[ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: 5. NSAIDs in the perioperative period
items.q: Evaluate the use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in the perioperative period.
items.a:
## Mechanism and effect

NSAIDs inhibit **cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2)**, reducing prostaglandin production (peripheral sensitisation, inflammation, fever). They give **good analgesia for mild to moderate pain** and **reduce opioid consumption**, with magnitude depending on drug, operation and background regimen (and opioid-related side effects such as nausea). Selective **COX-2 inhibitors** (celecoxib, parecoxib) largely spare platelet function and reduce, **but do not abolish**, GI ulcer/bleeding risk; renal and cardiovascular risks remain.

## Benefits

- Opioid sparing; effective for **musculoskeletal, dental, gynaecological and orthopaedic** surgery.
- Simple, oral or IV; useful in **day surgery**.

## Risks and cautions

| System | Risk |
|---|---|
| **Renal** | AKI (reduced afferent perfusion), especially with hypovolaemia, CKD, ACE inhibitors/ARBs and diuretics ("triple whammy") |
| **GI** | Ulceration and bleeding (non-selective), elderly, steroids, anticoagulants |
| **Bleeding** | Platelet inhibition (reversible with non-selective NSAIDs) |
| **Cardiovascular** | Increased risk of MI and stroke (COX-2 and high-dose diclofenac); hypertension and fluid retention; **contraindicated after CABG**; heart failure |
| **Respiratory** | **NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease** in some asthmatics |
| **Other** | Possible effects on **bone and anastomotic healing** (controversial, limited evidence), hyperkalaemia, pregnancy (avoid unless compelling benefit in early pregnancy; fetal renal/oligohydramnios risk from about 20 weeks; contraindicated in the third trimester under NZ guidance) |

## Preop

Assess risk and agree whether an NSAID is appropriate.

- Use **at the lowest dose for the shortest time** with a defined review/stop date, often only a few days, after assessing risk (renal function, volume status, age, cardiac disease, bleeding risk, asthma).
- Give with food; consider **gastric protection** in at-risk patients.
- Avoid in **AKI, hypovolaemia, advanced CKD, decompensated heart failure, active ulcer/bleeding, relevant hypersensitivity or unacceptable procedure-specific risk**. Stable mild CKD needs individual assessment rather than a blanket prohibition. Anastomotic concerns are drug/procedure dependent (notably diclofenac in some colorectal data); agree the plan with the surgeon.
- COX-2 inhibitors are an option where bleeding or GI risk is key, but with cardiac risk.

## Intraop

Confirm adequate perfusion/volume status and no duplicative NSAID dosing. Choose a route and timing consistent with the operation, bleeding risk and product guidance.

## Postop

Reassess renal function, bleeding, GI symptoms and ongoing need; stop promptly with dehydration/AKI or other harm. Provide a clear stop date at discharge.

## Conclusion

NSAIDs are valuable adjuncts in a multimodal plan for selected patients, with careful screening for renal, cardiac, GI and bleeding risk.

**Sources:** Evidence · [BJA Education NSAID review, 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10591119/); [Medsafe pregnancy advice](https://www.medsafe.govt.nz/profs/PUArticles/September2022/Non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory%20drugs-NSAIDs-avoid-use%20in-pregnancy.html).

## Self-marking checklist

- Mechanism and effect (COX-1/COX-2)
- Opioid-sparing benefit and settings of use
- Renal risk and the triple whammy
- GI and bleeding risk
- Cardiovascular risk and the CABG contraindication
- Asthma
- Practical rules: lowest dose and shortest duration, screening
- COX-2 selectivity and a balanced conclusion

[ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: 6. Opioid tolerance, physical dependence and opioid-induced hyperalgesia
items.q: Distinguish opioid tolerance, physical dependence and opioid-induced hyperalgesia, and outline their relevance to acute pain management.
items.a:
## Definitions

- **Tolerance**: a reduced response to the same dose with time, requiring more drug for the same effect; due to receptor desensitisation, downregulation and NMDA-mediated changes.
- **Physical dependence**: withdrawal symptoms when the drug is stopped or an antagonist is given (sweating, tachycardia, diarrhoea, yawning, anxiety, piloerection).
- **Opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH)**: **paradoxically increased pain sensitivity** (and allodynia) from opioid exposure; the pain may be diffuse, spread beyond the original site and **worsen with increasing doses**. It is mediated by **NMDA receptor activation and central sensitisation**, microglial activation, and descending facilitation.
- **Addiction**: a behavioural disorder (compulsive use despite harm), distinct from the first two.

## Distinguishing tolerance from OIH

| | Tolerance | OIH |
|---|---|---|
| Possible response to more opioid | May improve | May fail to improve or worsen; **not a diagnostic challenge test** |
| Pain quality | As original | Diffuse, new areas, allodynia |
| Management | Individualised rescue plus multimodal care; reassess cause | Specialist-guided reduction/rotation and selected adjuncts; avoid abrupt withdrawal |

**First exclude worsening pathology, inadequate delivery and withdrawal.** OIH is a clinical consideration without a simple validated bedside diagnostic test; tolerance, withdrawal-associated pain and OIH can coexist.

## Relevance

- **Intraoperative**: high-dose **remifentanil** is associated with acute tolerance and hyperalgesia; use lower doses, plan transition analgesia with multimodal drugs and regional blocks.
- **Opioid-tolerant patients** (chronic opioid use, buprenorphine, methadone) usually need an agreed **baseline-opioid continuation/replacement plan** to avoid withdrawal, plus titrated short-acting rescue and appropriate regional/non-opioid therapy. Adjust for toxicity, route and organ function; do not indiscriminately add lignocaine to blocks or gabapentinoids to a sedating regimen.
- **Management of OIH**: reduce or rotate the opioid, **ketamine** (NMDA antagonist), alpha-2 agonists, methadone, and non-opioid adjuncts; avoid reflex dose escalation when pain worsens.
- Monitor for **withdrawal**, sedation and respiratory depression.

Review timing and distribution before attributing worsening pain to an opioid effect. A new focal surgical finding warrants examination and investigation. Confirm baseline treatment and recent doses, look for withdrawal symptoms and establish functional goals. Management may require opioid stewardship, an appropriate non-opioid or regional plan, targeted dose adjustment with pain input and repeated monitoring rather than switching agents on the basis of pain severity alone.

Labelling a patient tolerant or dependent does not explain a sudden increase in postoperative pain. Evaluate the operation, withdrawal, missed baseline treatment and complications before escalating.

**Sources:** Evidence · [ANZCA acute pain evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence); [perioperative buprenorphine guidance](https://asra.com/the-asra-family/trainees/trainee-videos/videos/guidelines/2021/08/12/buprenorphine-management-in-the-perioperative-period).

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines tolerance, dependence, hyperalgesia and addiction
- Explains mechanisms (NMDA, central sensitisation)
- Distinguishes tolerance from OIH clinically
- Describes remifentanil and intraoperative opioid use
- Plans for opioid-tolerant patients (continue baseline)
- Manages OIH (reduce opioid, ketamine, alpha-2 agonist)
- Monitors for withdrawal and respiratory depression

[Australian Acute Pain Opioid Analgesic Stewardship Clinical Care Standard](https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/clinical-care-standards/opioid-analgesic-stewardship-acute-pain)

items.title: 7. Buprenorphine maintenance and major abdominal surgery
items.q: A patient maintained on buprenorphine for opioid use disorder requires major abdominal surgery. Outline your perioperative pain plan and justify whether you would stop buprenorphine.
items.a:
## Preop

Confirm indication, formulation, daily dose, last dose, adherence, other opioid/sedative use and the usual prescriber. Assess current pain, renal/hepatic function, OSA, prior perioperative experience, withdrawal/relapse risk and patient goals. Involve acute pain and addiction services early, with a written plan agreed with the patient.

Buprenorphine is a high-affinity **partial μ agonist**, not an antagonist equivalent to naltrexone. It can make added full-agonist dosing more challenging, but adequate analgesia remains possible. The multisociety recommendation is **not to routinely discontinue or taper maintenance buprenorphine**, because interruption can destabilise treatment and increase recurrence/overdose risk. Any exceptional high-dose adjustment should be specialist-led and shared with the patient/prescriber, not a routine instruction to stop for several days.

## Intraop

Continue the agreed maintenance regimen. Use an effective **regional or neuraxial technique** when appropriate and a procedure-specific non-opioid plan (paracetamol, NSAID if safe; selected ketamine). Do not stack sedating adjuncts or combine active regional LA with IV lignocaine analgesia.

If additional opioid is required, titrate a **high-affinity full agonist such as fentanyl or hydromorphone** with appropriate observation; requirements may exceed those of an opioid-naive patient. High receptor affinity does not mean full agonists can never work. Avoid a fixed opioid multiplier or unmonitored escalation.

## Postop

Continue maintenance treatment and multimodal analgesia. With specialist agreement, dividing the daily buprenorphine dose can improve analgesic coverage; temporary dose changes depend on formulation and the overall plan. Provide titrated rescue full agonist/PCA when needed, with dose and monitoring matched to tolerance and risk. Its respiratory-depression ceiling does **not** make concurrent opioid/benzodiazepine use safe.

Monitor pain, function, sedation/ventilation, withdrawal and craving; investigate unexpectedly severe pain rather than attributing everything to buprenorphine. Plan transition off additional acute opioids as pain improves, and return to the agreed maintenance schedule. Ensure discharge supply, direct handover to the usual prescriber, follow-up and overdose/naloxone education. Do not discharge with buprenorphine inadvertently omitted or a prolonged new full-agonist regimen without a stop plan.

Ask about the maintenance dose, dosing interval and indication, and plan to maintain access to medication during fasting and admission. Agree who will supervise supplements and communicate the resulting outpatient plan to the prescriber before discharge.

**Sources:** Evidence · [2021 multisociety perioperative buprenorphine recommendations](https://asra.com/the-asra-family/trainees/trainee-videos/videos/guidelines/2021/08/12/buprenorphine-management-in-the-perioperative-period). This stem concerns established treatment for opioid use disorder, not routine commencement of a postoperative patch.

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies maintenance indication, formulation/dose and the usual prescriber
- Explains partial agonism/high affinity and distinguishes naltrexone
- Does not routinely stop/taper maintenance treatment; balances relapse/overdose risk
- Uses Preop / Intraop / Postop with regional/non-opioid options
- Allows titrated high-affinity full-agonist rescue under monitoring
- Discusses specialist divided dosing rather than a universal dose change
- Includes sedation/respiratory, withdrawal and craving assessment
- Provides additional-opioid taper and explicit maintenance/discharge handover

[ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: 8. Converting a PCA to oral analgesia and planning discharge
items.q: On day two after uncomplicated abdominal surgery, a patient with stable renal function is mobilising and tolerating oral fluids. Outline how you would convert their morphine PCA to oral analgesia and plan safe discharge.
items.a:
## Assess readiness

Confirm improving pain, useful sleep and function, oral intake and absorption, stable observations, no escalating surgical concern and no unresolved opioid toxicity. Review the wound, pain at rest and on movement, adverse effects, bowel function and renal/hepatic status. Check whether opioid use before surgery affects the plan. Ask what pain control the patient needs for mobilisation and what support they have at home. High PCA use, a sudden new pain or unreliable absorption should prompt reassessment before conversion.

## Convert to a safe oral plan

Review actual PCA deliveries and other opioids over a representative 24-hour period, including recent trends and clinician-administered doses. Demands recorded by the pump are not doses delivered. Use the local equivalence reference and pharmacist or pain service if the route or drug changes. As an illustrative estimate only, 18 mg IV morphine may correspond to about 54 mg oral morphine using a 1:3 IV-to-oral ratio in a local reference. That estimate is not a prescription. Requirements usually decline as surgical pain improves. Use a lower initial regimen with titrated immediate-release rescue, especially with frailty, sedation, renal dysfunction or when rotating to a different opioid with incomplete cross-tolerance. Equation-derived doses should be reconciled against the patient at the bedside.

Continue regular non-opioids as appropriate, such as paracetamol and a short course of an NSAID if suitable. Choose an oral immediate-release opioid with a clear dose and interval only if needed. Define how the first oral dose and cessation of the pump will be coordinated so there is neither stacked opioid dosing nor an unplanned analgesic gap. Stop duplicate rescue prescriptions and notify nursing staff when switching. Recheck within the expected onset of effect, and review again during mobilisation. Check sedation, ventilation, nausea and constipation and provide an escalation plan if pain is uncontrolled.

## Discharge and follow-up

Discharge when the oral regimen provides adequate function with acceptable adverse effects. Explain the short expected course, taper or stop plan, safe storage and disposal, and avoidance of alcohol or unadvised sedatives. Prescribe only a necessary quantity. Give written instructions for severe or unexpected pain, marked sedation, breathing difficulty and who to contact for review. Communicate any ongoing opioid prescription, rationale and review date to the patient and usual prescriber.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence) · [Australian Acute Pain Opioid Analgesic Stewardship Clinical Care Standard](https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/clinical-care-standards/opioid-analgesic-stewardship-acute-pain)

## Self-marking checklist

- Checks oral absorption, pain trajectory, function and adverse effects
- Uses actual PCA delivery and all other opioids
- Explains conversion limitations and cautious titration
- Coordinates first oral dose, pump cessation and avoidance of duplication
- Reassesses activity, ventilation and adverse effects
- Provides a discharge stop plan, quantities and follow-up

items.title: 9. Opioid-induced respiratory depression on the ward
items.q: Describe the risk factors for opioid-induced respiratory depression on the ward and outline your management of a patient on PCA who is found drowsy with a respiratory rate of 6.
items.a:
## Risk factors

- **Patient**: age over 65, OSA and obesity, respiratory, renal or hepatic disease, opioid-naive, head injury, hypovolaemia.
- **Drug and prescribing**: background infusion, **PCA by proxy**, concurrent sedatives (benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids, alcohol), long-acting opioids, errors in programming or syringe change, neuraxial opioid together with systemic opioid.
- **System**: inadequate monitoring, ward and night-time.

## Management of the drowsy patient with a rate of 6

- **1.** **Stop the PCA** (clamp the line, remove the handset), call an **urgent medical emergency response now**: drowsiness with RR 6 is already dangerous. Preserve access, isolate opioid delivery safely and **do not flush retained opioid in the line** into the patient.
- **2.** **ABC**: open the airway (jaw thrust, airway adjunct), **100% oxygen**, assist ventilation with a bag-mask if needed.
