- **3.** **Naloxone**: 40 to 100 micrograms IV every 2 minutes titrated to adequate ventilation, airway patency and consciousness (aim for adequate breathing, not full reversal); consider **infusion or repeat dosing** because naloxone lasts 30 to 60 minutes and the opioid effect may outlast it; avoid unnecessary abrupt full reversal in a breathing opioid-dependent patient (withdrawal, severe pain and sympathetic effects). **Apnoea, profound hypoxaemia or impending arrest requires immediate ventilation and larger resuscitative naloxone doses as needed**; small-dose titration must not delay rescue.
- **4.** **Check** glucose, pulse oximetry and capnography, ABG if needed, and look for other causes (sedatives, hypercapnia, stroke, hypoxia, sepsis).
- **5.** **Look for causes in the system**: pump settings, syringe concentration, programming error, background rate, other opioids, renal function.
- **6.** Monitor on a higher dependency level, restart analgesia with a **reduced regimen** or a different technique, and inform the acute pain service.
- **7.** **Report** the incident and review.

## Prevention

Standard concentrations and order forms, no routine background infusion, **sedation scoring and respiratory rate** with set frequencies, appropriate continuous oximetry/capnography for risk, and education. Supplemental oxygen treats hypoxaemia but can conceal hypoventilation on SpO2; normal saturation on oxygen does not prove safe ventilation.

Do not rely on a reassuring SpO₂ on oxygen or wait for desaturation. Assign someone to support ventilation and call the response team, then review recent pump deliveries, clinician boluses and other sedatives, including neuraxial opioid. After apparent improvement consider renarcotisation, confirm repeated observations and review the original prescription before any opioid is restarted.

**Sources:** Evidence · [BJA Education, Opioid-induced respiratory depression, 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.12.007); [ANZCA PS41](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/558316c5-ea93-457c-b51f-d57556b0ffa7/PS41-Guideline-on-acute-pain-management).

## Self-marking checklist

- Patient, drug and system risk factors
- Stops the PCA and calls for help
- Supports the airway and breathing with oxygen
- Titrates naloxone with doses and duration of action
- Looks for other causes and programming errors
- Monitors, modifies analgesia and involves the pain service
- Reports the incident
- Prevention through monitoring and standardisation

[ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence) · [Australian Acute Pain Opioid Analgesic Stewardship Clinical Care Standard](https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/clinical-care-standards/opioid-analgesic-stewardship-acute-pain)

items.title: 10. The acute pain service: structure, role and benefits
items.q: Discuss the structure, role and benefits of an acute pain service in a hospital.
items.a:
## Structure

An **anaesthetist-led, multidisciplinary** service: a medical lead, **clinical nurse specialist(s)**, and pharmacist, with links to surgeons, ward nursing, psychology and physiotherapy. It requires **24-hour availability** (or on-call), defined referral criteria, written protocols, and links to the pain clinic, addiction and palliative services.

## Roles

- **Management of high-risk patients**: epidurals, regional catheters, PCA, ketamine and lidocaine infusions, opioid-tolerant or addicted patients, complex or neuropathic pain, trauma and major surgery.
- **Standardisation** of orders, monitoring, equipment, drug concentrations and protocols (for example, PCA order form, epidural management, treatment of side effects).
- **Daily review** of patients, with advice on analgesia, adjuvants, opioid weaning, and discharge planning.
- **Education** of nursing, medical and surgical staff and patients.
- **Safety and quality**: incident review, audit of pain scores, side effects and outcomes; guideline updates; **opioid stewardship** and discharge prescribing.
- **Persistent-pain risk management**: identify risk, optimise recovery and arrange early referral. Service involvement does not guarantee prevention of persistent pain.
- **Research** and quality improvement.

## Benefits

- Better **pain relief and patient satisfaction**, fewer side effects and complications (for example, fewer high-risk events with epidural and PCA).
- Earlier mobilisation and possibly shorter stay; safe use of advanced techniques.
- Improved knowledge and culture around pain, with a lower risk of opioid-related harm.

## Challenges

Resources and funding, staffing after hours, role clarity with the ward team, and demonstrating clear outcome improvements.

Define activation and handover at PACU discharge, after hours and in a stand-alone facility. Use ward eligibility criteria, clear charting and pharmacy-approved solutions. Agree who can initiate, modify and discontinue each technique, and design observation frequency and adverse-effect triggers around expected risk. A patient with unexpected weakness, marked sedation, poor ventilation or uncontrolled pain should have a reliable route to senior help. Scope covers transition to oral and discharge analgesic stewardship. Monitor functional outcomes, patient experience, naloxone use, rescue team calls, catheter complications, medication errors and prescribing on discharge. Review incidents with nursing, pharmacy, medical and surgical teams, feed results back and repeat measurement after the change. Include competence assessment, scenario training and accessible patient information for people needing interpreters or other communication support.

For a patient able to self-dose, PCA matches a fluctuating analgesic need and permits review of actual use. A background infusion increases exposure and monitoring needs. An independently prescribed continuous infusion requires a separate indication, a suitable monitored setting and specialist review. Intermittent oral or monitored IV dosing is useful for predictable pain or when a patient cannot manage a PCA, with reassessment between doses.

**Sources:** Evidence · [ANZCA PS41 acute pain statement](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/558316c5-ea93-457c-b51f-d57556b0ffa7/PS41-Guideline-on-acute-pain-management).

## Self-marking checklist

- Multidisciplinary, anaesthetist-led structure with nursing
- 24-hour availability and protocols
- Management of high-risk therapies (epidural, PCA, catheters)
- Standardisation, safety and audit
- Education of staff and patients
- Prevention of persistent pain and stewardship
- Benefits to patients and hospital
- Limitations and resource issues
- Compares patient-controlled delivery with continuous opioid infusion

[ANZCA acute pain statement PS41](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/558316c5-ea93-457c-b51f-d57556b0ffa7/PS41-Guideline-on-acute-pain-management) · [ANZCA professional documents including PS45 and PG67](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents)

items.title: 11. Epidural analgesia for open colorectal surgery and the epidural that is not working
items.q: A 65-year-old man has an epidural for open colorectal surgery. Discuss the indications, risks and benefits of postoperative epidural analgesia, and your approach to the epidural that is not working.
items.a:
## Indications and benefits

Thoracic epidural analgesia (TEA) with local anaesthetic (± opioid) suits **major open abdominal and thoracic surgery**, **rib fractures**, and patients with severe respiratory disease. Benefits: **superior dynamic analgesia**, fewer **pulmonary complications**, earlier return of bowel function, reduced opioid, and attenuation of the stress response. In modern **ERAS** pathways with laparoscopic surgery, the benefit is smaller and TEA may be omitted.

## Risks

- **Hypotension** (sympathetic block), motor block, urinary retention, pruritus and nausea (opioid).
- **Failure or incomplete coverage**: frequency varies with definition, technique and service; have a rescue plan.
- **Catheter-related**: dural puncture (headache), intravascular or intrathecal migration (toxicity, high block), **epidural haematoma** (rare but catastrophic; risk varies markedly by population, traumatic placement and antithrombotic exposure), **abscess**, nerve injury.
- Disconnect, local anaesthetic toxicity, and delayed mobilisation.

## The epidural that is not working

- **1.** **Assess**: check pain, block (cold/pinprick) level and distribution, catheter depth at skin, site, pump, connections, infusion running; **exclude surgical causes**.
- **2.** **First exclude red flags:** new weakness, severe back pain, fever, high block or systemic toxicity requires stopping infusion and urgent assessment, **not a test bolus**. If safe, a trained clinician may give a fractionated protocol-based bolus after checking aspiration, recent dose, BP and monitoring/resuscitation readiness. Repositioning or limited sterile withdrawal may help selected unilateral blocks; do not advance an externally exposed catheter back through the skin.
- **3.** **No block at all**: consider dislodgement, pump/connection error, wrong space or ineffective delivery. Replace only if indicated and safe after reviewing antithrombotic timing, infection risk and total LA exposure.
- **4.** **Pain outside the covered dermatomes:** reassess catheter level and whether the technique can cover the incision; repeated large boluses will not reliably rescue a catheter at the wrong level.
- **5.** **Rescue**: add **systemic multimodal analgesia** (paracetamol, PCA) or alternative regional techniques (paravertebral, erector spinae, TAP/rectus sheath).
- **6.** **Convert** to an alternative technique when repeated top-ups fail, considering anticoagulation; document and review by the pain service.

Before changing the infusion check whether the patient has a unilateral, patchy or absent block and whether the deficit matches the incision and catheter level. Review sites, tubing, drug delivery and anticoagulation. New severe back pain or motor deficit changes the pathway to urgent review rather than a routine test bolus. If hypotension limits efficacy, reassess volume, surgical causes and options for alternative analgesia.

**Sources:** Evidence · historical [Blue Book 2017 TEA chapter](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-(the-blue-book)); [ASRA antithrombotic guidance](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39880411/). Benefits depend on the operation, alternatives and service quality; ERAS does not automatically exclude TEA for open surgery.

## Self-marking checklist

- States indications and benefits (dynamic analgesia, respiratory outcomes)
- Notes reduced role in ERAS and laparoscopic surgery
- Lists risks: hypotension, failure, headache, haematoma, abscess
- Explains variable bleeding risk without an unsupported universal incidence
- Assesses a failing epidural systematically (block, catheter, pump)
- Uses bolus, repositioning, withdrawal and replacement
- Provides alternative analgesia
- Documents and involves the pain service

[ANZCA Blue Book 2017, Deacon and Hartley on thoracic epidural analgesia](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [ASRA antithrombotics and regional anaesthesia](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39880411/)

items.title: 12. New back pain and leg weakness with a thoracic epidural
items.q: A patient with a thoracic epidural infusion reports new back pain and leg weakness on day 2. Outline your assessment and management.
items.a:
## Recognition and differential

**New back pain plus leg weakness during an epidural is a spinal-compression emergency until excluded.** Epidural haematoma and abscess must be considered urgently. Other causes include excessive/misplaced LA, intrathecal/subdural migration, cord ischaemia, pre-existing spinal pathology and peripheral/positioning injury. The combination of pain and a new motor deficit must not be dismissed as expected LA block.

## Immediate assessment and actions

- **1.** **Stop the epidural infusion; do not give a bolus.** Call the senior anaesthetist/acute pain service and obtain **immediate spinal/neurosurgical advice**. Stabilise ABC, oxygenation and perfusion; record onset and progression precisely.
- **2.** Document motor power, sensory level/distribution, reflexes, bladder/bowel dysfunction and back/catheter-site findings. Check fever/sepsis and vital signs. Repeat examinations while arranging imaging; **do not wait 1–2 hours for block regression** before referral or imaging.
- **3.** Review insertion difficulties, prior neurology, catheter migration, all LA doses and **exact anticoagulant/antiplatelet doses and times**, including renal function. Check FBC/platelets and coagulation; inflammatory markers/blood cultures if infection suspected. Tests must not delay imaging.

## Imaging and definitive management

- Arrange **emergency MRI of the relevant spinal region**, extending coverage if the level is uncertain or abscess extent requires it. If MRI is unavailable/contraindicated, urgently discuss CT/alternative imaging and transfer with the spinal service; waiting for an ideal scan must not create avoidable delay.
- **Haematoma:** urgent decompression when indicated and coordinated reversal/correction of coagulopathy. Neurological recovery worsens with delay—aim for diagnosis and surgery as rapidly as possible, preferably within hours. Published 8–12-hour windows are **not permission to wait**.
- **Abscess:** obtain blood cultures without delaying treatment; start appropriate IV antibiotics (including staphylococcal/MRSA cover as locally indicated) and discuss urgent drainage, particularly with neurological deficit or compression.
- **Catheter removal is not automatic before assessment**: coordinate imaging, removal and anticoagulant reversal with the anaesthetic/spinal teams. Removal itself has bleeding implications. Culture a removed catheter if infection is suspected, but do not delay definitive care for a tip specimen.

## Ongoing care and prevention

Frequent documented neurological assessment, appropriate higher-acuity care and an alternative analgesic plan. Explain the event to the patient, document decisions/times and provide open disclosure and incident review.

Prevent through asepsis, careful selection, drug-specific antithrombotic intervals for both insertion **and removal**, and observations that reliably detect new weakness/back pain. Dilute LA may facilitate examination, but no monitoring regimen eliminates risk.

**Sources:** Evidence · [ASRA neurological complication advisory](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2869280/); [ASRA antithrombotic guideline, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39880411/).

## Self-marking checklist

- Treats new pain plus weakness as an emergency, with haematoma/abscess in the differential
- Stops infusion and avoids a further bolus
- Calls senior anaesthesia and spinal/neurosurgical teams immediately
- Documents onset and full neurological/bladder findings
- Reviews anticoagulants, renal function, platelets and coagulation
- Obtains emergency imaging without waiting for LA regression
- Coordinates urgent decompression or antibiotics/drainage and safe catheter handling
- Includes repeated assessment, alternative analgesia, disclosure and prevention

[ASRA antithrombotics and regional anaesthesia](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39880411/) · [ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: 13. Neuraxial opioids and their monitoring
items.q: Compare the neuraxial opioids used for postoperative analgesia and describe the monitoring required.
items.a:
## Physicochemical principles

Lipid solubility influences CSF persistence, systemic uptake, onset, duration and rostral spread. It is a continuum, not a simple binary classification. Hydrophilic **morphine** persists in CSF and can cause delayed ventilatory depression; lipophilic **fentanyl/sufentanil** act rapidly with shorter single-dose effects and more uptake into tissues/blood.

## Agents and use

| Agent | Typical use/examples | Key distinctions |
|---|---|---|
| **Morphine** | Preservative-free IT doses often 50–150 micrograms for obstetric/arthroplasty protocols; selected major surgery uses 100–300 micrograms. Epidural dosing is in **mg**, commonly low single-digit doses under protocol. | Prolonged early postoperative analgesia, commonly 12–24 h; early **and delayed** respiratory risk, pruritus, PONV, retention. |
| **Fentanyl** | IT commonly 10–25 micrograms with LA; epidural bolus or dilute LA–opioid infusion. | Lipophilic; rapid onset and shorter bolus effect. Continuous infusion remains a continuing risk and needs monitoring throughout. |
| **Diamorphine** | Used neuraxially in some UK pathways; dose is procedure/protocol specific. | **Lipophilic prodrug**, converted to active 6-monoacetylmorphine and then morphine; not itself a hydrophilic opioid. Duration/monitoring cannot be inferred solely from the parent drug. |
| **Hydromorphone** | Selected neuraxial use where available under specialist protocol. | Intermediate lipid solubility; duration/rostral spread between the extremes. Verify formulation and protocol. |

LA and neuraxial opioids can be synergistic, allowing lower doses. LA contributes hypotension and motor block; opioid contributes sedation, pruritus, PONV and respiratory impairment. No preparation should be used neuraxially without checking formulation/preservatives.

## General adult monitoring

Assess **consciousness/sedation, ventilation (rate, depth, apnoea/obstruction) and oxygenation**, alongside pain, block level, BP and bladder function. Higher-risk patients or concurrent systemic depressants need more intensive/longer surveillance.

- **Single hydrophilic opioid (e.g. morphine): ≥24 hours**, at least hourly for 12 hours, then every 2 hours for 12 hours.
- **Single lipophilic opioid (e.g. fentanyl): ≥2 hours**, continually for the first 20 minutes, then at least hourly until 2 hours; further observation depends on clinical condition and other drugs.
- **Continuous infusion/PCEA:** monitor for the entire infusion. The single-bolus schedule is not a stop point. Follow agent-specific guidance and local protocol, with increased surveillance after initiation/dose change and for risk factors.
- Low-dose obstetric morphine may have a **separate risk-stratified obstetric pathway**; do not generalise that reduced schedule to all adult surgical patients.

Supplemental oxygen can mask hypoventilation on oximetry. Use continuous monitoring/capnography where appropriate, trained staff and explicit escalation orders. Additional opioids/sedatives need an authorised plan. Respiratory depression requires airway/ventilatory support, urgent help and naloxone, sometimes repeated or infused; naloxone can wear off before neuraxial morphine.

**Sources:** Evidence · [ASA/ASRA neuraxial opioid respiratory-depression guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26655725/).

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains lipid solubility, uptake and rostral spread
- Compares agents without calling diamorphine hydrophilic
- Uses preservative-free formulation and distinguishes micrograms from epidural mg
- Includes early/delayed respiratory risk and other adverse effects
- States ≥24-hour hydrophilic and ≥2-hour single-lipophilic monitoring
- Continues observation throughout infusions/PCEA and adjusts for risk
- Assesses ventilation, consciousness and oxygenation rather than rate alone
- Includes additional-depressant precautions and rescue

[ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: 14. Hypotension when a thoracic epidural infusion is increased
items.q: After open abdominal surgery, a patient with a thoracic epidural becomes hypotensive when the infusion is increased for pain. Outline your assessment, management and revised analgesic plan.
items.a:
## Stabilise and diagnose

Call for help if unstable, confirm the BP reading and review ECG, heart rate, consciousness, oxygenation, ventilation and perfusion. Check the timing of the bolus or rate change, solution and dose, catheter level and recent observations. Pause or reduce the infusion while assessing the severity. Sympathetic blockade reduces venous return and vascular tone. Extensive block can affect cardiac accelerator fibres and cause bradycardia. Establish sensory level and motor power bilaterally. Dyspnoea, ascending weakness, severe bradycardia or impaired consciousness suggest an unexpectedly high block and require immediate airway and cardiovascular rescue.

Avoid anchoring on the epidural. Look for blood loss, hypovolaemia, sepsis, myocardial ischaemia, arrhythmia, anaphylaxis or medication effect. Review operation, drains, wound, fluid balance and recent medications. Check blood gas, haemoglobin, lactate, ECG and bedside ultrasound where indicated. Intravenous local anaesthetic exposure can cause toxicity if a catheter migrates into a vessel. Neurological symptoms, ventricular arrhythmia or unexplained collapse should trigger the relevant rescue pathway.

## Restore perfusion

Maintain oxygenation and ventilation. Give a small, reassessed fluid bolus when volume responsive or underfilled, and use blood and haemorrhage control if bleeding is likely. Avoid repeated empiric fluid boluses in a vasodilated or overloaded patient. Give an appropriate titrated vasopressor for sympathectomy, choosing according to heart rate, cardiac output and monitoring. Treat significant bradycardia early according to severity. Escalate to invasive monitoring or critical care if instability persists. Consider serious postoperative causes concurrently and ask the surgical team to review when indicated.

## Rebuild the analgesic plan

After stabilisation, assess surgical pathology, catheter site and depth, distribution and quality of block. Patchy or absent analgesia may reflect a displaced or unilateral catheter and should not prompt repeated unmonitored boluses. Use regular non-opioids where suitable and titrated opioid rescue with monitoring, avoiding duplicate routes or excessive sedation. Discuss restarting at a lower local anaesthetic concentration or rate only if findings and monitoring permit, or use an alternative regional or systemic plan. Review cumulative local anaesthetic exposure and anticoagulant timing if replacement or removal is considered. Record reassessment after any intervention, with explicit BP, sensory, motor and functional pain targets and escalation criteria. New focal deficit, severe back pain or sphincter symptoms requires urgent specialist investigation.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2017, Deacon and Hartley on thoracic epidural analgesia](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

## Self-marking checklist

- Confirms instability, assesses neuraxial extent and pauses the infusion as indicated
- Explains sympathectomy and considers other causes
- Provides tailored fluids, vasoactive support and escalation
- Recognises high block and toxicity red flags
- Rebuilds a safe multimodal plan without blind bolusing
- Defines monitoring, review and catheter decisions

items.title: 15. Continuous peripheral nerve catheters on the general ward
items.q: Discuss the benefits, risks and safe management of continuous peripheral nerve block catheters for postoperative analgesia on a general ward.
items.a:
## Benefits

- **Prolonged, targeted analgesia** (3 to 5 days or longer), with **opioid sparing**, fewer side effects, better rehabilitation (arthroplasty, amputation, shoulder surgery, rib fractures) and earlier discharge.
- Avoids some neuraxial effects such as bilateral sympathectomy; **deep plexus/deep peripheral blocks still require neuraxial antithrombotic precautions** and permits **ambulatory (home) use** in selected cases.

## Risks

- **Catheter problems**: displacement (common), kinking, leakage, failure of block, disconnection.
- **Local anaesthetic toxicity** (intravascular position, prolonged infusion, combined use with other blocks).
- **Motor block and falls**: quadriceps weakness with femoral catheters; pressure injury to an insensate limb; **masking compartment syndrome**.
- **Infection**, haematoma (rare), nerve injury.
- **Diaphragmatic paresis** with interscalene catheters.

## Safe management

- **Selection**: the patient able to understand the risks; exclude coagulopathy and infection at the site.
- **Technique**: ultrasound-guided placement, aseptic technique, secure fixation, and a documented tip position.
- **Infusion**: use **ropivacaine 0.2%** (or levobupivacaine 0.125 to 0.25%) at a site- and patient-specific prescribed rate (4–10 mL/h is an example range, not a universal safe rate) through a dedicated, labelled pump with a **bacterial filter** and avoiding Luer connections; set maximum **mg/hour and cumulative doses across all LA sources**. Do not combine with an IV lignocaine analgesic infusion. Use route-specific connectors where available.
- **Ward monitoring**: pain, sensory and motor block, sedation, vital signs and site checks at defined intervals; protocols for toxicity (stop, lipid emulsion) and **unexpected motor loss**.
- **Acute pain service** daily review; patient education (falls, limb protection, what to report).
- **Removal** when the pain is controlled, with oral analgesia established before cessation to reduce rebound pain; pharmacological tapering is not always required.
- **Compartment syndrome** suspicion: stop/reduce LA as part of an **immediate orthopaedic assessment**, with pressure measurement when needed and urgent decompression if diagnosed. Do not wait for block regression or a normal pulse to reassure you.
- **Home use:** only selected patients with a capable carer, written limb-protection/pump instructions, clear LAST/infection red flags, 24-hour contact and a reliable follow-up/removal plan.

Match the catheter to the incision, include a charted baseline sensory and motor examination and agree who reviews escalating pain. A loss of effect warrants checking pump, reservoir, line and site plus surgical examination. Reassess function after each approved change. Include additive local anaesthetic from infiltration or other blocks in the dose calculation.

**Sources:** Evidence · [ANZCA PS41](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/558316c5-ea93-457c-b51f-d57556b0ffa7/PS41-Guideline-on-acute-pain-management); [ASRA antithrombotic guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39880411/); [ASRA LAST checklist](https://asra.com/news-publications/asra-updates/blog-landing/guidelines/2020/11/01/checklist-for-treatment-of-local-anesthetic-systemic-toxicity).

## Self-marking checklist

- Benefits: prolonged analgesia, opioid sparing, rehabilitation
- Risks: displacement, toxicity, falls and motor block, infection
- Masking of compartment syndrome
- Patient selection
- Technique, infusion type and concentration
- Ward monitoring and acute pain service review
- Toxicity protocol
- Patient education and removal
- Checks function and dose exposure before and after adjusting a catheter

[ASRA antithrombotics and regional anaesthesia](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39880411/) · [ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: 16. Analgesia for a fractured femur before definitive surgery
items.q: A 30-year-old man with a fractured femur arrives in the emergency department in severe pain. Outline your approach to analgesia before definitive surgery.
items.a:
## Assessment and priorities

Treat as part of the **primary survey** (airway, breathing, circulation); pain control is part of resuscitation, but not at the expense of haemodynamics. Assess pain (numeric scale), associated injuries, neurovascular status, head injury, analgesia given, allergy, and the risk of **compartment syndrome**.

## Immediate measures

- **Splinting**; traction only for a suitable fracture after excluding associated pelvic/knee/other contraindicating injury, immobilisation, positioning, ice; reassurance.
- **Titrated IV opioid**: fentanyl 25 to 50 micrograms or morphine 2 to 3 mg every 3 to 5 minutes until pain is controlled; **intranasal fentanyl** or inhaled **methoxyflurane** or nitrous oxide as bridging.
- **Ketamine** 0.1 to 0.3 mg/kg IV (sub-dissociative) for opioid-sparing in the haemodynamically unstable or opioid-tolerant patient.
- **Paracetamol** IV 1 g; NSAIDs deferred if bleeding risk or renal injury.

## Regional analgesia (the preferred strategy)

- **Fascia iliaca block** or **femoral nerve block** (20 to 30 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine or 0.375% ropivacaine) under ultrasound in the ED: rapid relief and opioid sparing; delirium reduction evidence from older hip-fracture populations must not be assumed for a healthy 30-year-old femoral-shaft patient; give **before** moving the patient.
- Consider a **catheter** for ongoing pain. **PENG targets hip capsular pain and is not a general femoral-shaft block.** Calculate total LA in mg, accounting for weight, toxicity risks and any other LA rather than relying on volume alone.
- Document **neurovascular status before the block**, and avoid dense blocks if compartment syndrome is a concern (monitor and educate).

## Ongoing management

- Regular paracetamol, opioid by PCA or oral, antiemetic, and bowel care.
- Anticoagulation timing for neuraxial blocks; spinal or GA for fixation depending on stability.
- **Monitor for compartment syndrome** (pain out of proportion, paraesthesia, pain on passive stretch), and fat embolism.
- Acute pain service follow-up and a discharge plan.

Before and after applying traction or a block, document colour, temperature, pulses, sensation and power. Check for other injuries and use immobilisation and positioning as analgesic interventions. Record which pain remains on movement. If pain escalates or the examination changes, request urgent orthopaedic reassessment for compartment syndrome or bleeding even if pulses remain palpable. Do not use repeated boluses as an alternative to examination.

**Sources:** Evidence · [ANZCA acute pain evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence). Apply trauma and block safety principles to the actual fracture location; illustrative doses require weight/risk adjustment.

## Self-marking checklist

- Includes pain management within primary survey
- Splinting and positioning
- Titrated IV opioid with doses and alternatives (methoxyflurane, intranasal fentanyl)
- Ketamine as sub-dissociative option
- Fascia iliaca or femoral nerve block with local anaesthetic doses
- Neurovascular assessment and compartment syndrome awareness
- Multimodal ongoing analgesia
- Follow-up with the acute pain service

[Association of Anaesthetists regional analgesia and acute compartment syndrome guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9292897/) · [ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: 17. Sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis: analgesia and anaesthesia
items.q: A 24-year-old man with sickle cell disease presents with a vaso-occlusive crisis and severe limb pain. Outline your approach to analgesia and the anaesthetic issues if he requires surgery.
items.a:
## Pathophysiology and presentation

HbS polymerises when deoxygenated, causing **sickling, vaso-occlusion, haemolysis** and ischaemic pain (bone, chest, abdomen). Triggers: infection, dehydration, hypoxia, cold, stress, acidosis. Complications: **acute chest syndrome**, stroke, priapism, splenic sequestration, renal impairment.

## Analgesia (treat early and aggressively)

- **Rapid assessment**, usually using the patient's own report; check prior exposure rather than assuming tolerance; offer analgesia **within 30 minutes** of presentation and respect the individual pain plan.
- **Titrated IV opioid** (morphine 0.1 mg/kg or hydromorphone; fentanyl) every 15 to 30 minutes, then **PCA** with adequate bolus doses and monitoring; individualise to prior use; **avoid pethidine**.
- **Paracetamol** regularly, **NSAID** if renal function allows, **ketamine** in refractory pain, regional blocks for localised pain (cautiously).
- **Supportive**: oxygen if hypoxic (not routinely), warmth, **hydration** (avoid overload), treat infection, incentive spirometry (prevent chest syndrome), laxatives, antiemetics; haematology review. **Transfusion is not routine treatment for uncomplicated pain crisis**; severe acute chest syndrome, stroke or other specific complications may require simple/exchange transfusion.
- **Monitor** sedation and respiratory rate; consider an acute pain service.

## Anaesthetic considerations

- **Prevent sickling**: avoid hypoxia, hypothermia, dehydration, acidosis, venous stasis and tourniquets (use with caution).
- ### Preop

Haematology plan based on genotype, baseline Hb, previous complications and surgical risk. Where preoperative transfusion is appropriate, Hb around **90–110 g/L** is often targeted; avoid excessive Hb/hyperviscosity. **HbS <30% is not a universal target**: lower HbS targets are reserved for selected severe disease/high-risk surgery. Review organ function and minimise prolonged fasting with an individual fluid plan.
## Intraop

 warm, oxygenate, maintain euvolaemia and normocapnia, **regional anaesthesia** acceptable.
## Postop

Adequate analgesia, respiratory surveillance, oxygen **if hypoxaemic**, mobilisation/incentive spirometry and a low threshold to assess acute chest syndrome. Avoid overhydration and opioid oversedation while treating pain effectively.

A new oxygen requirement or fever prompts urgent reassessment for acute chest syndrome and other causes, with chest imaging and specialist involvement. Record baseline haemoglobin, previous crises, transfusion history and antibodies, and anticipate complex crossmatching if transfusion is considered. Adjust fluids to avoid dehydration and pulmonary oedema. Monitor pain, ventilation, sedation and function together, and reassess the diagnosis if pain differs from previous episodes. Include early escalation to haematology for neurological change, worsening hypoxia or suspected organ involvement.

**Sources:** Evidence · [NICE CG143 acute sickle pain recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg143/chapter/Recommendations); [ASH transfusion support guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6988392/).

## Self-marking checklist

- Pathophysiology and triggers
- Early, titrated opioid analgesia and PCA
- Avoids pethidine
- Adjuncts: paracetamol, ketamine, regional blocks
- Supportive care: hydration, oxygen, infection
- Anaesthetic prevention of sickling
- Transfusion and haematology input
- Postoperative monitoring for acute chest syndrome

[ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: 18. Acute herpes zoster pain and preventing post-herpetic neuralgia
items.q: A 71-year-old man presents with severe pain from acute herpes zoster involving the thoracic dermatomes. Discuss the options for the management of his acute pain and the prevention of post-herpetic neuralgia.
items.a:
## Background

Herpes zoster is reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the dorsal root ganglion, causing a **dermatomal vesicular rash with severe neuropathic and inflammatory pain**. Risk factors for **post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN)**: age over 50, severe acute pain, severe rash, prodromal pain, and ophthalmic involvement. PHN frequency depends on age, severity, follow-up and definition; it is a substantial risk in this older patient.

## Acute pain management

- **Antiviral** (valaciclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days, famciclovir, or aciclovir) started **within 72 hours** of the rash: reduces the duration and severity of the acute illness; a reliable reduction in subsequent PHN has **not** been established. Consider treatment beyond 72 hours if new lesions continue or there is immunocompromise/ocular or neurological involvement. Renally adjust antiviral dosing.
- **Analgesia**: regular **paracetamol** and/or **NSAID**; **topical** lignocaine for selected localised pain **only on intact skin**; never on active vesicles/broken skin. Capsaicin is generally a later option after healing; **opioids** (tramadol, oxycodone) for severe pain.
- **Neuropathic agents** early: a carefully selected **gabapentinoid** with renal dosing or another neuropathic agent. In a 71-year-old, tricyclic anticholinergic, cardiac and falls risks may outweigh benefit; if used, start very low and review. Do not promise that early neuropathic drugs prevent PHN.
- **Regional blocks** for severe pain: **thoracic paravertebral, epidural, intercostal or sympathetic blocks** in selected refractory cases after specialist assessment. Evidence for durable prevention is uncertain; do not routinely add steroid or undertake a neuraxial/deep procedure without bleeding/infection assessment.
- **Corticosteroids**: short course in selected severe cases (modest effect on acute pain, no effect on PHN).
- Skin care and prevention of infection.

## Prevention of PHN

- **Vaccination**: recombinant zoster vaccine prevents future zoster and its complications in eligible people. It **does not treat the current episode or established PHN**. Discuss vaccination after recovery according to current NZ eligibility/timing guidance; do not imply immediate vaccination prevents PHN from this episode.
- Early antivirals and adequate analgesia treat acute illness and suffering, but should not be advertised as proven prevention of PHN.

## Established PHN

Refer to a pain service; treat with gabapentinoids, tricyclics, SNRIs, lignocaine patches, capsaicin 8% patches and psychological support.

**Sources:** Evidence · [ANZCA acute pain evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence); [official shingles vaccine guidance](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/shingles-vaccination-guidance-for-healthcare-professionals/shingles-immunisation-programme-information-for-healthcare-practitioners). Distinguish treatment of this episode from prevention of future zoster.

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies zoster and PHN risk factors
- Antiviral timing and dose
- Analgesia: simple, opioid, topical
- Early neuropathic drugs
- Regional blocks with limited evidence
- Role of corticosteroids
- Vaccination for prevention
- Plan for established PHN

[ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: 19. Acute severe headache versus undifferentiated abdominal pain
items.q: Compare your initial assessment and analgesic management for a patient with an acute severe headache and for a patient with undifferentiated acute abdominal pain.
items.a:
## Identify time-critical disease while treating pain

In both patients assess vital signs and perfusion, establish onset, course and associated symptoms, review medications and pregnancy potential, and give appropriate analgesia while organising diagnostic work. Choose repeatable pain and functional assessments and document the response. Analgesia does not remove the need for examination or urgent investigation. Reassess if pain worsens, vital signs change or the initial working diagnosis no longer fits.

## Acute severe headache

Ask about thunderclap onset, new or changing pattern, fever, meningism, trauma, anticoagulation, focal symptoms, seizure, new hypertension in pregnancy or postpartum, immune compromise and analgesic use. Examine consciousness, neurology, BP, neck and fundi where feasible. Red flags warrant urgent investigation or specialist input for causes such as haemorrhage, meningitis, venous thrombosis or hypertensive disease. Do not assume post-dural puncture headache solely because the patient recently had a neuraxial procedure. A stable patient with a typical recurrent migraine and no concerning features may receive a suitable non-opioid, an antiemetic and a migraine-specific agent if indicated and safe. Check cardiovascular and pregnancy contraindications. Avoid using opioid as routine migraine treatment and assess for medication overuse if presentations recur. Give an explicit review plan if the diagnosis is uncertain.

## Acute abdominal pain

Identify shock, peritonism, bleeding, obstruction, sudden onset, pain out of proportion and relevant vascular or pregnancy risk. Evaluate focal examination, urine and pregnancy tests when relevant and arrange imaging or surgical assessment according to the suspected cause. Visceral pain may be poorly localised or colicky, while parietal irritation is often well localised and aggravated by movement. These patterns guide assessment but do not replace serial examination. Promptly address source control, perfusion and treatment of sepsis or bleeding when indicated.

Use oral or parenteral treatment according to severity, haemodynamics and absorption. Paracetamol may be suitable. An NSAID can be useful for selected renal colic when renal function, bleeding and pregnancy considerations permit. Use monitored titration of a short-acting opioid for severe pain when needed, with reassessment of ventilation and sedation. Add an antiemetic as indicated. Avoid forcing a single analgesic regimen across all abdominal pain. Arrange follow-up, observation or admission by diagnosis and trajectory, with explicit escalation for persistent severe pain, hypotension or peritoneal signs.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence) · [NICE CG150 headache guideline](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg150/chapter/recommendations) · [NICE NG118 renal colic guidance](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng118/chapter/recommendations)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises red flags and treats pain during investigation
- Describes an acute headache history and relevant examination
- Provides mechanism-directed headache treatment and opioid limitation
- Identifies abdominal pain red flags and likely mechanisms
- Individualises non-opioid and monitored opioid treatment
- Uses serial reassessment and dispositional planning

items.title: 20. Postoperative pain, delirium and cognitive dysfunction in older patients
items.q: Discuss the relationship between postoperative pain management and postoperative delirium or cognitive dysfunction in elderly patients, and strategies to reduce these risks.
items.a:
## Terminology

- **Postoperative delirium**: an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness, arising within the first postoperative week or until discharge. Frequency varies substantially by population and assessment.
- **Delayed neurocognitive recovery:** cognitive decline identified up to **30 days**. **Postoperative neurocognitive disorder:** from **30 days to 12 months**, requiring appropriate assessment, functional context and exclusion of delirium/other causes; not simply a low bedside score.

## Link with pain and analgesia

- **Unrelieved pain** increases the risk of delirium (stress response, sleep disturbance).
- **Opioids**, particularly pethidine and high doses, increase delirium, as do **benzodiazepines, anticholinergics (hyoscine, antihistamines), tricyclics, gabapentinoids** and ketamine in large doses.
- Pain and its treatment may therefore each cause delirium: the goal is **adequate, function-directed analgesia with the least harmful effective regimen; undertreating pain to avoid all opioid can itself worsen delirium**.

## Risk factors

Age, dementia or baseline cognitive impairment, frailty, polypharmacy, alcohol, sensory impairment, major or emergency surgery, hip fracture, infection, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, hypoxia, sleep deprivation, urinary retention and constipation.

## Prevention and management

- **Assess pain** with appropriate observational tools in cognitive impairment.
- **Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia**: regular paracetamol, **regional anaesthesia and nerve blocks** (e.g. evidence-supported hip-fracture peripheral blocks; do not assume equal delirium evidence for every newer block), minimise opioids; avoid pethidine, benzodiazepines and anticholinergics.
- Regional versus general anaesthesia (no clear difference for delirium); avoid excessive anaesthetic depth when possible; processed EEG may guide dosing but does not guarantee delirium prevention.
- **Non-drug measures**: reorientation, family, glasses and hearing aids, sleep, early mobilisation, hydration, nutrition, bladder and bowel care, avoid restraints and catheters.
- Treat the cause (infection, hypoxia, metabolic); consider a short, low-dose **antipsychotic** only for severe distress/danger after de-escalation and reversible causes are addressed. Check QT/drug interactions and avoid or obtain specialist advice in **Parkinson disease/Lewy body dementia**; **geriatrics co-management**.

Agree a daily functional goal and check whether pain is preventing sleep, deep breathing or supervised mobilisation. Review opioid dose and sedative co-medications, while also checking for undertreated nociceptive pain. Reassess after regional or medication changes. If new confusion develops, evaluate oxygenation, infection, constipation, urinary retention and hydration before attributing it solely to an opioid or the anaesthetic.

**Sources:** Evidence · [perioperative neurocognitive terminology consensus](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2017.11.087); [ANZCA acute pain evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence).

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines delirium and postoperative neurocognitive disorder
- Explains that unrelieved pain and opioids both increase risk
- Names drugs to avoid (pethidine, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics)
- Lists risk factors
- Observational pain assessment
- Opioid-sparing multimodal and regional strategies
- Non-drug measures
- Treats causes; co-management with geriatrics

[ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: 21. Non-pharmacological and alternative therapies for acute pain
items.q: Discuss the role of non-pharmacological and alternative therapies in the management of acute pain.
items.a:
## Rationale

Pain has sensory, affective and cognitive components, so non-drug therapies can reduce **pain, anxiety and drug requirements**. They are **adjuncts** to a multimodal plan, are generally low risk, and are particularly helpful when drugs are limited (pregnancy, children, opioid concerns).

## Physical and complementary

- **Positioning, immobilisation and splints**; **cold** (ice packs for swelling and pain) and **heat** (selected muscle spasm); massage. Protect skin and avoid thermal injury, especially with ischaemia, neuropathy or an insensate blocked limb.
- **TENS** (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation): gate-control and endorphin mechanisms; modest evidence for postoperative pain and labour.
- **Acupuncture and acupressure**: evidence for reduced pain and nausea (P6 acupressure for PONV) with variable quality; contraindicated with coagulopathy at needle sites.
- **Physiotherapy** and early mobilisation.

## Psychological and cognitive

- **Preoperative education and information**, reassurance, and setting realistic expectations.
- **Distraction**, relaxation, deep breathing, **guided imagery, hypnosis**, music (shown to reduce pain and anxiety), virtual reality, and cognitive behavioural therapy.
- Addressing **catastrophising, anxiety and depression**.

## Other

- **Sucrose, skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding** for selected brief neonatal procedures; sucrose is **not sufficient analgesia for major surgery or ongoing severe pain**.
- Presence of family and a supportive environment; sleep hygiene.

## Limitations

Variable evidence, small effect sizes, need for patient engagement and training, potential costs, and these methods **must not delay effective analgesia**.

## Conclusion

Offer suitable measures as part of multimodal care, tailored to the patient's preference and the setting.

Ask what the patient has used before, whether it was helpful and which components they would like to continue. Choose measures tied to a particular goal, such as positioning to reduce incision strain, coached breathing to permit coughing, or graded movement to restore function. Test effects within a realistic time frame and check for risks or interfering treatments. For a complementary product, document its ingredients and review interactions, bleeding and sedation alongside conventional drugs. For a technique such as acupuncture or TENS, explain uncertainty by indication; monitor whether it helps the agreed endpoint. Verify consent and scope of practice. If an intervention delays assessment or replaces necessary analgesia, change the plan. Coordinate nursing or physiotherapy input and give the patient options that can continue safely at home.

**Sources:** Evidence · [ANZCA acute pain evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence). Evidence varies by technique and setting; avoid promising a universal opioid-sparing effect.

## Self-marking checklist

- States rationale and role as adjuncts
- Physical measures (heat, cold, positioning, TENS)
- Acupuncture/acupressure with evidence and cautions
- Psychological methods (education, relaxation, hypnosis, music, CBT)
- Neonatal measures
- Limitations and evidence quality
- Integrates into a multimodal plan

[ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: 22. Psychosocial influences on acute pain
items.q: Discuss the psychosocial factors that influence a patient's experience of acute pain and how you would address them perioperatively.
items.a:
## Biopsychosocial model

Pain is not simply nociception: it is shaped by **cognitive, emotional and social context**. The same injury produces very different pain in different people.

## Factors

- **Anxiety and fear**: preoperative anxiety predicts higher postoperative pain and analgesic use.
- **Depression** and low mood; **catastrophising** (magnification, rumination, helplessness) predicts severe acute and chronic post-surgical pain.
- **Coping style**: **active coping** (staying active, problem-solving) is protective; **passive coping** (avoidance, reliance on others) worsens outcome.
- **Expectations and placebo/nocebo effects**: positive expectations reduce pain; negative information enhances it.
- **Previous pain experiences**, trauma, abuse, and chronic pain.
- **Illness behaviour**: how the patient responds to symptoms, including fear-avoidance.
- **Social**: culture, language, family and workplace support, **compensation and third-party issues** (litigation, workers' compensation) may be associated with outcome differences; **association does not establish causation or malingering**. Address practical stress and support without stigma.
- **Sleep, substance use** (opioid, alcohol, tobacco) and personality.

## Preop

- **1.** **Identify risk** at preoperative assessment (pain history, validated screening for anxiety, depression, catastrophising), and flag high-risk patients for the acute pain service.
- **2.** **Information and education**, with realistic expectations; reduce anxiety (premedication when appropriate, calm environment).
- **3.** **Treat** anxiety and depression; **cognitive behavioural strategies**, relaxation, distraction and hypnosis.
## Intraop

- **4.** **Multimodal analgesia** and regional techniques tailored to risk; avoid excessive reliance on opioids.
- **5.** **Communication**: listen, believe the patient's report, avoid negative language, involve family and interpreters.
## Postop

- **6.** **Follow-up** and early referral for persistent pain; multidisciplinary pain clinic and psychological services.

Explore expectations about postoperative movement, prior painful experiences, sleep, language, cultural preferences and worries about dependence or discharge. Use supported decision-making and an interpreter where needed. Assess anxiety and depression without treating either as proof that pain is psychogenic. Expectations and prior experiences can amplify or reduce symptoms; use clear, honest framing rather than false reassurance. Active coping can include paced mobilisation, relaxation and asking for support. Passive coping may reflect fear or previous disability and should invite practical support. Compensation issues do not establish pain exaggeration. Agree functional goals and review the effect of both analgesia and non-drug measures with the patient.

Agree on a measurable recovery goal with the patient, such as tolerating chest physiotherapy or walking to the bathroom. Document what helped and hand it over.

**Sources:** Evidence · [ANZCA acute pain evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence). Associations inform supportive care, not judgements about whether pain is real.

## Self-marking checklist

- Biopsychosocial model
- Anxiety, depression and catastrophising
- Coping style and expectations (placebo/nocebo)
- Illness behaviour and past experience
- Social, compensation and cultural factors
- Identifies high-risk patients preoperatively
- Interventions: education, CBT, relaxation, multimodal analgesia
- Communication and follow-up

[ANZCA professional documents including PS45 and PG67](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents) · [ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: 23. Palliative femoral fixation in metastatic prostate cancer
items.q: A 60-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer and severe bone pain on regular modified-release oxycodone presents for palliative surgical fixation of a femoral metastasis. Outline your approach to his perioperative pain management.
items.a:
## Assessment

Identify the **pain types** (nociceptive bone pain, neuropathic, incident pain), the **current opioid regimen** (morphine equivalents), other adjuvants (dexamethasone, gabapentinoid, bisphosphonate), renal and hepatic function, **opioid tolerance**, and the patient's goals. Involve the **palliative care and acute pain teams**.

## Principles

- **Continue the baseline opioid** (including the long-acting oxycodone on the morning of surgery) to prevent withdrawal and uncontrolled pain, and add **additional short-acting opioid** for acute pain (requirements may be higher but must be individually titrated; there is no dependable universal percentage).
- Treat **incident pain** and neuropathic features with adjuncts.

## Preop

 continue regular drugs; review constipation, sedatives; pre-block assessment.
## Intraop

 **regional anaesthesia** (spinal or epidural, or a nerve block such as fascia iliaca for femoral surgery), plus multimodal agents (**paracetamol, ketamine 0.25 to 0.5 mg/kg, dexamethasone** when indicated). **Do not combine IV lignocaine analgesia with active regional LA**; titrate short-acting opioid (fentanyl, hydromorphone) as required; avoid pethidine.
## Postop

 continuous regional analgesia if appropriate, **PCA** (higher bolus doses) in addition to baseline opioid, regular paracetamol, NSAIDs if safe (renal, bleeding), neuropathic drugs and **ketamine** for refractory pain; **opioid rotation** only with an explicit specialist conversion plan, allowing for incomplete cross-tolerance. Methadone conversions are nonlinear and cannot use a routine equianalgesic percentage; manage constipation, nausea and sedation.
- **Anticoagulation** and coagulopathy (platelets after chemotherapy) are checked before neuraxial block.

If oral baseline therapy cannot be given, arrange a conservative alternative-route regimen and review promptly. A PCA background may be appropriate for selected tolerant patients under specialist supervision; it is not routine.

## Other

Honest communication about goals, an advance care plan, and a smooth hand-back to palliative care at discharge.

Assess the broader pain experience, including immobility, fear, social support and the patient’s aims for the operation. Check whether bone pain is new or changing and consider another fracture, cord compression or other oncological emergencies if the pattern changes. Agree goals and ceilings of care, including whether procedures, monitored infusions or admission fit the patient’s priorities. Prepare a discharge and relapse-of-pain plan with the palliative team and usual prescriber. Evaluate any immediate-release rescue against function and ventilatory risk, alongside the established baseline regimen.

**Sources:** Evidence · [ANZCA acute pain evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence); [IV lignocaine safety consensus](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.15270).

## Self-marking checklist

- Assesses pain types, current opioids and goals
- Continues baseline opioid and adds extra short-acting opioid
- Uses regional anaesthesia and multimodal adjuncts
- Plans PCA and ketamine for tolerant patients
- Avoids pethidine; considers renal function
- Checks coagulation before neuraxial block
- Involves palliative and acute pain teams
- Considers goals of care and discharge

[ANZCA professional documents including PS45 and PG67](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents) · [ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

items.title: 24. Total knee arthroplasty with obstructive sleep apnoea: analgesia and rehabilitation
items.q: A patient with obstructive sleep apnoea is booked for primary total knee arthroplasty. Justify an analgesic plan that supports early rehabilitation and explain how you would judge success.
items.a:
## Plan around recovery and respiratory reserve

Ask about baseline knee pain, mobility, frailty, renal disease and existing opioid use. Review severity of OSA, home CPAP use and other sedatives. Agree a functional goal such as participation in supervised physiotherapy, safe transfers and reasonable sleep. Discuss expected pain, the recovery pathway, likely blocks, rescue analgesia and monitoring. Severe or unexpected pain after surgery requires reassessment for causes such as surgical bleeding, tight dressings or an evolving neurological problem.

## Choose a procedure-specific regimen

Use paracetamol and, if appropriate, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, considering renal, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal and bleeding risks. Consider intraoperative dexamethasone as appropriate and account for glycaemia. In many contemporary pathways, adductor canal block and periarticular local infiltration provide complementary analgesia. Coordinate the cumulative local anaesthetic dose. Adductor canal block generally better preserves quadriceps strength than femoral block, but weakness can still occur. Assess motor function before first mobilisation and use supervised mobilisation and fall precautions. Discuss posterior knee pain and whether an adjunct regional technique is appropriate for the service and surgical plan.

Choose general or spinal anaesthesia by individual and operative considerations. Routine intrathecal morphine adds respiratory risk and may offer limited incremental benefit if effective local infiltration and regional analgesia are already used. If considered, weigh the dose, alternatives and postoperative monitoring capacity, especially in OSA. Avoid routine sedating adjuncts that impair participation or compound ventilatory risk. Use titrated immediate-release rescue opioid when necessary. Escalate observation according to OSA severity, opioid exposure and recovery events, and continue prescribed positive airway pressure where appropriate.

## Assess the outcome and adapt

Measure pain on movement as well as at rest, ability to transfer, knee function and participation in physiotherapy. Follow quadriceps strength, nausea, dizziness, urinary retention, sedation, hypoxaemia and opioid use. Check whether rescue medication improves function without destabilising ventilation or increasing falls. Adapt the regimen if a block causes weakness, severe pain persists or respiratory events occur. Convert to a simple oral regimen as soon as appropriate and check readiness for discharge against mobility, support and respiratory criteria. Explain analgesic use and taper, red flags, follow-up and the role of rehabilitation. A lower pain score alone is an incomplete outcome if the patient cannot mobilise safely.

**Sources:** [BJA Education Anaesthesia and analgesia for total knee arthroplasty 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.03.004) · [ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence)

## Self-marking checklist

- Establishes OSA risk and functional recovery goals
- Chooses appropriate systemic drugs and limits sedating adjuncts
- Justifies motor-sparing regional analgesia and dose coordination
- Explains intrathecal morphine trade-offs and respiratory monitoring
- Measures mobility, motor function and adverse effects alongside pain
- Plans oral transition, safe discharge and follow-up

items.title: 2026.2 Q7: Inadvertent total spinal anaesthesia
items.source: Past SAQ 2026.2 Q7 · pass rate not reported
items.q: Describe the diagnostic features and clinical management of inadvertent total spinal anaesthesia.
items.model:
## Recognition

Rapidly ascending sensory/motor block with **arm tingling/weakness, difficulty speaking/breathing, hypotension and bradycardia** suggests a high neuraxial block; progression to unconsciousness/apnoea and collapse is a total spinal. **A T4 surgical level is ordinarily required for caesarean delivery and alone does not diagnose a pathological high block.** Consider excessive dose, unrecognised intrathecal epidural dosing, catheter migration or unusually extensive spread. Also consider haemorrhage, anaphylaxis, local anaesthetic systemic toxicity and embolic or cardiac causes. In pregnancy add aortocaval compression.

Assess the time course of a spinal injection or an epidural top-up, progressive sensory spread and neuromuscular findings. This can occur outside obstetrics. Treat apnoea or cardiovascular collapse on clinical findings, without waiting to map a precise level.

## Immediate management

- **1.** **Call senior anaesthetic and resuscitation help immediately. In pregnancy, also call the obstetric and neonatal teams.** Stop neuraxial dosing. Reassure the conscious patient and communicate with the team; obtain emergency airway/drug equipment.
- **2.** **Airway and breathing:** give oxygen, support the airway and **assist ventilation immediately** if inadequate. Intubate promptly for apnoea, loss of consciousness or inability to protect/maintain ventilation. Use an appropriate induction/sedation strategy for haemodynamics and awareness; do not delay oxygenation for a perfect RSI sequence. Release cricoid pressure if it obstructs ventilation/intubation.
- **3.** **Circulation with a pulse:** rapid IV access, manual left uterine displacement where pregnancy causes aortocaval compression, judicious fluid bolus and prompt vasopressor therapy. Treat bradycardia (e.g. **atropine 0.6 mg IV** under local protocol). Severe bradycardia/hypotension or peri-arrest collapse may need **titrated IV adrenaline in microgram boluses**, administered by an experienced anaesthetist. Do not allow repeated ineffective small doses to delay resuscitation.
- **4.** **Cardiac arrest:** start high-quality **supine CPR with manual uterine displacement when applicable**, standard ALS/defibrillation and **adult cardiac-arrest adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO** according to the algorithm. **10–100 microgram peri-arrest boluses are not the standard arrest dose.** Address reversible causes.
- **5.** **Resuscitative hysterotomy/delivery:** in maternal cardiac arrest with a uterus at or above the umbilicus, summon the delivery team and **prepare immediately at the arrest location**. Arrange delivery **as rapidly as feasible**; do not wait until minute 4 to begin preparing or transfer to theatre. ANZCOR states that evidence is insufficient to define a specific interval by which delivery should begin. Maternal resuscitation and urgent obstetric decisions proceed together—do not wait for complete stabilisation before discussing delivery.

## Continuing care

Maintain ventilation and haemodynamic support until block regression and reassess other diagnoses. Provide **sedation/anaesthesia after intubation** because paralysis/high block does not ensure unconsciousness. Plan HDU/ICU observation according to severity, fetal/neonatal care where relevant, documentation, patient/team debrief and open disclosure. Review dose, technique, catheter checks and incremental epidural top-up practice.

**Sources:** Examiner report unavailable in the reviewed archive. The model follows current resuscitation guidance.
rubric: Recognises pathological ascending block without calling an ordinary T4 level diagnostic
Calls for help and stops further neuraxial dosing
Supports airway/ventilation promptly and plans intubation/ongoing sedation
Treats hypotension and bradycardia promptly, including maternal positioning when applicable
Distinguishes titrated microgram adrenaline with a pulse from 1 mg adult arrest dosing
Starts standard ALS immediately and applies manual uterine displacement when appropriate
Prepares resuscitative delivery immediately when gestation/uterine size warrants
Includes ongoing support, differential diagnosis, debrief and prevention

items.title: 2026.1 Q6: Intrathecal morphine for postoperative analgesia
items.q: Evaluate the use of intrathecal morphine for post-operative analgesia.
items.model:
## Rationale

Intrathecal morphine is a **hydrophilic spinal opioid** acting at dorsal-horn μ receptors. Slow clearance from CSF gives prolonged analgesia, commonly **12–24 hours**, with rostral spread creating a risk of **delayed respiratory depression**. Morphine itself produces little motor or sympathetic block; accompanying spinal local anaesthetic does produce these effects.

## Advantages

- Effective early postoperative analgesia and reduced systemic opioid requirements in selected major operations, including caesarean delivery, arthroplasty and abdominal surgery.
- A single, inexpensive injection; particularly convenient when spinal anaesthesia is already planned. No catheter, pump, displacement or catheter-removal problem.
- Preserves motor function relative to local-anaesthetic epidural infusion, potentially supporting mobilisation. This does **not** eliminate systemic opioid adverse effects or guarantee better recovery.

## Disadvantages

- **Early or delayed ventilatory impairment**, including apnoea and airway obstruction. Risk is dose dependent and increased by OSA, frailty, obesity with sleep-disordered breathing and concurrent systemic opioids or sedatives. Delayed events can occur well beyond an initially normal PACU assessment.
- Pruritus, nausea/vomiting, urinary retention and sedation. Incidence varies greatly with dose, operation and patient population; a single percentage is misleading.
- Cannot titrate or withdraw the injected dose. Analgesia may be inadequate for movement and does not cover several postoperative days.
- Neuraxial procedural risks and contraindications, including infection, coagulopathy/antithrombotic timing and refusal.

## Dose and practical balance

Use **preservative-free morphine**, prescribe in **micrograms**, double-check preparation and choose the lowest effective **procedure-specific** dose. Around **50–150 micrograms** is commonly used for caesarean delivery or arthroplasty; selected major surgical protocols use **100–300 micrograms**. These are examples, not a universal weight-based regimen or ceiling of efficacy. Increasing the dose usually increases adverse effects.

## Safe use

- Assess OSA, previous opioid sensitivity, comorbidities, other sedatives and the ward's monitoring capacity; agree a rescue analgesia plan. Higher-risk patients need increased surveillance or an alternative technique.
- General adult ASA/ASRA guidance for a **single hydrophilic neuraxial opioid** recommends monitoring for **at least 24 hours**, at least **hourly for the first 12 hours, then every 2 hours for the next 12**. Assess consciousness, ventilation and oxygenation; enhance monitoring for risk or additional opioids. Obstetric low-dose pathways may use a separate risk-stratified protocol.
- Supplemental oxygen can conceal hypoventilation on pulse oximetry. Consider continuous oximetry/capnography according to risk; ensure staff can recognise and rescue deterioration.
- For respiratory depression: stop additional depressants, call for help, support airway/ventilation and titrate IV naloxone; repeat doses/infusion may be needed. Do not delay ventilation while obtaining naloxone. Treat PONV, pruritus and retention under the acute pain protocol.

## Evaluation

Useful when the expected analgesic benefit outweighs adverse effects **and monitored inpatient care is available**. It is not a generic shortcut to same-day discharge. Modern motor-sparing blocks and infiltration may reduce its incremental value, especially in knee arthroplasty.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · 2026.1 Q6 required evaluation, at least two advantages and recognition of delayed respiratory depression. Evidence · [neuraxial opioid monitoring](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26655725/); [BJA Education knee review, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.03.004).
rubric: Explains hydrophilic action, prolonged analgesia and rostral spread
Gives at least two advantages and avoids equating no pump with no monitoring
Includes delayed respiratory depression and other opioid adverse effects
Uses preservative-free, microgram, procedure-specific dosing
Assesses OSA, sedatives and monitoring resources
States general adult minimum 24-hour monitoring with ventilation, consciousness and oxygenation
Describes rescue including ventilation and naloxone
Reaches a balanced clinical conclusion rather than recommending routine day-case use

items.title: 2025.2 Q14: Emergency spinal surgery in a patient on high-dose oral naltrexone
items.q: Discuss the perioperative pain considerations for a patient on high-dose oral naltrexone requiring emergency spinal surgery.
items.model:
## Preoperative assessment

Naltrexone is a competitive opioid antagonist, predominantly at μ receptors. A recent high oral dose can substantially blunt opioid analgesia. Establish indication, dose, last administration, formulation, baseline pain, prior opioid exposure and recurrence risk. Emergency decompression or stabilisation should not be delayed for a washout. Hold further doses when opioid analgesia is expected and involve the acute pain, addiction/prescribing and surgical teams. Explain difficult analgesia and the possibility of delayed respiratory depression. Document baseline neurology, contraindications to regional analgesia and the constraints of postoperative examination. Arrange a monitored postoperative bed early.

## Intraoperative plan

Use procedure-appropriate non-opioid analgesia with regular paracetamol when suitable and an NSAID only if renal function, bleeding and the surgical plan permit. Discuss wound infiltration or a suitable fascial plane technique if it is compatible with the operation and the neurological assessment. Monitor total local anaesthetic exposure. Ketamine may be useful as a specialist adjunct. Dexmedetomidine may reduce opioid need in selected patients, but consider bradycardia, hypotension and delayed recovery when cord perfusion or examination is important. Use antiemetics and anticipate severe dynamic pain.

If opioids are needed despite residual blockade, titrate short-acting IV opioid in a fully monitored environment with immediate ventilatory support and specialist supervision. The dose required initially may be higher, but there is no safe fixed multiplier. Repeated large doses can have delayed consequences as blockade wanes and receptor sensitivity changes. Consider the individual rationale and specialist expertise for alternative opioid strategies. Buprenorphine is not a substitute for naltrexone nor an automatic way to bypass blockade.

## Postoperative and discharge plan

Use PACU and HDU/ICU monitoring as appropriate for the opioid exposure and risk, including ventilation, sedation and oxygenation. Avoid routine background opioid infusion, minimise other sedatives and reassess frequently. Reduce rescue doses as opioid responsiveness returns. Keep airway support and naloxone available and reassess neurological function and surgical causes of disproportionate pain.

Transition to oral non-opioids and limited immediate-release rescue if still required. Agree taper and restart with the naltrexone prescriber. Restart only when opioid analgesia is no longer needed and an adequate opioid-free interval has been confirmed. Starting too early can precipitate withdrawal. Where dependence makes the timing uncertain, specialist-led assessment and, where appropriate, a naloxone challenge may assist. Discuss lowered tolerance, overdose risk and follow-up, including naloxone when indicated.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Competitive antagonism, an explicit multimodal plan and postoperative higher-level monitoring. Strong answers addressed the restart and post-discharge period.
rubric: Identifies competitive antagonism and variable opioid response
Balances emergency surgery with medication interruption and specialist input
Builds a specific multimodal plan with neurological assessment
Explains cautious monitored IV rescue and delayed respiratory risk
Plans HDU or ICU and decreasing opioid requirements as blockade resolves
Coordinates safe restart, discharge and relapse or overdose support

items.title: 2025.2 Q6: Analgesic strategy for above-knee amputation in critical limb ischaemia
items.q: Justify your perioperative analgesic strategy for a patient with critical ischaemic leg pain requiring an above knee amputation.
items.model:
## Preop

**Assess the pain and the patient.** Establish severity at rest and on movement, ischaemic versus neuropathic features, sleep, function, existing opioid exposure, previous pain treatment and the patient's goals. Critical ischaemia commonly coexists with diabetes, vascular disease, renal impairment and frailty, but assess these rather than assuming them from the stem. Explain residual-limb pain, painless phantom sensations and possible phantom pain; involve the acute pain service early.

Treat severe rest pain now: regular weight/risk-adjusted paracetamol, **titrated opioid**, and a regional catheter or epidural where feasible. Do not withhold adequate opioid merely to avoid escalation. Continue or safely replace established baseline opioids. Consider a cautiously titrated neuropathic agent for an established neuropathic component, adjusting for renal function and falls/sedation risk; **routine pre-emptive gabapentin or amitriptyline has not reliably prevented phantom pain**.

Check antiplatelet/anticoagulant treatment, renal function, infection and baseline neurology before neuraxial or deep peripheral techniques. Deep plexus/deep peripheral blocks require neuraxial antithrombotic precautions.

## Intraop

- **Regional analgesia** is valuable for limiting systemic opioid burden. A spinal/epidural may provide surgical anaesthesia if appropriate; otherwise combine GA with a regional analgesic plan.
- **Above-knee amputation requires more than a sciatic plus femoral block.** Consider obturator and lateral/posterior femoral cutaneous contributions and the level of incision/tourniquet. Fascia iliaca alone is incomplete. Choose appropriate proximal coverage, supplementation or neuraxial anaesthesia; do not promise complete surgical anaesthesia from two nerves.
- A surgeon-placed sciatic perineural catheter can provide postoperative analgesia but may not cover all incisional pain. Specify aseptic insertion, documentation of location and a cumulative local-anaesthetic dose limit if multiple sites are used. For example, dilute ropivacaine infusion is titrated by the pain service to patient size, site and other LA exposure, not a mandatory rate/duration for all patients.
- Paracetamol, selected low-dose ketamine and titrated opioid as needed. NSAIDs depend on renal, cardiovascular, bleeding and perfusion risks and are often unsuitable in critical ischaemia. **Do not combine an IV lignocaine analgesic infusion with an active regional LA technique.**

## Postop

- Continue catheter/epidural if effective, non-opioid baseline and rescue opioid, with pain, sedation, ventilation and neurovascular review. Adjust drug/route for renal function. Consider PCA when cognition and observation resources allow; avoid routine new modified-release opioid.
- **Anti-neuropathic medication is an option, not automatic prophylaxis:** assess burning/shooting pain or allodynia and trial one appropriate agent with slow titration, renal adjustment, review and a stop rule. Avoid stacking sedating drugs in frail patients. Ketamine may be a specialist rescue adjunct.
- Daily acute pain review; investigate worsening pain for ischaemia, infection, haematoma or neuroma. Begin rehabilitation, residual-limb care, psychological support and desensitisation; mirror therapy/graded motor imagery may be tried with realistic expectations.
- Establish an oral regimen before catheter cessation, taper additional opioids as pain improves, and provide a written discharge plan and early follow-up. Refer persistent or disabling pain promptly rather than waiting three months to offer help.

## Justification

Regional and individualised multimodal care treats severe acute pain and supports rehabilitation. **Effective acute analgesia is worthwhile even though no single perioperative drug or catheter regimen reliably prevents chronic phantom pain.**
