**Sources:** Examiner feedback · 2025.2 Q6 expected preoperative rest-pain assessment, regional and multimodal analgesia, consideration of anti-neuropathic medication and multidisciplinary care. That does not establish routine prophylactic drug efficacy. Evidence · [BJA Education, Pain after lower limb amputation, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.11.006); [ASRA antithrombotic guidance, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39880411/).

Treats preoperative pain without undertreatment
Uses Preop / Intraop / Postop headings
Accounts for above-knee nerve coverage and incomplete sciatic-catheter analgesia
Checks antithrombotics, renal function, frailty and cumulative LA exposure
Uses multimodal baseline and monitored rescue opioids

items.title: 2024.2 Q14: Principles of opioid stewardship
items.q: Outline the principles of opioid stewardship.
items.model:
## Definition

**Opioid stewardship** is the responsible, evidence-based use of opioids to **maximise benefit to the patient while minimising harm to the patient, their family and the community** (misuse, diversion, overdose, persistent use). It extends from the theatre to the community. Structure: handling, perioperative prescribing, discharge and system.

## 1. Safe handling

- Comply with **regulations and local policy**: secure storage, registers and counts, double-checking, labelling.
- **Documentation** of every dose and the record of wastage with a witness; **discard** according to policy (not into the sink or bin); report discrepancies and theft; protect colleagues (impairment).

## Preop
- Identify risk: opioid-naive or tolerant, chronic pain, mental illness, substance use, OSA, sedatives, age and renal function.
- Plan **opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia** appropriate to the procedure and patient; avoid additive toxicity or sedation from indiscriminate combinations.

## Intraop
- Titrate to need; consider short-acting agents and **regional blocks**; avoid unnecessary long-acting opioids.

## Postop
- **Lowest effective dose** and shortest duration; oral over IV; avoid fixed long-acting opioids in opioid-naive patients and **avoid routine modified-release opioids**; reassess pain and function regularly; acute pain service involvement.

## 3. Discharge

- **Small, limited supply** (days, not weeks) guided by procedure-specific guidance; use **immediate-release** agents for new acute-pain prescriptions; reconcile established long-term therapy separately; give a **tapering plan** and a **review date**; hand over to the GP.
- **Educate** the patient: safe use, storage, disposal of leftover tablets, avoiding driving, sedative and alcohol combinations; consider **take-home naloxone** for high-risk patients.
- Check prescription monitoring (real-time prescription monitoring where available).

## 4. System and community

- Audit prescribing and outcomes; education and guidelines; collaboration with surgeons, pharmacists and GPs; recognise the **community impact** (supply, diversion, overdose deaths).
- Address opioid tolerance and dependence early, with addiction services where needed.

Ask about baseline opioid and sedative exposure, pain and function, and the patient’s goals. Involve pharmacy, nursing, the acute pain service and the usual prescriber when risks are high. Monitor actual opioid use, functional improvement and adverse effects before prescribing on discharge. Involve the patient in deciding quantity and a stop or taper plan, using teach-back when literacy or language could affect safe use. Audit duplicate prescriptions, discharge quantities and persistent use, and use the results to improve the pathway.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · safe handling (including documentation and disposal), responsible prescribing and community impact. Evidence · [ANZCA PS41](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/558316c5-ea93-457c-b51f-d57556b0ffa7/PS41-Guideline-on-acute-pain-management); [Australian Opioid Analgesic Stewardship standard](https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/clinical-care-standards/opioid-analgesic-stewardship-acute-pain).

Describes discharge prescribing (limited supply, immediate release, taper, review)
Includes patient education, disposal and naloxone

items.title: 2024.1 Q1: Severe postoperative pain in a stand-alone day surgery unit
items.q: You are asked to review a healthy 20-year-old patient for severe post-operative pain in a stand-alone day surgery unit. Describe your assessment and justify your management.
items.model:
## Assessment

Treat as an emergency until a serious cause is excluded.

- **Airway, breathing, circulation**: vital signs, SpO2, sedation score; do not assume pain is only surgical.
- **Pain**: site, character, onset, severity (numerical scale), movement; compare with the **expected pain for the procedure**.
- **Exclude serious causes**: surgical (bleeding, haematoma, compartment syndrome, infected or tight dressing/cast, nerve injury, torsion, perforation), anaesthetic (block failure or complication), **malignant hyperthermia, myocardial ischaemia, pneumothorax**, urinary retention, nausea/distension.
- **Analgesia already given** (drugs, doses, times; PONV, drug allergy), regular medication, opioid use or tolerance.
- **Psychosocial**: anxiety, expectations, social support, transport home.
- **Examine** the wound and limb; discuss with the surgeon if findings are unexpected.

## Management (justified)

- **1.** **Treat promptly**: oxygen if needed; titrate **IV opioid** in small increments (for example fentanyl 25 micrograms IV, repeated after assessment of effect) to tolerable pain and function, with continuous observation and airway/resuscitation equipment. Longer-acting opioids need slower reassessment and prolonged observation; IV oxycodone is not interchangeable with fentanyl for short offset.
- **2.** **Multimodal baseline** (if not already given): paracetamol 1 g, **NSAID** (ibuprofen 400 mg or parecoxib) unless contraindicated, local anaesthetic infiltration or a **rescue regional block**, after checking previous LA dose/timing and excluding a surgical emergency. Dexamethasone is an adjunct/PONV preventive, not immediate rescue analgesia.
- **3.** **Antiemetic** for nausea; consider small-dose **ketamine** (0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg) if opioid-resistant.
- **4.** **Reassess** after each step; call the surgeon/senior anaesthetist and arrange **transfer to an acute hospital** if pain remains uncontrolled, a complication is suspected, monitoring requirements exceed unit capability or respiratory depression develops. A stand-alone day unit may have no admission facility: establish an ambulance/receiving-hospital plan early.
- **5.** **Discharge only when** pain is controlled on oral analgesia, the patient is alert and safe, with an adult carer.

## Discharge plan

Short supply of **immediate-release** opioid only if needed, regular paracetamol and NSAID, clear written instructions (when to seek help), review call at 24 hours, and a stewardship focus (no long-acting opioids).

Ensure the patient is awake enough for a meaningful examination and repeat observations after each rescue intervention. A rising opioid requirement, unexpected abdominal distension, early neurological change or disproportionate pain warrants senior surgical review. If the facility cannot adequately monitor the patient, arrange supervised transfer with a receiving team, handover of cumulative drugs and ongoing monitoring during transport.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · focused assessment, prompt analgesia and a safe plan for the stand-alone unit. Evidence · [ANZCA PS41](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/558316c5-ea93-457c-b51f-d57556b0ffa7/PS41-Guideline-on-acute-pain-management).

Takes a pain history and compares it with the expected pain

items.title: 2023.2 Q1: Long-acting opioids for acute pain
items.q: Evaluate the use of long-acting opioids in the treatment of acute pain.
items.model:
## Definition

**Long-acting** covers drugs with a long half-life (**methadone**, buprenorphine patches, **modified-release** morphine, oxycodone, tapentadol and fentanyl patches) and long-acting formulations of short-acting agents.

## Rationale

Acute pain is **variable and time-limited**, so analgesia should be **titratable and quickly reversible**. Long-acting drugs/formulations are harder to adjust promptly and may accumulate, so their convenience can be outweighed by delayed toxicity.

## Advantages (in selected cases)

- Stable levels and **less peak-and-trough pain** in opioid-tolerant patients; **continue the baseline opioid** in those on long-term treatment to avoid withdrawal.
- **Methadone** is useful for refractory pain or opioid tolerance (NMDA antagonism, long half-life); **buprenorphine** has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression and can be continued perioperatively.
- Fewer doses and convenience for the patient with ongoing pain.

## Disadvantages

- **Prolonged risk of opioid-induced ventilatory impairment**, particularly when the pain stimulus falls (the effect outlasts the pain), and **accumulation** with renal or hepatic impairment.
- Less readily titrated to rapidly changing pain; onset and offset depend on the drug and formulation.
- **Persistent opioid use** after discharge and misuse or diversion; deaths reported from modified-release opioids in the opioid-naive.
- Unpredictable pharmacokinetics (methadone QT prolongation, CYP interactions; fentanyl patch absorption varies with heat and fever).
- Greater vulnerability in **elderly, renal impairment, OSA, obesity**, and with other sedatives.

## Position

ANZCA PS41 states that **routine modified-release opioid prescription is best avoided unless there is a demonstrated need, close monitoring and a cessation plan**. Transdermal fentanyl is inappropriate for acute postoperative pain, especially in opioid-naive patients. Use **short-acting titrated opioids** (oxycodone, morphine, hydromorphone) with multimodal and regional analgesia.

## Role

Individualised roles include **continuation of established baseline therapy**, cancer/palliative pain and selected perioperative **single-dose methadone** protocols with experienced clinicians and prolonged monitoring. Methadone is not equivalent to routine modified-release oxycodone prescribing. **Buprenorphine for opioid use disorder should not routinely be stopped**; an agreed perioperative plan can add non-opioid/regional therapy and titrated full agonists. Its respiratory ceiling does not eliminate overdose risk, especially with sedatives. Reconcile and review baseline doses if toxicity, altered route or organ dysfunction occurs.

A once-daily or patch formulation is difficult to adjust after a sudden reduction in pain, respiratory deterioration, or an unexpected renal decline. Even an apparently stable patient may become temporarily more vulnerable during sleep. Assess actual opioid use and function each day, plan when to stop rescue medication and explain the discharge risks.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · evaluate prolonged ventilatory risk, vulnerable patients and the role of long-acting agents rather than just listing drugs. items.title: 2023.1 Q12: Paracetamol dose modification and toxicity
items.q: Outline the circumstances where the dosing of paracetamol requires modification (50%). Describe the management principles of paracetamol toxicity (50%).
items.model:
## Metabolism and toxicity

Most therapeutic paracetamol undergoes glucuronidation/sulphation; a smaller fraction is oxidised to **NAPQI**, normally detoxified by glutathione. Excess production or depleted glutathione causes hepatocellular injury. Early clinical wellness does not exclude serious poisoning.

## Circumstances requiring dose modification (50%)

| Circumstance | Practical modification and reason |
|---|---|
| Neonates and young infants | Use a **neonatal/paediatric formulary** incorporating gestational/postnatal age, weight and route. Immature clearance requires different intervals and daily limits; adult/older-child schedules must not be extrapolated. |
| Low body weight | Dose by actual weight. For **IV paracetamol in adults/adolescents ≤50 kg**, a common product regimen is 15 mg/kg per dose, at least 4–6 hours apart, maximum **60 mg/kg/day and no more than 3 g/day**; verify the specific product. Oral limits may differ. |
| Frailty, malnutrition, prolonged poor intake, dehydration or other hepatotoxicity risks | Reassess the indication, duration and daily maximum; often use a reduced maximum (e.g. 2–3 g/day) under local guidance. Individualise for frailty. |
| Liver disease / alcohol-related risk | Severe active hepatic disease may contraindicate use. Stable liver disease is not synonymous with toxicity at every therapeutic dose: individualise dose/duration, nutritional status and monitoring. Avoid a universal “halve for all liver disease” rule. |
| Severe renal impairment | Extend the interval according to product/local guidance, commonly **at least 6 hours**, and consider comorbidity and repeated dosing. |
| Multiple preparations/routes | Count **all oral, IV and combination products** towards the daily total. For short courses, healthy adults >50 kg commonly have a maximum of **4 g/day**. |

Prescribe in mg and check the concentration, volume and infusion time against the product.

## Management of poisoning (50%)

- **1.** **Resuscitate and contact the Poisons Information Centre/toxicologist.** Obtain timing, formulation (immediate or modified release), amount, weight, single versus repeated/staggered exposure, co-ingestants and risk factors. Check glucose and treat co-ingestant toxicity.
- **2.** **Investigations:** paracetamol concentration at **4 hours or later** after a single acute ingestion, ALT/AST, renal function; INR, acid–base/lactate and glucose according to severity/timing. Earlier concentrations cannot exclude toxicity. Serial levels are needed for modified-release ingestion or delayed absorption.
- **3.** **Nomogram:** use only for an acute ingestion with a reliably known time in the appropriate time window. **Do not use it for repeated supratherapeutic ingestion, unknown time or as the sole assessment of modified-release poisoning.** Follow the relevant separate pathway. **Deliberate staggered immediate-release ingestion is distinct from repeated therapeutic excess**: the Australasian pathway can use the earliest reliably known ingestion time, with repeat levels when needed; obtain toxicology advice.
- **4.** **Activated charcoal:** consider early for a potentially toxic ingestion if the airway is safe; selected large or modified-release ingestions may benefit later. Timing/dose depend on formulation and toxicology advice; do not delay antidote.
- **5.** **N-acetylcysteine (NAC):** start when the concentration crosses the treatment line, when indicated by the unknown-time/repeated-ingestion pathway, or empirically if a potentially toxic ingestion cannot be assessed in time to start treatment within **8 hours**. Benefit persists in late presenters and hepatic injury.
- **6.** The standard Australasian **two-bag IV regimen is 200 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours (20 hours total)**. Use local weight caps/fluid adjustments; massive poisoning may require increased NAC and additional measures under toxicology advice. Treat infusion reactions and resume appropriately rather than abandoning indicated treatment.
- **7.** Before stopping, reassess paracetamol concentration, ALT/AST, INR and clinical progress against **protocol stopping criteria**; continue NAC if ongoing drug or evolving injury. Manage hypoglycaemia, acidosis, encephalopathy and renal failure; involve ICU/liver-transplant services early for severe toxicity.
- **8.** Arrange psychosocial assessment and follow-up.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · cover both dose modification and toxicity, including age/weight, nutrition/liver risk and antidote timing. Evidence · [Australasian paracetamol-poisoning guideline](https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2020/212/4/updated-guidelines-management-paracetamol-poisoning-australia-and-new-zealand). Use the current local poisons protocol for the exact exposure.

items.title: 2022.2 Q2: Pain management for semi-elective below-knee amputation after trauma
items.q: Discuss the intraoperative and postoperative pain management of a trauma patient who requires a semi- elective below knee amputation for an isolated injury.
items.model:
## Preop: planning context

The stem specifies an **isolated traumatic injury**, not a particular age or otherwise normal health. Establish current pain, prior opioid/neuropathic treatment, renal function, anticoagulation, infection, baseline neurology and psychological distress. Explain acute residual-limb pain, phantom sensations and possible persistent pain. Agree the analgesic and rehabilitation plan with the patient, surgeon and acute pain service; then focus the answer on the requested intraoperative and postoperative phases.

## Intraop

- Choose **spinal/epidural or GA plus regional analgesia**, according to patient preference, contraindications and surgical requirements. Avoid assuming that GA is needed for unmentioned polytrauma.
- A **sciatic block/catheter plus saphenous or femoral coverage** is useful for below-knee surgery; select a block level proximal to the incision/tourniquet and allow for incomplete coverage. A surgeon-placed perineural catheter is another option, with documented placement and secure fixation.
- Use dilute local anaesthetic with an individualised total-dose limit. Check neuraxial/deep-block antithrombotic timing and infection risk; multiple catheters/infiltration share the same systemic LA toxicity budget.
- Regular paracetamol and an NSAID only if renal perfusion, bleeding and other risks permit. Titrate opioid to need. Low-dose ketamine may help severe pain, tolerance or hyperalgesia; a monitored example is 0.1–0.3 mg/kg slowly IV with an infusion around 0.1–0.2 mg/kg/h under local protocol. It is not required for every patient.
- **Do not run an IV lignocaine analgesic infusion concurrently with regional local anaesthetic.** Choose one strategy and respect the applicable separation interval.

## Postop

- Continue an effective peripheral catheter/epidural for the period of clinical benefit, with daily review rather than a compulsory 3–5-day course. Specify observations for pain/function, sedation/ventilation, motor/sensory change, catheter site, pump settings and LAST symptoms.
- Continue appropriate non-opioids and offer **titrated immediate-release opioid or PCA** for breakthrough. Maintain established baseline opioid needs, then taper the added acute-pain component as recovery permits.
- **Discuss anti-neuropathic medication** if neuropathic pain develops or established treatment needs continuation. Gabapentin/pregabalin or a tricyclic may be trialled selectively with renal, sedation and anticholinergic precautions; they are **not established routine prophylaxis against phantom pain**. Avoid commencing several sedating agents together.
- Reassess escalating pain for residual ischaemia, haematoma, infection or another complication. Arrange residual-limb care, physiotherapy, prosthetic planning and psychological support; mirror therapy or graded motor imagery may be tried without promising prevention.
- Establish oral analgesia before stopping a catheter to limit rebound pain. A short LA infusion does not inherently require pharmacological tapering. Give written discharge/taper instructions and early pain-service follow-up for persistent or disabling pain.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · the 2022.2 report discussed regional/perineural techniques, multimodal and anti-neuropathic options. **Current evidence changes the prevention claim:** acute benefit does not prove prevention of chronic phantom pain. [BJA Education amputation review, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.11.006); [IV lignocaine safety consensus](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.15270).

items.title: 2022.1 Q4: Safety and quality of a ward-based postoperative epidural service
items.q: Describe the factors that ensure the safety and quality of a ward-based postoperative epidural analgesia service.
items.model:
## A safe service begins before insertion

Use agreed selection and contraindication criteria, including patient consent, appropriate surgery, anticipated benefit, infection and bleeding risk, and availability of trained ward staff. Check and document the baseline neurological examination and an insertion and removal plan coordinated with anticoagulants. Explain how the patient should report inadequate analgesia, dizziness, weakness or back pain. Handover catheter level, depth, last bolus, sensory and motor findings and planned observation frequency. Establish a named anaesthetist and acute pain service with daily review, continuous access to advice and an emergency escalation pathway.

## Standardise equipment and prescription

Use a dedicated labelled pump with a drug library or agreed programming limits, clearly distinguished epidural connections such as NRFit where implemented, a dedicated line and standard pharmacy-prepared solutions. Keep the solution, concentration, infusion rate, permitted bolus, lockout and maximum dose explicit. Independently check the patient, route, line tracing, prescription and programming at initiation and handover. Store neuraxial and IV drugs separately. Prevent unauthorised changes and specify who may give top-ups. Reconcile systemic opioids, sedation and other local anaesthetic exposure.

## Monitoring and response

Record pain at rest and movement, blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, sedation and oxygenation, sensory level and motor power. Inspect the catheter site and connections and check urinary retention, pruritus and nausea. Use higher surveillance after initiation, boluses or changes and in high-risk patients. Nurses must be competent in the equipment, motor and sensory assessments and first actions for problems. In inadequate analgesia reassess the surgical cause, catheter and block distribution before escalating the rate. For hypotension pause or reduce infusion as appropriate and assess bleeding, sepsis or unexpectedly extensive block. Treat significant respiratory depression immediately with airway and ventilation support and naloxone where appropriate.

New weakness, severe back pain, sphincter dysfunction or unexpected regression failure requires urgent anaesthetic and spinal review and emergency imaging as indicated. Stop the infusion and avoid blind bolusing or catheter removal without reviewing coagulation. Ensure appropriate monitoring and rescue equipment on the ward.

## Assure quality

Train ward nurses and junior doctors, rehearse escalation and use a structured handover and accessible protocols for common adverse effects. Audit functional analgesia, side effects, unplanned cessation, prescribing or connection errors, escalation times and patient experience. Review incidents with the ward and acute pain team. Update practice and reaudit.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Ward and site monitoring, dedicated equipment, staff training, daily pain team review and out-of-hours access, escalation protocols and audit.
rubric: Describes patient selection, consent and antithrombotic planning
Specifies dedicated pump, connections, medications and prescription

items.title: 2020.1 Q5: Spinal surgery in a patient with past opioid dependence now on naltrexone
items.q: A 36-year-old with a history of opioid dependence is booked for spinal surgery. The patient is no longer on opioids and is maintained on 50mg of oral naltrexone daily. Discuss the implications of the history of opioid dependence and current naltrexone treatment for the provision of effective analgesia, including an analgesia plan upon hospital discharge.
items.model:
## Assess analgesic and recurrence risks

The patient takes oral naltrexone, a competitive opioid antagonist, and reports no current opioid use. Do not assume ongoing tolerance or withdrawal. Establish the last dose, indication, duration of treatment, other sedatives, baseline pain and function, prior opioid response and recurrence risk. Clarify the extent of spinal surgery and likely postoperative pain. Discuss the plan jointly with the patient, naltrexone prescriber, surgery and acute pain service. Make an explicit plan for pain relief and continuity of addiction care before changing therapy.

For elective surgery likely to require opioids, the 2023 Blue Book suggests stopping oral naltrexone around 72 hours beforehand. Coordinate the date and consider whether the patient can safely interrupt recurrence prevention. If the operation is limited and opioid-free analgesia is realistic, continuation may be reasonable by agreement. The oral interval does not apply to depot or implant therapy. Naltrexone does not itself provide acute surgical analgesia.

## Perioperative analgesia

Plan regular paracetamol and, where appropriate, an NSAID depending on renal function, haemostasis and the operation. Consider surgical infiltration or a regional technique if compatible with the approach and postoperative neurological assessment. Use specialist ketamine or other adjuncts selectively. Account for cumulative local anaesthetic exposure and avoid excessive sedation. Explain how the plan will cover movement and rehabilitation.

If opioid rescue is needed, use small titrated doses of a short-acting agent and frequent reassessment in an appropriate setting. Residual blockade may limit response, whereas sensitivity may rise after the blockade wanes and previous tolerance may be lost. Avoid speculative large doses or prescribing an unmonitored background infusion. Provide closer monitoring for sedation and ventilatory impairment where exposure or clinical risk warrants it. Rule out complications when pain is unexpected. Review daily and convert to an oral plan when function and intake permit.

## Hospital discharge

Use non-opioids where possible, plus a limited supply of immediate-release opioid only if necessary. Specify the indication, dose and stop or taper schedule, and arrange early review with the prescriber and surgical or pain team. Discuss CNS depressants, secure storage and returns. Reintroduce naltrexone only under prescriber supervision after opioids are no longer required and an appropriate opioid-free interval is confirmed. Outline how recurrent pain will be treated after restarting. Discuss recurrence risk and overdose after abstinence or antagonist withdrawal, and offer naloxone education as appropriate.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Treat the patient as currently opioid-free. Detail concrete analgesia and discharge, and distinguish naltrexone from buprenorphine.

items.title: 2019.2 Q12: Opioid-free approaches for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy
items.q: List the advantages and disadvantages of opioid-free approaches for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. (50%) Justify your choice of opioid-free technique for this procedure. (50%)
items.model:
## Advantages (50%: balance against disadvantages)

Opioid-free anaesthesia (OFA) avoids intraoperative opioid exposure; **opioid-sparing** anaesthesia reduces it. For sleeve gastrectomy, obesity/OSA make avoidance of unnecessary opioid sedation, airway obstruction and PONV attractive. Non-opioid multimodal analgesia may reduce opioid requirements and PONV. However, an opioid-free intraoperative period does **not** establish fewer respiratory events, shorter PACU stay or less persistent opioid use. Postoperative rescue opioids may still be needed.

## Disadvantages

- Limited and heterogeneous procedure-specific evidence; “opioid-free” regimens vary substantially. Benefits must be patient-centred rather than simply a lower opioid total.
- **Dexmedetomidine:** bradycardia, hypotension and delayed recovery. **Ketamine:** dysphoria, hallucinations and sympathetic effects. **IV lignocaine:** LAST and additive toxicity with blocks/infiltration. **Magnesium:** hypotension and potentiation of neuromuscular block. NSAIDs have renal/GI/bleeding and procedure-specific concerns.
- Polypharmacy, dosing errors in obesity, extra infusions and monitoring, cost and incomplete visceral analgesia. TAP/port-site LA mainly treats abdominal-wall pain, not all visceral nociception.
- **POFA trial (2021):** general non-cardiac surgery, not a bariatric-specific trial. Dexmedetomidine-based OFA was stopped early after **five severe bradycardia events**; the primary adverse-event composite occurred in **78% versus 67%** with remifentanil (RR **1.16**, 95% CI **1.01–1.33**). It cautions against assuming that substituting non-opioids is intrinsically safer; it does not invalidate every opioid-sparing technique.

## Preop: selected technique and justification (50%)

Assess OSA/CPAP use, airway, reflux/aspiration risk, existing opioids, renal and cardiovascular function. Explain OFA as an option with **rescue opioid available**, not a promise to avoid all opioids at any cost. Choose drug-specific dosing scalars in obesity; ideal, lean and actual body weight are **not interchangeable**.

## Intraop

I would choose a **regional-based multimodal technique**: standard GA, regular paracetamol, an NSAID if appropriate, dexamethasone/PONV prophylaxis, and surgeon port-site infiltration **or** a suitable abdominal-wall block within a calculated total LA limit. Use low-dose ketamine selectively (e.g. 0.1–0.3 mg/kg slowly, with further dosing according to response and local protocol). This addresses several mechanisms without requiring every available infusion.

I would **omit IV lignocaine when regional/infiltrated LA is active**. Dexmedetomidine is optional, not obligatory; if chosen, avoid an aggressive loading dose, titrate cautiously and stop for significant bradycardia/hypotension. Magnesium is not needed routinely. Monitor haemodynamics, anaesthetic depth where appropriate and quantitative neuromuscular recovery. Treat haemodynamic responses by checking depth, surgical factors and analgesia; give a titrated short-acting opioid if necessary.

## Postop

Awake extubation after complete reversal, appropriate positioning, CPAP and respiratory surveillance according to OSA risk. Continue non-opioid analgesia and assess pain/function; provide titrated rescue opioid with monitoring when needed. A safe, comfortable recovery matters more than retaining an “opioid-free” label.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · list both advantages and disadvantages and **justify a specific regimen**. **Primary evidence:** [POFA](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33630043/); [IV lignocaine consensus](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.15270).

items.title: 2018.2 Q3: Fentanyl patches as discharge analgesia after hip replacement
items.q: One of your anaesthetic colleagues is prescribing fentanyl patches as discharge medication for patients following total hip joint replacement. Evaluate this practice.
items.model:
## Verdict

This is an **inappropriate and unsafe practice**: transdermal fentanyl is licensed for **stable, opioid-tolerant, chronic pain** and not for acute postoperative pain or opioid-naive patients.

## Why it might seem attractive

- Convenience, continuous delivery, avoids oral tablets (swallowing, nausea), and fewer doses.
- Constant plasma levels and less peak-and-trough pain.

## Problems

- **Respiratory depression**: the patch has a **delayed onset (12 to 24 hours)** and **long offset** (slow, variable decline over many hours after removal because a skin depot persists), so the effect outlasts the pain, with **fatalities after discharge** in the opioid-naive.
- **Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic mismatch**: acute pain **falls quickly over days**, while the patch delivers constant, non-titratable fentanyl; greater sensitivity or altered kinetics in frailty and hepatic disease. Renal impairment still requires caution, although fentanyl lacks morphine-like active renally cleared metabolites.
- **Variable absorption**: fever and external **heat** can increase uptake; skin condition, application and cachexia can alter absorption unpredictably. Do not cut patches or expose them to warming devices.
- **Interactions**: CYP3A4 inhibitors (macrolides, azole antifungals), other sedatives, alcohol.
- **Misuse, diversion and accidental exposure** (children, pets); risk of **persistent opioid use** after surgery; disposal issues.
- **Opioid-induced hyperalgesia and constipation**.
- Not consistent with **professional guidance** (ANZCA/FPM and TGA product information: not for acute pain or opioid-naive patients), and there are medico-legal consequences.

## Better practice

Multimodal analgesia (paracetamol, NSAID unless contraindicated), regional or neuraxial techniques, and a **short supply of immediate-release oral opioid** (oxycodone) with a clear plan to stop, patient education, and follow-up. For established patch users, make an individualised baseline-opioid plan with the pain service: continuation may be appropriate, but major surgery, warming and altered absorption may require a carefully supervised route conversion. Removal does not immediately abolish fentanyl exposure.

I would speak to my colleague, review the patients concerned, and report through the hospital's medication safety processes.

Check whether the patient already uses a patch for another indication. Reconcile baseline therapy separately with the usual prescriber and institute a plan for acute analgesia. If a patch was newly applied in error, remove it, document dose and time, observe for persistent toxicity and provide ventilatory support and naloxone as indicated. Removal does not end exposure immediately.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · evaluate patch kinetics, post-discharge respiratory risk and safer alternatives. Evidence · [ANZCA PS41](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/558316c5-ea93-457c-b51f-d57556b0ffa7/PS41-Guideline-on-acute-pain-management).

items.title: 2018.1 Q15: Intravenous lignocaine infusions for perioperative analgesia
items.q: Evaluate the use of intravenous lignocaine infusions for perioperative analgesia.
items.model:
## Mechanisms and rationale

IV lignocaine (lidocaine) has sodium-channel, anti-hyperalgesic and anti-inflammatory actions at systemic concentrations. It is an **adjunct**, not reliable sole surgical analgesia. Hepatic metabolism and active metabolites make low cardiac output, hepatic disease, prolonged infusion and renal dysfunction relevant to toxicity. Analgesic effects are not equivalent to performing a peripheral block with an IV dose.

## Evidence: historical enthusiasm versus current evaluation

- The **2017 Blue Book** and the **2018 examiner report** discussed promising small studies, especially abdominal surgery: reduced early pain/opioid use and possibly faster bowel recovery. Trials were heterogeneous and often small; statistical significance does not necessarily imply meaningful recovery benefit.
- **ALLEGRO** (online 2024; JAMA 2025) tested perioperative IV lignocaine in elective **minimally invasive colonic surgery**. In the **557-patient primary analysis**, GI-3 recovery by 72 hours was **57.3% versus 59.0%** (adjusted RR **0.97**, 95% CI **0.88–1.07**); no significant benefit was found in the secondary outcomes. Do not continue teaching routine improved bowel recovery or shorter stay in that population.
- This negative result is not proof of no benefit in every operation. Any selected use needs a procedure-specific rationale, acknowledgement of uncertain clinical benefit and comparison with safer/effective alternatives. Prevention of chronic postsurgical pain is not an established indication.

## Safe regimen and governance

Treat IV lignocaine as a **high-risk medicine**, generally off-label for this indication, with informed discussion, an approved protocol and an acute pain/anaesthetic service responsible for prescription and review.

The 2021 international consensus recommends **no more than 1.5 mg/kg ideal body weight over 10 minutes**, followed by **no more than 1.5 mg/kg/h** (maximum **120 mg/h**) for **no longer than 24 hours**, with reassessment. This is a ceiling framework, not a requirement to use the maximum; the consensus advises **against use below 40 kg**, and this framework must not be extrapolated to children or high-risk organ dysfunction.

**No concurrent local-anaesthetic techniques:** do not overlap an analgesic IV infusion with active epidural, nerve-catheter, wound-infusion or block/infiltration LA. The consensus specifies at least **4 hours after a nerve block before starting IV lignocaine**, and at least **4 hours after stopping IV lignocaine before a block**; also respect the duration of action of the other LA and the local protocol. Simply “counting the combined dose” is insufficient. **Small-dose single-shot spinal LA and intrathecal opioid are exceptions in the consensus**, not the same as an active LA nerve/epidural/wound infusion. A non-bolus wound/epidural infusion transition may be permitted 30 minutes after stopping IV lignocaine under that protocol; boluses need the longer separation. Follow the actual transition protocol rather than assuming all techniques share one interval.

## Risks, observations and rescue

- Early toxicity may include perioral tingling, tinnitus, metallic taste, dizziness or agitation; progression can cause seizures, conduction disturbance, hypotension and cardiac arrest. Sedation/GA can mask warning signs.
- Review conduction disease, low cardiac output, liver/renal dysfunction, interacting antiarrhythmics and all LA exposure. Specify approved location, trained staff, pump/concentration checks, ECG/vital-sign monitoring and stop/escalation criteria.
- Suspected **LAST:** stop LA, summon resuscitation help, oxygenate/ventilate, treat seizures and give **20% lipid emulsion according to the current LAST algorithm**. Modified resuscitation dosing applies; have the algorithm and lipid immediately available.

## Conclusion

IV lignocaine is a selectively considered adjunct with a narrow safety margin and uncertain procedure-specific benefit. It should **not** be described as routinely beneficial for colorectal recovery or casually added to a regional-based multimodal regimen.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Evaluate small procedure-dependent benefits against toxicity.

items.title: 2016.2 Q7: Ward guidelines for ketamine infusions
items.q: A new hospital is setting up its pain service and you have been asked to write the administration guidelines for ketamine infusions on the ward. Outline the information you would include in these guidelines.
items.model:
## Purpose and indications

Low-dose (sub-anaesthetic) ketamine is an **NMDA antagonist adjunct** for acute pain that is opioid-resistant: **opioid-tolerant patients**, severe pain after trauma or major surgery, neuropathic features, hyperalgesia, and when opioids cause intolerable side effects. It is **not** a sole analgesic.

## Patient selection

- **Contraindications/cautions:** allergy; active psychosis; significant uncontrolled cardiovascular disease/hypertension and severe hepatic disease require avoidance or specialist review. Pregnancy and acute neurological disease require individual risk–benefit assessment. **Raised ICP is not a universal absolute contraindication**; consider pathology, ventilation and cerebral perfusion.
- **Caution**: elderly, hepatic or renal impairment, history of drug misuse or psychiatric disease.

## Dose, route and administration

- **IV or subcutaneous** infusion by a pump with a **dedicated line (or anti-reflux valve)**; premixed standard concentration (for example, 1 mg/mL or 2 mg/mL); commonly **0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg/h** (typically 5 to 20 mg/h), with a **ceiling dose** (for example, 20 mg/h or 0.3 mg/kg/h) without senior review.
- Optional bolus 0.1 to 0.25 mg/kg only by the acute pain service or an anaesthetist.
- Use within an individualised multimodal plan; **PCA/continuous opioid is not compulsory**. Review concurrent opioids and other sedatives. SC administration is off-label and service-specific; define route-specific prescribing and line safety.
- **Duration**: define a short review/stop date, assess daily and stop when benefit no longer outweighs harm. A short low-dose infusion need not always be tapered; longer exposure needs an individual plan. Consider liver testing with prolonged/repeated exposure.

## Location, staffing and monitoring

- Approved wards, trained nurses, and a pain service **daily review**.
- **Monitoring**: sedation score, respiratory rate, SpO2, pain, BP and HR hourly for the first 4 hours then 2- to 4-hourly; **record psychotomimetic effects** (hallucinations, nightmares, dysphoria).

## Adverse effects and actions

- **Psychotomimetic** effects, sedation, nausea, dizziness, diplopia, raised BP/HR, excess salivation, urinary effects (with prolonged use).
- **Actions**: stop/reduce infusion, assess ABC and other sedatives, and escalate. Define the **named sedation scale** and local early-warning thresholds; a score of “2” is not equivalent across scales. New difficulty rousing, hypoventilation, airway compromise or haemodynamic instability requires urgent emergency response. Severe distressing psychotomimetic effects need senior review; do not reflexively add a benzodiazepine to an already sedated patient. Specify trained personnel and an adequately monitored setting for any bolus.

## Documentation, education, audit

Prescription chart, patient information, nurse training and competency, incident reporting, and regular audit.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · dose, route, method of administration, critical safety issues and when to call for help. Evidence · [ANZCA acute pain evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence). Example ward doses/observation schedules require a locally approved protocol, not a universal national ceiling.

items.title: 2015.2 Q4: Trigeminal neuralgia: features and treatment efficacy
items.q: a. Describe the clinical features of trigeminal neuralgia. (50%) b. Discuss the efficacy of the treatment modalities available for this condition. (50%)
items.model:
## Clinical features

- **Unilateral**, brief **stabbing, lancinating, electric-shock-like** attacks in the distribution of one or more branches of the **trigeminal nerve** (V2 and V3 most often, V1 least), lasting seconds to two minutes, repeated many times a day.
- **Triggered** by light touch, chewing, talking, brushing teeth, cold wind or washing the face; there are **trigger zones** and pain-free intervals (refractory periods).
- Usually **no sensory loss** in classical trigeminal neuralgia (neurological examination normal); sensory loss or other signs suggest a secondary cause (tumour, multiple sclerosis).
- Mostly **after age 50**, more common in women; may lead to weight loss, fear of eating, depression and sleep disturbance.
- **Classical** (neurovascular compression with morphological nerve changes, not merely incidental vascular contact; commonly at the root entry zone), **secondary** (MS, tumour) and **idiopathic**.
- Diagnosis is clinical; **MRI is recommended for all patients**, with appropriate trigeminal/root-entry-zone sequences to identify compression and exclude secondary causes. Normal examination does not exclude a secondary cause.

## Treatment efficacy

**Pharmacological** (first line, adequate in most)
- **Carbamazepine** (sodium channel blocker) 100 to 200 mg twice daily, titrated up to 800 to 1200 mg/day: often effective initially, although long-term tolerability limits use. **Oxcarbazepine is also first line**, with fewer enzyme interactions but important hyponatraemia risk. Side effects: dizziness, ataxia, hyponatraemia, rash (consider **HLA-B15:02** testing in relevant ancestry and **HLA-A31:01** according to prescribing guidance), hepatic effects, drug interactions.
- **Second-line or add-on**: lamotrigine, baclofen, gabapentin or pregabalin, phenytoin; weaker evidence.
- Conventional opioids generally do not control the brief TN paroxysms and are not routine treatment. Severe acute exacerbations may need specialist monitored IV lignocaine or fosphenytoin rescue rather than escalating oral opioids.

**Interventional (for drug failure, intolerance or progression)**
- **Microvascular decompression**: offers the most durable relief for **classical TN with demonstrated compression** in a suitable surgical candidate. Published observational series vary; recurrence remains possible. Balance benefit against craniotomy risks including hearing loss, CSF leak, stroke and rare death.
- **Percutaneous ablative procedures** (radiofrequency thermocoagulation, glycerol rhizotomy, balloon compression): often produce good initial relief, but recurrence, facial sensory loss, corneal injury (V1) and dysaesthesia/anaesthesia dolorosa are important trade-offs. They may suit patients unsuitable for decompression.
- **Stereotactic radiosurgery** (gamma knife): lower risk, slower response, recurrence over time.
- **Botulinum toxin** and peripheral nerve blocks: limited evidence.

**Summary:** drugs are effective for most; surgery is for the refractory, with trade-offs between durability and risk.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · distinguish clinical features from comparative treatment efficacy. Evidence · [EAN guideline](https://doi.org/10.1111/ene.13950); [practical guide](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/8461413/).

items.title: 2013.2 Q11: Role of tramadol in acute and chronic pain
items.q: Evaluate the role of tramadol in acute and chronic pain management.
items.model:
## Pharmacology

Tramadol is a **synthetic centrally acting analgesic** with **dual action**: a weak **mu-opioid agonist** (mostly via the active metabolite **O-desmethyltramadol**, M1, formed by **CYP2D6**) and **inhibition of serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake**. Oral bioavailability is about 70 to 75%; half-life 6 hours; **renal excretion** (about 90%), so reduce the dose in renal impairment (and lengthen the interval in the elderly). Maximum usual immediate-release adult dose is 400 mg/day; some product guidance limits patients **over 75** to 300 mg/day. Severe renal impairment requires a longer interval/lower maximum and some formulations are unsuitable; use the local product information.

## Role in acute pain

- Effective for **moderate acute pain** in selected patients (potency varies with route and CYP2D6 activity) when used as an alternative or adjunct to NSAIDs and paracetamol; **limited efficacy** at 50 to 100 mg for moderate to severe pain.
- **Potential advantages**: some studies find less respiratory depression or constipation at analgesically comparable doses; this is not absence of opioid risk or a guarantee of better tolerability. Dependence and serious respiratory depression still occur.
- **Disadvantages**: nausea, vomiting, dizziness, sedation; **seizure risk** (high dose, epilepsy, other drugs), **serotonin syndrome**; ineffectiveness in CYP2D6 **poor metabolisers** or with CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine), and excessive opioid effect in **ultra-rapid metabolisers**; hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia; misuse potential (not risk-free).

## Role in chronic pain

- **Neuropathic pain**: some short trials show benefit, but evidence is limited/low certainty; it is generally a later-line or short-term rescue option after first-line neuropathic therapies. Osteoarthritis/back-pain benefits are modest and do not establish favourable long-term benefit–harm balance.
- Long-term use has **opioid-class risks** (dependence, hyponatraemia, falls) and uncertain long-term benefit.

## Interactions and cautions

SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, MAOIs and linezolid increase serotonergic/seizure risk. **Ondansetron may reduce tramadol analgesia through 5-HT3 antagonism; a clinically established causal serotonin-syndrome interaction should not be asserted from that mechanism alone.** Other interactions include carbamazepine (reduces effect); warfarin (INR rise); renal and hepatic impairment; pregnancy and children (avoid in under 12 and after tonsillectomy).

## Conclusion

Tramadol is a **second-line adjunct** for mild to moderate acute pain and neuropathic pain, with the advantage of fewer opioid side effects, but its efficacy is variable, it has distinct risks, and it is not a safe opioid substitute.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · dual mechanism, acute/chronic roles, renal elimination and interactions. Evidence · [ANZCA acute pain evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence); [CPIC opioid guidance](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33387367/).

items.title: 2013.1 Q8: Acute neuropathic pain after surgery: diagnosis and management
items.q: (a) In a patient who complains of post operative pain, which features of the history and examination suggest a diagnosis of acute neuropathic pain? (50%) (b) How would the diagnosis affect your postoperative pain management plan? (50%)
items.model:
## Features on history and examination (50%)

Consider an acute lesion or dysfunction of the somatosensory system in the operative or injured territory. Ask about burning, electric shocks, shooting pain, tingling, numbness, painful cold and pain evoked by normally innocuous touch. Map the onset and distribution against the operation and positioning. Ask about spontaneous versus movement-related symptoms, severity at rest and activity, sleep and function. A dermatomal or peripheral nerve distribution supports the diagnosis. Establish pre-existing pain and neuropathy, prior nerve injury, diabetes and surgery likely to involve nerve trauma. Compare with the time course of regional anaesthesia and obtain any preoperative sensory and motor documentation.

Assess light touch, pinprick and temperature if appropriate, comparing sides and mapping hypoesthesia, allodynia and hyperalgesia. Assess motor power and perfusion, examine the surgical site and check positioning or compression risks. Screening tools such as DN4 may support the assessment but do not establish the mechanism alone. Mixed inflammatory and neuropathic pain is common. Progressive weakness, severe escalating pain, tense swelling or new sphincter symptoms demand urgent evaluation for causes such as compartment syndrome, haematoma or neuraxial compression rather than an assumption of uncomplicated neuropathy.

## How the diagnosis changes management (50%)

Treat reversible causes promptly: review dressings, positioning and possible surgical nerve entrapment or injury with the relevant teams. Escalate urgent findings and organise appropriate imaging or referral. Explain the possible mixed mechanism and agree functional targets. Use regular non-opioids for nociceptive components where safe, with titrated rescue opioid only as needed. Repeated escalation of opioid alone is unlikely to address all symptoms and increases risk.

For significant neuropathic features, consider a monitored trial of an appropriate agent with acute pain input, accounting for renal function, sedation, falls and concomitant opioids. Gabapentinoids or other neuropathic options may be appropriate selectively, with defined treatment goals and stop review. Routine perioperative gabapentinoid prophylaxis is unsupported. Consider regional or specialist adjuncts such as ketamine in selected severe cases if compatible with neurological assessment. Use positioning, desensitisation as tolerated, mobilisation and reassurance, and address anxiety and distress. Document repeat examination and pain/function measures to detect progression and determine treatment response. Arrange a discharge plan and early specialist follow-up for persistent pain or deficit, with advice about what should prompt urgent reassessment.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Identify populations at risk and support diagnosis through history and examination. Explain how mechanisms, psychosocial context and treatment choice change management.
rubric: Elicits characteristic symptoms and maps neuroanatomical distribution
Looks for sensory gain and loss and records motor findings
Recognises at-risk patients, mixed pain and limits of screening tools
Excludes reversible or urgent surgical and neurological causes
Explains mechanism-based treatment and selective neuropathic agents
Plans reassessment, functional support and follow-up

items.title: 2012.2 Q1: Dementia and fractured neck of femur: pain assessment and analgesia
items.q: You are asked to anaesthetise an 80-year-old lady with dementia and a fractured neck of femur. She is on no other medication. 1. What are the issues in assessing pain in this patient? (50%) 2. What would you prescribe for postoperative analgesia and why? (50%)
items.model:
## 1. Assessing pain in dementia

- **Communication**: cognitive impairment, aphasia, inability to use the numerical or visual analogue scales; reduced reporting (under-treatment is common).
- **Degree of dementia**: mild patients can often use simple verbal descriptors; severe patients need **observational tools**.
- **Confounders**: delirium, **dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, anaemia, infection, hypoxia, urinary retention, constipation**; agitation may be pain, or not.
- **Tools**: **Abbey Pain Scale**, PAINAD, or Doloplus, assessing vocalisation, facial expression, body language, behavioural and physiological change, with attention to **movement-evoked pain** and function.
- **Third-party information** from family and carers about her usual behaviour.
- Reassess regularly (at rest and on movement); do not rely on a single score.

## 2. Postoperative analgesia and rationale

**Principles**: age-related changes in pharmacokinetics (variable volume of distribution, often reduced renal/hepatic clearance) and pharmacodynamics (increased sensitivity), the risk of delirium and respiratory depression, and ease of administration.

- **Regional analgesia first**: **fascia iliaca or femoral nerve block**, continued/repeated if appropriate, provides opioid-sparing analgesia and may reduce delirium. PENG is an alternative for selected hip pain but is not interchangeable evidence for every outcome. Spinal is a surgical anaesthetic option; adding intrathecal morphine requires separate risk/monitoring assessment, and choosing spinal over GA alone does not reliably prevent delirium.
- **Regular paracetamol** with a weight-, nutrition- and liver-risk-adjusted daily limit; do not automatically prescribe 4 g/day to a frail low-weight patient.
- **NSAIDs**: avoid or use cautiously (renal function, gastric, cardiac risk).
- **Opioid**: **oxycodone 2.5 to 5 mg** orally as needed, reduced doses and extended intervals, avoid **pethidine** and **codeine**; avoid long-acting opioids and patches; monitor sedation and respiration.
- **Adjuncts**: low-dose ketamine if refractory; avoid tricyclics, benzodiazepines and anticholinergics (delirium).
- **Non-drug**: reorientation, family presence, glasses and hearing aids, repositioning, early mobilisation, bladder and bowel care.
- **Reassess** often, involve the acute pain service and geriatric team, and schedule safe non-opioid baseline therapy. Because she may not request analgesia, use proactive behavioural/function assessments to offer carefully titrated rescue opioid; do not interpret this as compulsory fixed-dose opioid regardless of sedation.

Compare the observed pain behaviour with relatives’ or carers’ description of their usual interaction and mobility. Repeat the same assessment during a gentle movement or transfer and after treatment. A calm patient may still have significant pain. Look for delirium, fear, urinary retention or positioning discomfort and assess whether an analgesic trial improves function rather than merely increasing sedation.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · give equal attention to assessment barriers and justified prescriptions. Evidence · [ANZCA acute pain evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence).

items.title: 2012.1 Q11: Starting an opioid PCA service: safety and order form
items.q: You are asked to initiate an opioid patient-controlled analgesia service in your hospital. a. How would you ensure patient safety? (70%) b. What are the key components to include in designing an order form? (30%)
items.model:
## a. Patient safety (70%)

**Governance**
- **Dedicated guidelines/protocol** approved by the hospital, led by an **acute pain service** (anaesthetist and nurse) with a multidisciplinary committee; audit and incident reporting.

**Patient selection**
- Suitable: moderate to severe acute pain, **able to understand and press the button**.
- **Caution**: extremes of age, **cognitive dysfunction**, language barriers, OSA, renal or hepatic failure, respiratory disease, opioid tolerance or addiction, sedatives. **No PCA by proxy** (no one else presses the button).

**Equipment and drug preparation**
- Standard **pumps** with lockout, **anti-reflux valves** or dedicated lines (with an anti-siphon device), tamper-proof locking, **failure alarms**, servicing and training; **pre-filled standard syringes** (for example, morphine 1 mg/mL) with clear labelling.
- Defined drug and **standard concentration**; double-checking when programming and changing syringes.

**Monitoring**
- **Pain score, sedation score, respiratory rate, SpO2** (and nausea) at defined intervals (for example, hourly for 4 hours then 2- to 4-hourly), recorded in a chart; **supplemental oxygen** if indicated, while recognising that it may mask hypoventilation. Include ventilation/airway assessment, continuous oximetry and, where appropriate, capnography for higher-risk patients.
- Defined **action thresholds** using a **named sedation scale** and local early-warning criteria (e.g. new difficulty rousing, apnoea/obstruction or a low respiratory rate) with naloxone available and **when to call** the pain team.

**Education**
- Patient education before surgery; **staff training and competency**, 24-hour support; processes for **complaints**, unauthorised use and tampering.

## b. Order form (30%)

- Patient identifiers, weight, allergies, **drug and concentration**, **bolus dose, lockout interval**, **background infusion** (none routinely in opioid-naive patients; specialist exceptions in selected tolerant patients), **4-hour limit** where used, duration.
- Clear **instructions** for monitoring, antiemetics, naloxone and that **additional opioids or sedatives require an explicitly authorised pain-service plan**, not unsupervised duplication.
- **Prescriber signature**, date and time, and review/stop times; instructions for changes.
- A section for **other analgesic drugs** (paracetamol, NSAID) and for contact numbers.

Before launch, simulate wrong concentration, proxy pressing and a sedated patient with inadequate ventilation. Confirm clear responsibilities from pump set-up to transfer, clear labels, independent programming checks and dedicated monitoring. Provide a 24-hour contact and standard actions after an event. Audit adverse effects, functional pain control, unplanned discontinuation and near misses, then adjust policy and staff training.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · service safety (70%) plus explicit order-form components (30%). Evidence · [ANZCA PS41](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/558316c5-ea93-457c-b51f-d57556b0ffa7/PS41-Guideline-on-acute-pain-management); [BJA Education opioid respiratory depression](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.12.007).
rubric: Dedicated guidelines and an acute pain service
Patient selection criteria and cautions
Equipment: pumps, lockouts, anti-reflux valves, labelling
Monitoring with frequency and action thresholds
Supplemental oxygen and naloxone

items.title: 2011.1 Q11: Codeine: pharmacology and pharmacogenetics
items.q: (a) Describe the clinical pharmacology of codeine including an outline of its therapeutic use. (70%) (b) Describe the influence of pharmacogenetics on the variability of patient response to codeine. (30%)
items.model:
## a. Clinical pharmacology and therapeutic use (70%)

- **Codeine** is a weak μ-opioid with relatively low receptor affinity. Much of its clinically relevant opioid analgesia depends on conversion to **morphine by CYP2D6**; describe it as a prodrug with variable activation, rather than a reliably titratable weak morphine.
- Other pathways include **glucuronidation to codeine-6-glucuronide** and CYP3A4 N-demethylation to norcodeine. Morphine subsequently forms M3G and active **M6G**. A small proportion of the dose undergoes CYP2D6 activation, but the clinical effect varies considerably; precise population percentages do not predict an individual's response.
- Orally absorbed, with onset commonly within 30–60 minutes and an elimination half-life of roughly 3 hours in healthy adults. Renal elimination of codeine/metabolites makes **renal dysfunction a toxicity risk**, including prolonged sedation and respiratory depression.
- Effects: analgesia, cough suppression, constipation, nausea/vomiting, sedation, ventilatory impairment and physical dependence. A “weak opioid” label does not imply weak toxicity. Combination products can cause inadvertent paracetamol/NSAID overdose when patients escalate tablets for poor analgesia.
- Historically used for mild–moderate pain, often in combination with paracetamol. A usual adult immediate-release dose is **30–60 mg every 4–6 hours, maximum 240 mg/day**, subject to product restrictions and patient factors. It is a poor choice when reliable rapid analgesia is needed; use alternatives rather than repeatedly escalating an ineffective prodrug.
- Prescription-only in Australia and New Zealand. Follow current restrictions: avoid in **children under 12**, under-18s after tonsil/adenoid surgery where restricted, known ultra-rapid metabolisers and breastfeeding. Respiratory disease, OSA, frailty, renal dysfunction and concomitant sedatives increase risk. Antitussive/antidiarrhoeal uses are product- and jurisdiction-dependent, not routine perioperative indications.

## b. Pharmacogenetics and clinical consequence (30%)

| CYP2D6 phenotype | Expected effect | Practical response |
|---|---|---|
| **Poor** | Little morphine formation; inadequate analgesia | Avoid codeine; use an alternative not dependent on CYP2D6 activation. |
| **Intermediate** | Reduced activation; effect may be inadequate | Monitor response; change analgesic if ineffective rather than escalating blindly. |
| **Normal** | Expected activation at standard doses | Usual precautions still apply; normal genotype does not exclude toxicity. |
| **Ultra-rapid** | Rapid/excessive morphine formation; toxicity possible at usual doses | Avoid codeine. |

Genotype frequencies vary across populations; ancestry alone is not an individual phenotype test. **CYP2D6 inhibitors** (e.g. fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion) can cause **phenoconversion** to reduced metabolism. CYP2D6 is **not considered clinically inducible** in the manner of CYP3A4. Interactions and organ function modify genotype–response relationships.

CPIC recommends avoiding codeine in poor and ultra-rapid metabolisers when genotype is known. Morphine or another suitable direct-acting analgesic may be preferable; **tramadol is also CYP2D6-dependent** and is not a reliable workaround. Choice must still consider renal function and respiratory risk.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · pharmacology/uses first, then a distinct explanation of variable pharmacogenetic activation. Evidence · [CPIC CYP2D6/opioid guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33387367/); [ANZCA acute pain evidence](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/acute-pain-management-scientific-evidence).

Includes other metabolic pathways, renal accumulation and opioid adverse effects

Distinguishes poor, intermediate, normal and ultra-rapid phenotypes
Explains CYP2D6 inhibition/phenoconversion without claiming induction
Avoids deterministic ancestry percentages
Chooses an appropriate alternative and recognises tramadol also needs CYP2D6

items.title: 2010.1 Q11: Opioid-dependent patient with severe pain after an osteotomy
items.q: A 34 year old, opioid-dependant woman is complaining of severe pain on the day after a first metatarsal osteotomy. The nurses are concerned she is drug-seeking. (a) How would you assess this patient? (60%) (b) Outline your pain management plan. (40%)
items.model:
## Assessment (60%)

See the patient promptly and take her report seriously. Clarify the onset, progression, location, quality and impact of pain, including pain at rest and with movement. Ask about pre-existing pain, expectations, sensations suggesting nerve injury and what has helped. Establish what opioid she takes, why, the formulation, dose, route, usual timing and last dose. Confirm prescriptions and actual use where possible. Ask non-judgmentally about non-prescribed substances, alcohol, benzodiazepines and previous experiences of withdrawal or overdose. Look for sweating, yawning, diarrhoea, restlessness or autonomic changes. Consider tolerance, withdrawal and opioid-induced hyperalgesia as distinct possibilities.

Review the operation, any infiltration or block, possible rebound pain, and the anaesthesia record, prescriptions and administration chart. Ask the nurses what they observed and which doses were offered, withheld or given, without treating the label “drug-seeking” as a diagnosis. Check sedation, ventilation and vital signs. Examine dressings, swelling, wound, tenderness, peripheral perfusion, sensation and motor function. Severe or escalating pain warrants assessment for a tight dressing, haematoma, ischaemia, infection, compartment syndrome or a nerve complication and early surgical review when indicated. Reassess after initial treatment and document function, distress and adverse effects.

## Management (40%)

Explain the findings and agree on immediate relief and functional targets with the patient and nursing team. Involve acute pain and, where applicable, the medication prescriber or addiction team. Verify and generally continue the baseline prescribed opioid or opioid agonist treatment to prevent withdrawal, with additional treatment for surgical pain. Consider paracetamol, a suitable NSAID if risks permit and procedure-specific regional or local analgesia after urgent surgical causes have been considered. Consider specialist ketamine for severe refractory pain when appropriate.

Use titrated short-acting opioid rescue in a monitored environment if simple and regional measures are insufficient. If PCA is suitable, individualise the bolus for established tolerance and specify monitoring and escalation. Coordinate any background opioid with the specialist plan and avoid duplicate parenteral and oral dosing. Monitor sedation, ventilation and function after dose changes. Plan the oral transition, expected duration, taper back to baseline, limited discharge quantities when needed and arranged follow-up. Discuss secure storage, overdose risk and naloxone where appropriate.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Weight assessment at 60%. Obtain the patient and nursing histories, examine for complications and review prescriptions and perioperative drug administration. Negotiate a plan that covers baseline and rescue opioid needs.
rubric: Elicits the pain history, trajectory and functional effect
Reviews medication exposure, missed doses and signs of withdrawal
Obtains chart, staff and patient accounts without stigma
Examines the foot and excludes urgent surgical causes
Agrees a practical multimodal plan and maintains verified baseline treatment

items.title: 2009.2 Q5: Analgesia in early pregnancy with a tibial shaft fracture
items.q: A woman who is 10 weeks pregnant presents to the Emergency Department with a closed tibial shaft fracture. 1. Classify the drugs used in pain management according to their safety to use at this stage of pregnancy. (40%) 2. What are the options available for perioperative pain management for this patient? (30%) 3. What would you recommend? Justify your choice. (30%)
items.model:
## 1. Safety classification at 10 weeks (40%)

This is **first-trimester organogenesis**, but untreated severe pain, maternal hypoxaemia/hypotension and delayed necessary fracture care also cause harm. TGA categories describe the type/amount of evidence and potential harm; they are **not a numerical ranking**, and “A” does not mean unlimited-dose safety.

| Drug/group | Current TGA examples and clinical interpretation |
|---|---|
| **Paracetamol — A** | Preferred baseline analgesic when indicated, at the lowest effective dose/duration and within the total daily limit. |
| **Local anaesthetics** | **Lignocaine A; bupivacaine A; ropivacaine B1.** Regional use is reasonable with standard dose/toxicity precautions. |
| **Opioids** | Do not assign one category to the whole class: **codeine A**, whereas **morphine/fentanyl/oxycodone/tramadol are C**. Short-term titrated opioid is acceptable for severe fracture pain. Categories do not make codeine a better acute analgesic; it has variable activation. Prolonged exposure and near-delivery respiratory depression/withdrawal are separate issues. |
| **NSAIDs — commonly C** | Not my routine choice here. Early-pregnancy risks and alternatives need discussion; later risks are gestation-dependent: **from 20 weeks** fetal renal dysfunction/oligohydramnios, and later pregnancy ductal constriction, especially **from 30 weeks**. Avoid conflating all pregnancy stages. |
| **Ketamine B3; gabapentin B3** | Limited human pregnancy data; not routine first-line drugs for this isolated fracture. Specialist use depends on need and alternatives. |

The 2009 examiner accepted a correct clinical safety classification as well as an appropriate recognised category system. Avoid filling an analgesia answer with unrelated anticonvulsants/ACE inhibitors. No currently used standard anaesthetic agent has been shown to be a human teratogen at usual clinical concentrations; regional anaesthesia should not be justified by claiming GA necessarily exposes the fetus to proven teratogens.

## 2. Options (30%)

- Reassurance, splintage/reduction, elevation/positioning and carefully protected cold therapy when appropriate.
- Oral/IV paracetamol and titrated IV morphine or fentanyl for severe pain with respiratory observation; oral immediate-release opioid when suitable.
- **Sciatic plus saphenous coverage** can treat tibial/lower-leg pain; select the approach for incision and tourniquet. Fascia iliaca/PENG are not complete tibial-shaft analgesic techniques. Neuraxial anaesthesia or GA are options for fixation.
- Tibial fracture carries **acute compartment-syndrome risk**. Agree surveillance with orthopaedics, document baseline neurovascular findings, avoid prolonged dense blocks and ensure rapid pressure measurement/assessment if suspected. No block is automatically “compartment-sparing”.

## Preop

Provide paracetamol (e.g. **1 g orally/IV**, only if weight/liver risk and daily totals permit) plus monitored titrated opioid (e.g. **fentanyl 25 micrograms IV**, repeated after assessing effect) promptly, splint/reduce, and assess for compartment syndrome. Involve orthopaedics and obstetrics; confirm gestation and discuss maternal/fetal implications. Necessary surgery should not be delayed solely because of trimester. At 10 weeks, continuous fetal CTG is not applicable; fetal assessment/documentation follows gestation and obstetric advice.

## Intraop

For fixation, choose an appropriate neuraxial or carefully planned regional/GA technique according to the operation, preference and surveillance needs. Maintain maternal oxygenation, perfusion and normal ventilation. Left uterine displacement is not routinely needed for a 10-week uterus. Calculate LA doses and avoid excess sedation.

## Postop

Regular appropriate-dose paracetamol, titrated short-term rescue opioid, ongoing objective limb/compartment observations and early mobilisation as feasible. Individualise thromboprophylaxis for pregnancy, trauma and immobility; coordinate **LMWH with neuraxial/deep-block insertion and removal**. Provide clear follow-up and red-flag advice.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Use the correct pregnancy classification, provide options and justify a plan in light of compartment risk.
rubric: Addresses 10-week gestation and balances drug risk against untreated pain/delayed care
Uses a correct classification without treating categories as a safety ranking
Correctly distinguishes ropivacaine B1 and codeine A from other examples
Discusses paracetamol, opioid, regional and non-drug options
Chooses appropriate tibial coverage and an explicit compartment-surveillance plan
Uses Preop / Intraop / Postop headings with a justified recommendation
Avoids asserting standard GA is a proven teratogen
Coordinates obstetric input and individualised VTE/neuraxial precautions

items.title: 2008.1 Q13: Role of gabapentin in postoperative pain
items.q: Evaluate the role of gabapentin in acute and chronic post surgical pain management.
items.model:
## Applied pharmacology

Gabapentin is an **analgesic for selected neuropathic pain conditions**, binding the **α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels** and reducing excitatory neurotransmitter release. It is structurally related to GABA but is not a GABA-receptor agonist. Oral absorption is saturable; bioavailability falls as the dose increases. It is not substantially metabolised and is **renally excreted unchanged** (usual half-life about 5–7 hours), requiring dose adjustment in renal dysfunction.

Adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, ataxia, visual disturbance, confusion and oedema. Few CYP-mediated pharmacokinetic interactions does **not** mean no important interactions: opioids and other sedatives increase respiratory/sedation risk. Chronic treatment should not be stopped abruptly without a withdrawal/taper plan.

## Acute postsurgical pain: current evaluation

- Early small studies suggested opioid sparing and analgesia after preoperative doses, explaining the optimistic **2008 examiner commentary**. Those historical expectations must be distinguished from present evidence.
- **Verret et al. (2020)** pooled **281 trials / 24,682 participants**: reductions in postoperative pain were **not clinically meaningful**; dizziness and visual disturbance increased. A reduced opioid total alone did not establish a favourable recovery benefit–harm balance.
- **GAP (2025)**, a large placebo-controlled trial in major surgery, found no improvement in hospital stay or patient-centred recovery from short perioperative gabapentin. Small opioid reductions did not translate into clear clinical benefit; the trial also reported a higher incidence of pain at four months, a secondary finding that does not support a prevention claim.
- Therefore **do not recommend routine initiation** for all postoperative patients or automatic prophylaxis for amputation, mastectomy or thoracotomy. Frailty, OSA, renal dysfunction and concurrent opioids make adverse effects particularly relevant.
- Continue established therapy when appropriate or consider a carefully monitored, symptom-targeted trial for a convincing neuropathic component, with an explicit goal and review/stop date. Opioid tolerance or a particular operation alone does not prove benefit.

## Established chronic postsurgical pain (CPSP)

First exclude treatable surgical/pathological causes and establish whether pain has neuropathic features. Gabapentin may be trialled within multidisciplinary care, with slow titration, renal adjustment and assessment of pain **and function**. Start low (e.g. 100–300 mg at night in an appropriate adult, lower/slower in frailty); higher divided doses depend on tolerance, renal function and benefit, not a mandatory target.

Evidence for diabetic neuropathy or postherpetic neuralgia **cannot be relabelled evidence for CPSP**: those are not postsurgical diagnoses. Evidence varies by surgical syndrome; benefit in phantom limb pain remains uncertain. Do not claim it is universally equivalent to tricyclics or a proven treatment for every neuropathic CPSP syndrome.

## Prevention and conclusion

Perioperative gabapentin has **not reliably prevented chronic postsurgical pain**. Its established place in some neuropathic pain conditions supports selective therapeutic trials, while contemporary evidence argues against routine acute perioperative initiation. Balance any individual benefit against sedation, falls, respiratory risk and withdrawal.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · answer both acute and chronic **postsurgical** roles, with brief applied pharmacology. Evidence · [Verret systematic review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32667154/); [GAP primary trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12416896/).
