items.title: 2008.1 Q5: Intrathecal morphine for total knee replacement
items.q: A 65-year-old female who weighs 85kg and is 165 cm tall (BMI 31) is scheduled for total knee replacement surgery. She has no other health problems. Discuss the pros and cons of intra-thecal morphine for post-operative analgesia in this patient.
items.model:
## Patient-specific balance

TKR causes substantial early pain, particularly during movement and physiotherapy. This patient is **65 with BMI 31**, but the stem says no other health problems. Screen for OSA and respiratory risk; **do not diagnose probable OSA from BMI alone**. The 2008 examiner mentioned passive-motion devices; modern rehabilitation usually prioritises active mobilisation rather than routine continuous passive motion.

## Pros

- Low-dose IT morphine can provide **12–24-hour analgesia** and reduce systemic opioid requirements, including during initial rehabilitation.
- Convenient if spinal anaesthesia is already being performed: single inexpensive injection, no postoperative catheter or pump.
- Morphine itself does not produce motor block; however, accompanying spinal LA does. Avoid attributing all benefits of spinal versus GA to the morphine component.

## Cons

- **Early and delayed respiratory depression**; an initially normal recovery does not remove the later risk. Age, OSA, sedatives and additional opioids affect risk. Obesity prompts assessment and appropriate surveillance, not automatic exclusion.
- Pruritus, PONV, retention and sedation may hinder recovery. Pain on movement may still require other analgesia.
- Cannot titrate or remove the dose; finite duration for a multi-day pain problem. Neuraxial procedural/antithrombotic risks remain.
- Absence of a pump does **not** mean reduced observation requirements or suitability for same-day discharge.

## Dose, alternatives and current practice

If selected, **100 micrograms preservative-free morphine** is a common TKA dose within an approved inpatient pathway; larger doses may add adverse effects without useful extra benefit. Use paracetamol, NSAID/COX-2 inhibitor if safe, and a motor-sparing regional plan. Current **PROSPECT** favours **adductor canal block plus periarticular local infiltration**; IT morphine is not routine when these work well. The **2026 BJA Education** review allows selected use when pain is expected to be difficult, with appropriate surveillance.

## Monitoring and rescue

For general adult single-shot hydrophilic neuraxial opioids: **at least 24 hours** of ventilation, consciousness and oxygenation assessment—at least hourly for 12 hours, then every 2 hours for 12 hours—with enhanced monitoring if risk warrants. Continuous oximetry/capnography may be indicated; supplemental oxygen can mask hypoventilation.

Have trained staff, rescue analgesia orders and naloxone available. Respiratory compromise requires immediate airway/ventilatory support and titrated naloxone, sometimes repeat dosing/infusion. Treat pruritus, PONV and retention under the pain-service protocol.

## Conclusion

It can be reasonable after individual assessment and informed discussion, **if inpatient monitoring is available**. For this patient, an effective motor-sparing block/infiltration regimen may offer a better benefit–harm balance; BMI alone neither mandates nor prohibits IT morphine.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · 2008.1 Q5 required an integrated, patient-specific discussion, dose, adverse effects and respiratory monitoring. **Current evidence:** [BJA Education TKA, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.03.004); [neuraxial opioid monitoring](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26655725/).

Assesses age/BMI without inventing OSA
Balances single-shot analgesia/opioid sparing against non-titratability and adverse effects
Includes early/delayed respiratory depression and neuraxial risks
Uses preservative-free low-dose morphine and an inpatient protocol
States at least 24-hour general adult monitoring and rescue requirements
Discusses ACB plus infiltration and the limited incremental role of IT morphine

items.title: 2006.2 Q4: Phantom limb pain
items.source: Past SAQ 2006.2 Q4 · pass rate not reported
items.q: Describe the features and management of phantom limb pain.
items.model:
## Definitions (keep these separate)

- **Phantom sensation**: non-painful awareness of the amputated part (tingling, position), present in most amputees.
- **Phantom limb pain (PLP)**: painful sensation referred to the absent limb.
- **Stump (residual limb) pain**: pain in the remaining limb (neuroma, ischaemia, infection, poor prosthetic fit).

## Features of phantom limb pain

- **Common and potentially persistent**; estimates vary with definition, timing and population. It can begin early or later and may continue for years; do not reassure that only a small fixed proportion remains affected.
- **Character**: burning, shooting, stabbing, cramping or squeezing; **intermittent**, distal limb (hand or foot) and may be triggered by weather, stress or touching the stump; **telescoping** of the limb.
- **Risk factors**: preoperative limb pain (especially ischaemic), severe acute postoperative pain, proximal amputation, anxiety and depression, and female sex.
- **Mechanisms** include peripheral (neuroma, ectopic discharge) and spinal/supraspinal sensitisation and altered sensorimotor processing; cortical reorganisation is one proposed mechanism, not a complete proven explanation. Psychological factors modulate pain without making it imaginary.

## Management

**Prevention**
- Good perioperative analgesia: appropriate regional and individualised multimodal care for acute benefit. **No single drug or catheter regimen reliably prevents chronic PLP.** Discuss risk and arrange follow-up.

**Treatment (neuropathic strategy)**
- **Individual drug trials**: gabapentinoids, tricyclics or other neuropathic agents may be considered, but PLP-specific evidence is limited and general neuropathic-pain recommendations are partly extrapolated. Choose by renal function, frailty, comorbidity and prior response; define goals and stop ineffective therapy.
- **Specialist options**: selected short-term ketamine or opioid trials may relieve refractory pain, but durable efficacy and harms require review. Memantine and calcitonin are not established routine second-line treatments. Topical treatment is more relevant to focal residual-limb pain than pain in an absent limb.
- **Non-drug**: **mirror therapy**, graded motor imagery, virtual reality, TENS, desensitisation, acupuncture, and cognitive behavioural therapy.
- **Interventional**: targeted assessment/blocks for a symptomatic neuroma; selected **targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR)** or regenerative peripheral nerve interfaces (RPNI) in specialist centres, and neuromodulation for refractory cases. Evidence and suitability vary; invasive/destructive procedures are not routine.
- **Multidisciplinary pain service** and treatment of the causes of stump pain (prosthetic fit, infection).

Explain the condition, set expectations, and support psychologically.

Begin by examining the stump and reviewing how the symptoms affect sleep and function. Distinguish a painful neuroma or pressure from the prosthesis from pain perceived distally in the absent limb. Liaise with prosthetics and rehabilitation and document the response to each treatment trial.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · distinguish phantom pain, painless phantom sensation and residual-limb pain. Evidence · [BJA Education, Pain after lower limb amputation, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.11.006).
rubric: Distinguishes phantom limb pain, phantom sensation and stump pain
Describes incidence, timing and character of PLP
States risk factors
Mentions mechanisms (peripheral, central, cortical)
Describes prevention with perioperative analgesia
Explains limited PLP-specific evidence and a goal-based neuropathic-drug trial
